## Majjhima Nikāya
## Uparipaṇṇāsa Commentary
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Devadaha Vagga
## 1. Devadaha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Devadaha Sutta. In that Devadaha Sutta, regarding the name "Devadaha," kings are called "Devas." In that place, there was a pleasant and well-guarded ceremonial pond (maṅgalapokkharaṇī) belonging to the Sakyan kings. Because it was the pond (daha) of the kings (devas), it became known as "Devadaha." Taking that name into account, the market town (nigama) also came to be called "Devadaha." The Blessed One, depending on that Devadaha market town, dwelt in the Lumbinī grove. "Sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetu" means it is because of the cause which is kamma performed in previous lives. By this statement, the Buddha shows that they [the Niganthas] reject the feelings associated with productive kamma (janaka-kamma) and the feelings associated with functional consciousness (kiriya-citta), and only accept the single feeling associated with resultant (vipāka) kamma. By the words, "Monks, those Niganthas who hold such a view," the Buddha specifies the meaning by the name Nigantha, which was previously mentioned without such specification.

In the words, "We were (in the past)," the Blessed One, while knowing the ignorance of those Niganthas, asks this only because he wishes to impose upon them the teaching of their failure. For those Niganthas who do not even know "We existed in the past," how will they know whether kamma was performed or not performed? This same method applies to the subsequent questions as well.

"Evaṃ sante" means, in the Cūḷadukkhandha Sutta, "if the words of the Great Nigantha were true"; however, in this Devadaha Sutta, it means "if you Niganthas do not know these many matters." "Na kallaṃ" means it is not proper.
2:
Gāḷhūpalepenāti means thick smearing, or repeatedly smearing with poison; it is not like a cloth smeared with rice paste. Esaniyā means with a probe (esani-salākā), or even with a small strip of rag. Eseyyā means one should investigate whether it is deep or shallow. Agadaṅgāraṃ is the powder of burnt gallnut (harītakī) or emblic myrobalan (āmalaka). Odaheyyā means one should apply it to the wound. The passage beginning with "Arogo" has already been explained in the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.

In the phrase "Evameva kho," what follows is the comparison between the simile and the meaning. Just as for a man pierced by an arrow, the time of the pain is clear when he is pierced, so too for these Niganthas, there should be a time of knowing: "Did we exist in the past or not? Did we perform evil kamma or not? Did we perform such evil?" Just as the pain is clear during the four times such as the cutting of the wound, there should be a time of knowing: "This much of our suffering has been exhausted; when this much is exhausted, all suffering will be exhausted; we shall be those established in the pure practice." Just as the time of knowing the state of comfort in the future, there should be a time of knowing in the present life for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states. Thus, in this context, three meanings are shown by one simile, and one meaning is illustrated by four similes.

However, these Niganthas do not know even one of those matters. Like a man who was not hit because the arrow missed, yet develops the perception "I am hit" and falls into suffering merely by accepting the word of an enemy who says "I have hit you," they believe all this solely by the authority of the Great Nigantha's word. Being unable to counter the Blessed One's refutation through the arrow simile, they are like a weak, thin dog that rouses the prey and brings it before the master hunter, then retreats itself; in the same way, they throw the burden of the view onto the Great Nigantha and say, "Venerable Nigantha..." and so on.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to refute those Niganthas along with their teacher, spoke the words beginning with "Pañca kho ime." Regarding those five things, by the phrase "Kā atီtaṃse satthari saddhā," he asks: what is the faith in the teacher who speaks of the past? What is that faith you Niganthas have in the Great Nigantha Nāṭaputta, who holds the view concerning the past? Does it have a true meaning or a false meaning? Does it have a true benefit or a false benefit? This is the question. The same method should be understood for the remaining terms such as mindfulness (sati) and oral tradition (anussava). Sahadhammikaṃ means being with reason. Vādapaṭihāraṃ means a view that can be brought back [defended]. This is the extent.
3:
“Does it have a true meaning, or an untrue meaning? Does it have a true result, or an untrue result?” He asks. In the remaining words, the method should be understood in this same way. “Sahadhammika” means occurring with a cause (having a logical reason). “Vādapaṭihāra” means a view that can return (a rebuttal). By this much, He shows the view that cuts off faith, which those people stated as: “Remove faith; this faith is very weak.”

“Avijjā aññāṇa” means [occurring] because of ignorance (avijjā) and because of lack of knowledge (aññāṇa). “Sammoha” means [occurring] because of delusion (sammoha). “Vipaccetha” means to believe in a perverted way, or it means to hold a perverted view.

“Diṭṭhadhammavedanīya” is kamma that gives results in this very existence (this life). “Upakkama” means [occurring] through effort and exertion (in the bodily door). “Padhāna” means [occurring] through energy (in the mind door). “Samparāyavedanīya” is kamma that gives results in the second or third existence. “Sukhavedanīya” is wholesome kamma (kusala kamma) that gives pleasant results (iṭṭhārammaṇa). The kamma opposite to that is called “dukkhavedanīya.” “Paripakkavedanīya” is kamma whose results are experienced in a matured (completed) existence; this is a synonym for diṭṭhadhammavedanīya. “Aparipakkavedanīya” is kamma whose results are experienced in an immature existence (to be born in the future); this is a synonym for samparāyavedanīya. Even though this is so, the distinction here is: kamma performed in the first stage of life that gives results in the first, middle, or last stage of life is called diṭṭhadhammavedanīya. Kamma performed in the middle stage of life that gives results in the middle or last stage of life, and kamma performed in the last stage of life that gives results in that same stage, is called diṭṭhadhammavedanīya. Whichever kamma gives results within seven days is called paripakkavedanīya. That kamma can be either wholesome or unwholesome.

In that matter (of giving results within seven days), there are these stories—In the city of Rājagaha, a poor man named Puṇṇa lived depending on the Treasurer Sumana. One day, when the festival was proclaimed in the city, the Treasurer said, “If you go to plow today, you will get two oxen and a plow. Will you play at the festival or will you plow?” Puṇṇa said, “What benefit is there for me in the festival? I will plow.” The Treasurer said, “If so, take the oxen you desire and plow.” Thus, he went to plow. On that day, the Elder Sāriputta, having arisen from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), reflected, “Whom shall I favor?” Seeing Puṇṇa, he took his bowl and robes and went to the place where he was plowing. Puṇṇa stopped plowing, offered a tooth-stick to the Elder, and gave him water for washing the face. The Elder, having attended to his body, [waited] for the work...
4:
(The Elder Sāriputta) sat in a place not far away, looking out for the path by which the food would be brought. Then, seeing Puṇṇa's wife bringing the food, he showed himself right on the way.

That wife offered the food she had brought for her husband into the Elder's bowl, then returned home, prepared and cooked another meal, and went [to the field] when the sun was high. Puṇṇa, having plowed once, was sitting down. His wife, bringing the food, said, “Lord... I brought food for you early in the morning, but seeing the Elder Sāriputta on the way, I offered that food to him and had to cook and bring another meal, so it has become late; Lord, please do not be angry.” He said, “Dear, you have done a good thing. I also offered a tooth-stick and face-washing water to the Elder early in the morning. The Elder has also partaken of our alms-food. Today, we have become sharers of the ascetic practice performed by the Elder,” and he gladdened his heart. At that moment, the place he had plowed once became solid gold. After eating, Puṇṇa looked at the plowed area and, seeing it shining, stood up and struck it with his goad. Realizing it was red gold, he thought, “It is not proper to use this without informing the King,” and went to report it to the King. The King had all that gold carried by carts and piled in the royal courtyard, then asked, “Who in this city has this much gold?” When it was said that no one had such, he granted him the position of Treasurer. He became known as the Treasurer Puṇṇa.

There is another story—In that same city of Rājagaha, there was a poor man named Kāḷaveḷiya. His wife cooked sour gruel made with leaves. The Elder Mahākassapa, having arisen from the attainment of cessation, reflected, “Whom shall I favor?” and seeing him, stood at the door of the house. That wife took the bowl, put all the sour gruel into it, and offered it to the Elder. The Elder went to the monastery and offered it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One took only enough for his own sustenance, and the remaining gruel was sufficient for five hundred monks. Kāḷaveḷiya also arrived at that place and received a small portion. The Elder Mahākassapa asked the Blessed One about the result for Kāḷaveḷiya. The Blessed One said, “On the seventh day from today, he will receive the Treasurer's parasol.” Kāḷaveḷiya heard those words and went to tell his wife.

At that time, as the King was touring the city, he saw a man sitting on an impaling stake (impaled) outside the city. Seeing the King, the man cried out in a loud voice, “O King, please grant me your royal meal.” The King said, “I shall grant it,” but when the royal meal arrived in the evening, he remembered and asked, “Is there anyone who can go and deliver this food?” and had it proclaimed in the city that he would give a thousand coins. When it was proclaimed for the third time, Kāḷaveḷiya's wife accepted it. Then, when she was presented to the King, she took the form of a man, equipped herself with the five kinds of weapons, took the bowl of food, and went out of the city. At the foot of a palm tree outside the city, an ogre named Dīghatāla was sitting.
5:
"Great King, please grant me the royal meal," said the man (who was on the stake). The King said, "I shall grant it," and when the royal meal was brought in the evening, he remembered and asked, "Do you know anyone capable of taking this meal?" He had a bag of a thousand coins proclaimed throughout the city. On the third time, the wife of Kāḷaveḷiya accepted it. Then she was presented to the King; she took the form of a man, equipped herself with the five weapons, took the bowl of rice, and departed from the city.

A Yakkha named Dīghatāla, who lived in a palmyra tree outside the city, saw her passing by the foot of the tree and said, "Stop, stop! You are my food." She said, "I am not your food; I am a royal messenger." When asked, "Where are you going?" she replied, "To the man sitting on the stake." He asked, "Can you also carry a message for me?" She said, "Yes, I can." He said, "Please announce that Kāḷī, the wife of Dīghatāla Yakkha and daughter of the celestial king Sumanadeva, has given birth to a son. There are seven large treasure pots at the foot of this palmyra tree; you may take those treasure pots." She went along proclaiming, "Kāḷī, the wife of Dīghatāla Yakkha and daughter of the celestial king Sumanadeva, has given birth to a son."

When the celestial king Sumanadeva, sitting in the assembly of Yakkhas, heard this, he said, "A human is bringing us pleasant news; call that person." Having heard the message and being pleased, he said, "I give you the treasure pots located within the spread of this tree's circular shadow." After the man sitting on the stake had eaten the meal and was wiping his face, he realized it was the touch of a woman and bit her topknot. She cut off her own topknot with a sword and went straight to the King. The King asked, "How shall it be known that the meal has been fed?" She replied, "It can be known by the sign of the topknot," and after informing the King, she had those riches brought. The King asked, "Does anyone else possess such wealth?" They replied, "No, Great King." The King appointed her husband as the wealthy treasurer (Setthi) in that city. The story of Queen Mallikā should also be told. These are the stories related to wholesome kamma (kusala kamma).

However, the youth Nanda behaved wrongly towards the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā; as he rose from the couch and was leaving, the great earth split open to give way, and he fell into the great hell right there. Nanda the butcher also practiced the trade of cattle slaughter for fifty years; one day at mealtime, not finding any meat, he cut off the tongue of a living ox, roasted it over coals, and prepared to eat it. Then his own tongue was severed at the root and fell into his rice bowl. He died screaming in agony and was reborn in hell. A Yakkha named Nanda, while traveling through the air with another Yakkha, saw the Venerable Sāriputta sitting in the open air at night with his hair newly shaven. Wanting to strike him on the head, he informed the other Yakkha, and although the other Yakkha forbade him, he struck him. Crying out, "I am burning! I am burning!" he sank into the earth right there and was reborn in the great hell. Thus it should be known. These are the stories showing the results of unwholesome kamma (akusala kamma). At the very least, whatever kamma is performed near the time of death gives results in another existence; all such...
6:
While the Yakkha was traveling through the air with another Yakkha, he saw the Venerable Sāriputta sitting in the open air at night with his hair newly shaven. Wanting to strike him on the head, he informed the other Yakkha, and although the other Yakkha forbade him, he struck him. Then, crying out, "I am burning! I am burning!" he sank into the earth right there and was reborn in the great hell. These are the stories showing the results of unwholesome kamma. At the very least, whatever kamma is performed even near the time of death gives results in another existence; all such kamma is called samparāyavedanīya kamma (kamma to be experienced in a future life). Among those, whatever result of an unimpaired jhāna will arise, that result is said to be "a result produced in this very life." Although the kamma that is the root of that result is not analyzed as either diṭṭhadhammavedanīya or samparāyavedanīya, it should be understood that the kamma arising from this cause is indeed samparāyavedanīya. The result of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) occurring in another existence for those on the first path (magga), etc., is merely called "an excellence produced in this life." Even though it is so called, the kamma associated with the path should be understood as paripakkavedanīya (ripened to be experienced). This is because the volition of the path (magga-cetanā) alone gives results most swiftly, as the fruition follows immediately after the path.

Bahuvēdanīya refers to kamma leading to an existence with perception (saññā-bhava). Appavēdanīya refers to kamma leading to an existence without perception (asaññā-bhava). Savedanīya refers to kamma that yields a result. Avedanīya refers to kamma that does not yield a result. In this way, even when effort is made in kammas such as diṭṭhadhammavedanīya, if the cause for becoming samparāyavedanīya, etc., is not obtained, it is called "aphala." Aphala means fruitless or futile. By this sequence of words, showing the fruitlessness of exertion in the teachings of the heretics which do not lead to liberation from the round of suffering, it should be understood that the doctrine of the "severance of effort" (padhānacchedaka-vāda) is shown. "Sahadhammikā vādānuvādā" means that due to the reasons stated by others, the doctrines of the Nigaṇṭhas and the derivative doctrines spoken by their followers, being based on those reasons, reach a state deserving of censure by the wise. There is also a reading "vādānuppattā gārayhaṭṭhānā." The meaning of that reading is: being based on reasons stated by others, they follow the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas, and while making that doctrine dry and withered, they reach the ten blameworthy grounds such as being "doers of evil deeds" (dukkaṭakammakārī). Saṅgatibhāvahetu means due to the cause of fixed destiny (niyati). Pāpasaṅgatikā refers to those fixed in evil deeds. Abhijātihetu means the cause of the six classes of birth (chaḷabhijāti).
7:
Having shown the fruitlessness of the Niganthas' efforts, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Kathañca bhikkhave" to show the fruitfulness of effort and energy in the emancipating teaching (Niyyanika Sasana). In that passage, "anaddhabhūtaṃ" refers to an existence (attabhāva) that is not oppressed. An existence not oppressed by suffering is called the human existence. Not oppressing that existence is the meaning of "anaddhabhūtaṃ." One who subjects that very existence to various difficult practices is said to oppress it with suffering. Those who have gone forth in the teaching and live in forests or at the foot of trees are said not to oppress themselves with suffering. In the emancipating teaching, effort and energy are called Right Effort (Sammāvāyāma).

Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, however, said this: One who is born into a noble family and, at the age of seven, while adorned and sitting on his father's lap, attains Arhatship when the four noble truths are proclaimed during the thanksgiving (anumodanā) by the Saṅgha of monks who had finished their meal at the house; or one who, when asked by his parents, "Dear son, will you become a monk?" replies, "Yes, I will," and is bathed, adorned, and taken to the monastery, where he learns the meditation on the five parts ending in skin (taca-pañcaka kammaṭṭhāna) and attains Arhatship at the very moment the razor touches his hair; or a newly ordained monk who, with his head anointed with realgar oil, eats the food sent by his parents the next day and attains Arhatship while sitting in the monastery—such a person is said not to oppress himself with suffering. This is one with extraordinary honor and offerings. Even one born from the womb of a slave woman, wearing at least a silver ring and anointing the body with only a small amount of yellow pigment (gora-kapiyaṅgu), who is taken to be ordained and attains Arhatship either while his hair is being shaved or on the following day, is also said not to oppress his un-oppressed existence with suffering.

Righteous happiness (dhammika sukha) refers to the happiness derived from the four requisites obtained from the Saṅgha or a group. "Anadhimucchito" means not being infatuated by craving. One should not be greedy for it, thinking, "I will not give up this righteous happiness." One who uses the food distributed by tickets (salāka-bhatta) or the rainy-season robes (vassāvāsika) obtained from the Saṅgha, discerning that "this is for this purpose," and partakes of them among the monks in the midst of the Saṅgha, prospers in virtue, concentration, insight, the path, and its fruition, like a lotus flower among lotus leaves. "Imassa" refers to the cause of the present five aggregates. "Dukkha-nidānassa" refers to craving (taṇhā). This is because craving is the root cause of the suffering of the five aggregates. "Saṅkhāraṃ padahato" refers to one who makes a well-exerted effort...
8:
For the person who exerts effort, "dispassion (virāga) occurs" means dispassion occurs through the Path. The meaning is: "Through the exertion of effort in formations, the fading away of this origin of suffering (samudaya-sacca) occurs for me"—thus he understands. By this, the easy practice with swift realization (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā) is described. By the second turn, the state of equanimity (majjhattatākāro) of that person with well-exerted effort is described.

In the passage "So yassa hi khvāssa," the summary meaning is: For that person, through the exertion of effort in formations regarding the origin of suffering, dispassion occurs; he exerts effort in those formations, exerting effort by way of the Path. For the person who, observing with equanimity the origin of suffering and developing equanimity, dispassion occurs; he develops equanimity therein, developing it by way of the development of the Path. "Tassa" means for that person.

"Paṭibaddhacitto" means one whose mind is bound by intense lust. "Tibbachando" means one with thick desire. "Tibbāpekkho" means one with strong longing. "Santiṭṭhantiṃ" refers to a woman standing together (with someone). "Sañjagghantiṃ" refers to a woman laughing a great laugh. "Saṃhasantiṃ" refers to a woman smiling.

In the words "Evameva kho bhikkhave," this is the illustration of the simile: A certain man, being intensely attached to a certain woman, provides her with food, clothing, flowers, perfumes, ornaments, and so on, and has her live in his house. That woman, transgressing against her husband, consorts with another man. The man thinks, "Surely, I am not providing her with suitable care," and increases his care. That woman continues to transgress even more. The man thinks, "This woman, even when cared for, still transgresses; if she stays in my house, she might even cause me harm. I will expel her." Having made a statement in the midst of people that they are separated, he releases her, saying, "Do not enter my house again." That woman, unable to regain intimacy with that man by any means, wanders about with dancers and performers. Seeing her, the man does not feel displeasure; rather, only joy arises in him.

In that simile, the time when the man was intensely attached to the woman should be understood as this monk's attachment to his own existence (attabhāva). The time when he provided food, clothing, and so on, and had her live in the house, should be understood as the time of caring for the existence. The time when the woman transgressed should be understood as the state of ill health due to the provocation of bile and so on, even while the existence is being cared for. Just as he increased his care, thinking, "She transgresses because she does not receive suitable care," so too [he thinks], "This (pain) occurs because I do not have medicine"...
9:
Noting the time for medical treatment, even if care and attendance are increased, there is a tendency for relapse; while one illness among bile and others is being treated, another becomes aggravated due to the corruption of phlegm, bile, or wind, leading to pain again. Just as one might be driven out of a house after being spoken to with reproachful words in the midst of an assembly, thinking, 'Now I am neither your slave nor your worker; I have wandered through the beginningless Saṃsāra serving only you; what benefit do I have from you? Let it be cut or let it be broken,' one should, without any regard for this body, make firm effort and eradicate the defilements with the Path. Just as that man, seeing that woman wandering and dancing with other dancers, does not feel distress but only joy, even so, an Arahant monk, seeing his own body afflicted by causes such as the corruption of bile, does not feel distress but only joy, thinking, 'Indeed, I shall be released from the suffering of bearing the five aggregates.' This analogy should be understood as having come to clarify this meaning: 'Distress arises only for one whose mind is attached to his wife, but not for one who is unattached,' and knowing this, one abandons strong lust for women. Similarly, only a monk who strives regarding formations or develops equanimity can abandon craving, which is the root of suffering; knowing that it cannot be done otherwise, he fulfills both and abandons craving, the cause of suffering.

'I, living with the desired happiness, striving' means one whose mind is directed towards Nibbāna. Herein, for some, the 'pleasant practice' of wearing fine robes and living in an inspiring monastery is unsuitable and the mind becomes distracted. Only the 'painful practice' of wearing torn and coarse robes and living in cemeteries or at the foot of trees is suitable, and the mind becomes concentrated. This was said in reference to one who has such a practice of painful progress (dukkha-paṭipadā).

'Even so'—here, the correspondence between the analogy and the thing illustrated should be understood. The yogi, oppressed by the fears of birth, aging, and death, should be understood as the fletcher. The crooked mind should be understood as the crooked arrow. Physical and mental effort should be understood as the two firebrands. Faith (saddhā) should be understood as the clarified oil used to straighten the arrow. The Supramundane Path should be understood as the straightening tool. Just as the fletcher, having greased the crooked arrow with clarified oil and heated it over the firebrands, straightens it with the straightening tool, so should be understood the straightening of this monk's crooked mind by greasing it with faith, heating it with physical and mental effort, and using the Supramundane Path. Just as only the fletcher, having shot the enemy with the arrow thus straightened, achieves success...
10:
...and enjoys prosperity, so should this yogi be understood as destroying the mass of defilements with the mind thus straightened, and reaching the sublime plane of Nibbāna in an inspiring monastery, enjoying the bliss of Fruition Attainment (phalasamāpatti).

In this Dispensation, the Blessed One has already taught the practices of the monk of pleasant progress and quick intuition (sukhā-paṭipadā khippābhiññā) and the monk of painful progress and slow intuition (dukkhā-paṭipadā dandhābiññā). Since the practices of the remaining two monks (pleasant progress with slow intuition and painful progress with quick intuition) had not yet been taught, He began this discourse to teach those practices. Alternatively, when these two practices are taught, the others are also considered taught. However, the practice of insight (vipassanā) known as the 'attainable practice' (āgamanīya-paṭipadā) leading to the Path and Fruition had not been taught, so He began this discourse to teach that practice. Alternatively, the practice along with the attainable practice had indeed been taught. However, He began this discourse to show a previously unshown arising of a Buddha and the renunciation of a clansman, ending the teaching with Arahantship. The rest of the terms are clear in all respects.

## The Commentary on the Devadaha Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya (Papañcasūdanī) is finished.
## 2. Commentary on the Pañcattaya Sutta

The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Pañcattaya Sutta. Therein, 'eke' (some) refers to certain recluses and brahmins. 'Samaṇabrāhmaṇā' means they are recluses (samaṇas) because they have approached the state of wanderers, and brahmins (brāhmaṇas) by birth. Alternatively, they are those designated by the world as 'recluses' and 'brahmins.' They are called 'aparantakappikā' (speculators of the future) because they grasp the future by speculating and specifically conceptualizing it. Alternatively, they are called 'aparantakappikā' because they possess speculation about the future (aparanta-kappa).

In this context, by the word 'anta' (end/part), the meaning of 'portion' or 'section' is intended, as in the passage: 'Friends, identity (sakkāya) is one end' (A.Ni. 6.61). 'Kappa' refers to craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). It has also been said: 'Regarding "kappa," by way of summary, there are two kappas: the kappa of craving and the kappa of views.' Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: they are 'aparantakappikā' because they stand speculating on the future portion of the aggregates by the power of craving and views. For those who thus stand speculating on the future, their views follow only the future by way of repeated arising; thus they are 'aparantānudiṭṭhino' (those who hold views following the future). Having such views, they cause other people to also hold such views, based on, arriving at, and depending on that future...
11:
They speak various words expressing views. 'Anekavihitāni' means of various kinds. 'Adhivuttipadāni' refers to words that express views. Alternatively, because they overcome the true meaning and speak without grasping the nature of things as they are, views (diṭṭhi) are called 'adhivutti'. The words that point out those views are 'adhivuttipadāni', meaning words that indicate views.

'Saññī' means one who is endowed with perception. 'Arogo' means one who has a permanent (nicca) nature. 'Ittheke' means 'thus some'. By this statement, the sixteen doctrines of a percipient self (saññīvāda) are taught. By the word 'asaññī', the eight doctrines of an unpercipient self (asaññīvāda) are taught; by the word 'nevasaññīnāsaññī', the eight doctrines of a neither percipient nor non-percipient self; and by the words 'sato vā pana sattassa', the seven doctrines of annihilationism (ucchedavāda) are taught. In that context, 'sato' refers to an existing being. 'Uccheda' means cutting off, 'vināsa' means destruction, and 'vibhava' means the passing away of existence. All these words are merely synonyms (vevacana) for one another. By the words 'diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ vā', the five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life are taught. In that context, 'diṭṭhadhamma' refers to the present self-identity (attabhāva). It is a name for the self-identity obtained in various lives. 'Diṭṭhadhammanibbāna' means reaching Nibbāna in the present life, which means the subsiding of suffering in this very self-identity. 'Santāṃ vā' refers to a peaceful self through three modes, such as 'saññī'. In the phrase 'tīṇi honti', the doctrine of a percipient self is one by way of a peaceful self, and the other two—annihilationism and the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life—together make three.

'Rūpiṃ vā' means holding the view that the self has form, either by way of the physical body (karajarūpa) or the kasiṇa-form. Among them, the attainer (lābhī) takes the kasiṇa-form as the self. The speculator (takkī) takes both kinds of form as the self. 'Arūpiṃ' means designating the self either as the object of a formless attainment or as the remaining mental states excluding the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha). Both attainers and speculators designate it in this way. The third view arises by way of a mixed grasp (missakagāha). The fourth view arises only by way of speculative grasp (takkagāha). In the second tetrad, it should be understood that the first view is taught regarding those who enter attainments, the second view regarding those who do not, the third view by way of kasiṇa-preliminary work the size of a saucer or a bowl, and the fourth view by way of an expansive kasiṇa.

'Etaṃ vā panekesaṃ upātivattataṃ' means the view of those who have surpassed the seven perceptions (saññāsattaka) mentioned briefly by the term 'saññī'. Other teachers, however, say it refers to those who have surpassed eight perceptions (aṭṭhaka). Both of these will be explained clearly later. The summary meaning here is that some people are able to surpass these seven or eight perceptions...
12:
...some are able to surpass the seven or eight perceptions, while some are not. Among them, only those who are able to surpass them are taken here. Among those who are able to surpass them, just as among people who have crossed the Ganges, one might go to Dīghavāpi and stay there, while another might go further to Mahāgāma and stay there; even so, some stay saying that the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) is immeasurable and imperturbable, while others stay in the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). Between those two attainments, in order to show the sphere of infinite consciousness first, it is said: 'viññāṇakasiṇameke'. Later, He will say: 'ākiñcaññāyatanam-eke'. 'Tayidaṃ' refers to this wrong view, the cause of the wrong view, and the object of the wrong view. 'Tathāgato abhijānāti' means that He knows with His superior omniscient knowledge that 'this particular view is held because of this cause'.

Now, wishing to explain the cause of that view in detail, He said: 'ye kho te bhonto', and so on. 'Yā vā pana etāsaṃ saññānaṃ' refers to the perceptions already mentioned, such as 'yadi rūpasaññānaṃ'. 'Parisuddhā' means being free from defilements. 'Paramā' means supreme. 'Aggā' means foremost. 'Anuttariyā akkhāyati' means declared to be unsurpassed. By the passage 'yadi rūpasaññānaṃ', the four fine-material sphere perceptions are taught. By the passage 'yadi arūpasaññānaṃ', the perception of the sphere of infinite space and the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness are taught. By the remaining two terms, the cycle of attainment and the cycle of non-attainment are taught. Thus, these perceptions are eight by way of groups, but seven in terms of essence. This is because the cycle of attainment is already included in the previous six.

'Tayidaṃ saṅkhataṃ' means that the entire collection of perceptions along with the wrong view is a conditioned (saṅkhata) phenomenon, produced by the meeting of causes. Because it is conditioned, it is called 'oḷārika' (gross). 'Atthi kho pana saṅkhါရာနံ nirodho' means that there is indeed Nibbāna, which is the cessation of those formations called conditioned. Having known that Nibbāna 'exists', the Buddha, who is accustomed to seeing the escape from the conditioned, has perfectly surpassed that conditioned state.

'Tatra' refers to those eight doctrines of an unpercipient self. The words 'rūpiṃ vā', etc., should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the doctrine of a percipient self. Since this is the doctrine of an unpercipient self, the second tetrad is not mentioned here. 'Paṭikkosanti' means they reject or deny.
13:
In the passages starting with "Perception is a disease" (saññā rogo), it is called a disease (rogo) in the sense of being oppressive; a boil (gaṇḍo) in the sense of being faulty; and a dart (sallaṃ) in the sense of repeatedly piercing. In the passages starting with "Coming or going" (āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā), "coming" (āgati) is by way of rebirth-linking; "going" (gati) is by way of death; "passing away" (cuti) is by way of shifting; "reappearance" (upapatti) is by way of approaching rebirth; "growth" (vuddhi), "increase" (virūḷhi), and "expansion" (vepullaṃ) are by way of arising again and again and developing successively.

Although the occurrence of consciousness without form (rūpa) indeed exists in the four-constituent existence (catuvokārabhavo), there is no occurrence of consciousness apart from the remaining three mental aggregates. However, this question is spoken by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhavo). Indeed, in the five-constituent realm, there is no such thing as the occurrence of consciousness apart from these aggregates.

In this matter, a Sophist (Vitaṇḍavādī) might say, based on the words "apart from form" (aññatra rūpā) etc., that form also exists in the formless existence (arūpabhava), consciousness exists in the non-percipient existence (asaññabhava), and likewise, consciousness exists for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti). To him, it should be said: "If you obstruct the meaning by following the shadow of the words, then because of the words 'coming or...' (āgatiṃ vā), you would fall into the error of saying that consciousness flies like a bird, a two-legged or four-legged creature, or walks on feet, or grows like a cow's horn or a creeper. Furthermore, the three types of existence taught by the Blessed One in hundreds of discourses would become only two, due to the non-existence of the formless existence. Therefore, do not speak thus; bear in mind the meaning as it has been stated."

"Therein" (tatra) is a locative case used in the eight views of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Here too, the terms starting with "Possessing form" (rūpī vā) should be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned. "Non-perception is delusion" (asaññā sammoho) means that the state of being without perception is a basis for delusion (sammohaṭṭhāna). Indeed, when someone knows nothing at all, people say, "This person is one without perception" (asaññī). "By the mere extent of formations of the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized" (diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabbasaṅkhāramattena) means by the mere extent of the occurrence of perception that cognizes the seen visible object, the heard sound, and the sensed smell, taste, and touch. Here, it is called "cognized" (viññātabba) because it is known. The meaning here is: by the mere extent of the occurrence of perception in the five doors, as indicated by the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. "By the mere extent of formations" (saṅkhāramattena) means by the mere extent of the occurrence of gross formations. "Of this sphere" (etassa āyatanassa) means of this meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "Attainment" (upasampadaṃ) means acquisition (paṭilābha). "It is a ruin" (byasanaṃ hetaṃ) means it is destruction; "it is an emergence" (vuṭṭhānaṃ hetaṃ) means it is a rising. One should enter that meditative attainment by making the occurrence of perception in the five doors or the occurrence of gross formations cease. It is intended to show that emergence from that attainment occurs through the re-occurrence of those perceptions. "It is not said to be reached by the attainment of formations" (saṅkhārasamāpattipattabbamakkhāyati) means it is not said to be reached by the occurrence of gross formations. "It is reached by the attainment of the remnants of formations" (saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattipattabbaṃ) means it is reached by the occurrence of those formations which are the only remnants and have reached an extremely subtle state through the power of meditation. When such formations are occurring...
14:
There is no such thing as reaching this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [by gross formations]. "This" (tayidaṃ) means that even though this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle, it is conditioned (saṅkhata), and because it is conditioned, it is gross.

"Therein" (tatra) is a term used in the locative case regarding the seven annihilationist views (ucchedavāda). The view that runs towards the future saṃsāra is called "running upwards" (uddhaṃsarā); the meaning is that they run towards the future saṃsāra. They speak only of attachment (āsatti), which is craving (taṇhā). In the variant reading "attached" (āsatta), the meaning is also that they speak only of craving. In the phrase "thus we shall be hereafter" (iti pecca bhavissāma), the method should be understood as: "we shall be kings, we shall be brahmins," and so on. "I think it is like a merchant" (vāṇijူpama manye) means it appears to my knowledge as if it were a merchant, or similar to a merchant. "Fear of personality" (sakkāyabhaya) means it arises from the fear of personality (sakkāya, the five aggregates).

Those people fear like the four types of creatures that fear what is not to be feared. Great King, those four are: (1) The earthworm, fearing "lest the earth be exhausted," does not eat earth and lives in fear. (2) The crane, fearing "lest the earth sink," stands on one leg and lives in fear. (3) The lapwing (kikī), fearing "lest the sky fall," sleeps on its back with its legs pointing upwards and lives in fear. (4) The Brāhmaṇadhammika brahmin, fearing "lest the world be cut off," does not practice the holy life and lives in fear. In this way, those people fear personality. "Loathing of personality" (sakkāyaparijigucchā) means the loathing of that very personality consisting of the three realms.

"Like a dog bound by a leash" (sa gaddulabaddho) means like a dog bound by a rope passed through a pole. Here, personality (sakkāya) consisting of the three realms should be seen as the firm post or stake. The person with wrong view is like the dog; the wrong view is like the pole; and craving is like the rope. Just as a dog bound by a rope to a pole or stake is unable to break free by its own nature and only runs around the post, so too should it be understood that the person with wrong view, bound by the rope of craving passed through the pole of wrong view and tied to personality, only runs around personality.

"Only these five bases" (imāneva pañcāyatanāni) means these five causes. Although five were established in the table of contents (mātikā) and five in the conclusion, only four (percipient, non-percipient, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, and annihilationist) were analyzed in the detailed exposition. If it is asked, "Where is the view of Nirvana in this life (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda) included?", it should be understood that it is included in the two terms "unity" (ekatta) and "diversity" (nānatta).

Having thus shown the forty-four views of those who speculate about the future (aparantakappika), he now says "There are, bhikkhus..." (santi bhikkhave) etc., to show the eighteen views of those who speculate about the past (pubbantakappika). Therein, they are called "speculators about the past" (pubbantakappika) because they conceive and grasp the past (pubbanta), which is called the past portion.
15:
Pubbantakappika refers to those who speculate about the past. Similarly, the remaining terms should be understood as previously stated. In the statement "The self and the world are eternal," they take one of the aggregates, such as form (rūpakkhandha), as the self and the world, asserting, "It is eternal, deathless, and remains stable forever." As the Buddha taught: "They designate the self and the world, saying 'Form is the self, form is the world, and it is eternal,'" and this should be understood in detail. The same method applies to "non-eternal" (asassata) and so forth. Here, the first discourse teaches the four types of Eternalism (Sassatavāda), and the second discourse teaches the seven types of Annihilationism (Ucchedavāda).

If one asks, "Why are these Annihilationist views mentioned again here when they have already appeared below?"—below, they are mentioned to show the meaning "when one dies in such and such a life, one is annihilated in that very life." Here, however, a person with wrong views who has attained the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-abhiññā) sees the past but not the future. Thus, he thinks, "The self that has come from the past is annihilated in this very life and does not go beyond this." This is included to show that meaning. The third discourse teaches the four types of Partial-eternalism (Ekaccasassatavāda), and the fourth discourse teaches the four types of Eel-wriggling (Amarāvikkhepavāda). "Antavā" means finite, limited, or having a circumscribed boundary. One who does not expand the meditation device (kasiṇa) takes that kasiṇa as the self and the world, and thus such a view arises. The second discourse is taught regarding one who expands the kasiṇa. The third discourse is taught regarding one who expands it horizontally but not vertically. The fourth discourse is taught regarding a logician (takkī). The next set of four (catukka) follows the same method as stated below.

"Ekantasukhī" refers to one who experiences continuous happiness. This view arises through the power of those who have attained supernormal knowledge, those who remember past births, and logicians. When one who has attained supernormal knowledge recollects his past lives in royal families and so forth, where he was consistently happy, this view arises. Similarly, when one who remembers past births (jātissara) is experiencing happiness in the present and recollects a similar state of existence in seven past lives, this view arises. For a logician, however, because he is endowed with happiness in this life, the view arises through mere reasoning: "In the past, I was just like this."

The view "Ekantadukkhī" (exclusively suffering) does not arise for one who has attained supernormal knowledge. This is because such a person is certainly happy in this life through the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna). This view arises only for a jātissara person or a logician who is experiencing suffering in this life. The third view, regarding those with mixed happiness and suffering, arises for all those who experience mixed happiness and suffering in this life. The fourth view arises in the same way. One who has attained supernormal knowledge, now being in a state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (upekkhā) through the power of the fourth jhāna, and recollecting the Brahma world of the fourth jhāna in the past...
16:
...recollecting [that state]. This view arises for a jātissara person who is neutral in the present and recollects a state of neutrality, and for a logician who is neutral in the present and assumes through reasoning, "It will be like this in the past as well." By this sequence of words, the eighteen doctrines of those who speculate about the past (pubbantakappika) are taught: four types of Eternalism, four types of Partial-eternalism, four types of Finitism and Infinitism, four types of Eel-wriggling, and two types of Fortuitous Origination.

Now, wishing to extract and remove these views, the Buddha said, "Monks, regarding those views," and so forth. In that context, "knowledge within oneself" refers to direct knowledge (paccakkhañāṇa). "Pure" means free from defilements. "Bright and clear" means radiant. All these terms refer to insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa). While the five qualities such as faith (saddhā) exist in external traditions, insight knowledge exists only in the Buddha's Dispensation. In those views, they purify only a portion of knowledge, saying, "We know this," and thus they enter into a portion of knowledge. "It is called clinging (upādāna)" means that because that state is not true knowledge but wrong view, even that portion of knowledge for those beings is called clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna). Alternatively, because it has the characteristic of mere knowing, it could be a portion of knowledge; nevertheless, because they cannot transcend that view and because it is a condition for clinging, it is called simply "clinging." "One who transcends that clinging" refers to one who has gone beyond that view.

Thus, all sixty-two views mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta are taught: four types of Eternalism, four types of Partial-eternalism, four types of Finitism and Infinitism, four types of Eel-wriggling, two types of Fortuitous Origination, sixteen doctrines of percipient existence, eight doctrines of non-percipient existence, eight doctrines of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, seven types of Annihilationism, and five types of Nibbāna in the here and now. However, by merely teaching the Brahmajāla Sutta, this sutta is not yet considered taught. Why? Because this sutta contains matters concerning identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) that go beyond the Brahmajāla Sutta. But if this sutta is taught, the Brahmajāla Sutta is considered already taught.

Now, to show that these sixty-two views arise with identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) as the forerunner, the Buddha said, "Monks, here a certain person," and so forth. In that context, "relinquishing" means giving up. "Not clinging to the fetters of sensual desire" means having abandoned the craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Rapture born of seclusion" refers to the rapture (pīti) of the first and second jhānas, which are accompanied by rapture. "Ceases" means it ceases through the cessation of jhāna. For one who has emerged from an attainment (samāpatti), it is said to have ceased.
18:
"Where do water, earth, fire, and air find no footing? Where do long and short, small and great, fair and foul cease? Where do name and form cease without remainder?"

The answer to that question is: "It is Nibbāna, which is to be known through the knowledge of the path and fruition of Arahantship, which is not visible to eye-consciousness, which is infinite, and which is radiant in every way."

In this context, Nibbāna is shown by the rejection of formations. However, in this sutta (Saḷāyatana Sutta), it is shown by the rejection of the six sense bases. In other suttas, Nibbāna is shown by the term "liberation without clinging" (anupādā-vimokkha), but in this Pañcattaya Sutta, it refers to the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti). The remaining words are clear in all suttas.

## Papañcasūdanī, Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya
## The Explanation of the Pañcattaya Sutta is Finished.
## 3. Explanation of the Kinti Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Kinti Sutta. There, "at Pisinārā" means in the district of that name. "At Baliharaṇa" means that because people brought offerings (bali) to the spirits in that forest grove, it is called Baliharaṇa. "For the sake of robes" (cīvara-hetu) means because of robes, desiring robes. "For the sake of various types of existence" (itibhavābhava-hetu) means teaching the Dhamma with the intention of experiencing happiness in various lives by relying on this merit-making activity consisting of teaching; the meaning is the question "Does it occur to you thus?"

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness, are taught in terms of both the mundane and the supramundane. "Therein" (tatra) means among those thirty-seven factors. "Should be" (siyaṃsu) means they would exist. "In the higher Dhamma" (abhidhamme) means in the distinguished Dhamma, specifically in these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. "And therein" (tatra ca) is also used in the locative case referring to the factors of enlightenment. In the phrase "different in meaning and different in phrasing," if one says "the body is a foundation of mindfulness, feeling is a foundation of mindfulness," there is a difference in meaning. If one says "foundations of mindfulness," there is a difference in phrasing. "By this also" (tadamina-pi) means "you should know that meaning by this reason as well." Thus, by comparing meaning and phrasing, it shows the taking of a meaning other than the true meaning, and the incorrect placement of phrasing. In the passage "Whatever is the Dhamma, whatever is the Vinaya," the cause that makes the meaning and phrasing known is called both Dhamma and Vinaya. "It agrees in meaning" (atthato hi kho sameti) means only mindfulness should be taken as the foundation of mindfulness. "Different in phrasing" (byañjanato nānaṃ) means they incorrectly apply the mere phrasing as "foundation of mindfulness" (singular) or "foundations of mindfulness" (plural). "A mere trifle" (appamattakaṃ kho)...
19:
When it is said "Satipaṭṭhānā," it is distinct in terms of phrasing (byañjana). "Tadamināpi" means "You should also know this meaning through this reason." By reconciling the meaning and the phrasing, it demonstrates the wrong grasping of meaning and the incorrect presentation of phrasing. In the Pali "Yo dhammo yo vinayo," the very cause that makes the meaning and phrasing understood is called both Dhamma and Vinaya.

"Atthato hi kho sameti" means that by way of meaning, only mindfulness (sati) is taken as Satipaṭṭhāna. "Byañjanato nānaṃ" means that they incorrectly present the mere phrasing as either "Satipaṭṭhāno" or "Satipaṭṭhānā." "Appamattakaṃ kho" means that in the Suttanta Pali, phrasing is of little consequence. This is because even if one recites by making a slight aspirated (dhanita) sound, it is possible to reach Nibbāna.

Regarding the recitation of an unaspirated (sithila) letter as aspirated (dhanita), there is this story: An Arahant Elder residing in Vijayārāma Monastery, while bringing forth the Pali and teaching meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) to two monks, said "Samuddho samuddho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano bhāsati," pronouncing it with an aspirated (dhanita) sound. One monk said, "Venerable, it is only Samudda (unaspirated)." The Elder replied, "Friend, whether I say it with an aspirated sound as Samuddho or as Samudda, we only know the salty ocean. You are not seekers of meaning, but seekers of phrasing. Go to Mahāvihāra and have your phrasing purified in the presence of monks who are proficient in phrasing." Thus, he made them leave without continuing the meditation teaching. Later, that Arahant Elder had a drum beaten at Mahāvihāra, and only after teaching the monks a problem concerning the four paths did he attain Parinibbāna. In this way, in the Suttanta Pali, phrasing is of little consequence.

However, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, phrasing is not of little consequence (it is important). Even the novice ordination (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) is valid only if there is purity on both sides. Vinaya rituals such as the higher ordination (upasampadā) can be invalidated merely by pronouncing an unaspirated (sithila) sound as an aspirated (dhanita) one. But here, this was said with reference to Suttanta phrasing.

Why is there a dispute in the fourth view? The dispute is due to perception (saññā). Their perception is: "I say only mindfulness is Satipaṭṭhāna, but this person says the body is Satipaṭṭhāna." The same logic applies to phrasing (byañjana).
20: One should not hastily bypass by means of accusation; one should not act hurriedly for the sake of accusation. For a certain person, when told, "There is a mustard-seed-sized sore on your forehead," replies, "You see the mustard-seed-sized sore on my forehead, but you do not see the ripe-palm-fruit-sized large boil on your own forehead." Therefore, a person should be carefully examined. "Adaḷhadiṭṭhi" means not having a firmly held view; one does not grasp firmly, like putting a crocodile into the heart. "Upaghāta" means the arising of mental suffering, similar to the pain of one whose wound is touched with a harsh manner. "Suppaṭinissaggi" means that even if one says once or twice, "What offense have I committed? When did I commit it?" or "You have committed an offense; your preceptor has committed an offense," when reminded, "Venerable, you committed such an offense on such a day, please remember slowly," they remember and relinquish the offense at that very moment. "Vihesā" means the weariness of body and mind that occurs to one who has to bring forth many meanings and reasons. "Sakkomi" (I am able) means that such a person, after giving permission, when told, "Venerable, you have committed an offense," asks, "When and regarding what matter?" and when told, "On such a day regarding such a matter," says, "Friend, I do not remember." Then, after being reminded repeatedly, "Venerable, remember slowly," they remember and relinquish the offense. Therefore, He said, "Sakkomi." In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places. "Upekkhā nātimaññitabbā" means equanimity should not be overstepped; it should be practiced and developed. If someone sees such a person urinating while standing and says, "Friend, should one not sit?" that person is said to have overstepped equanimity. "Vacīsaṃhāra" means the carrying of speech (tale-bearing). It means bringing what these people said to those people, saying, "You were told such and such by these people," and bringing what those people said to these people. By the terms "diṭṭhipalāsa" and so on, the unpleasing nature of the mind is described. It means: "If the Teacher (the Buddha) knows of this tale-bearing, He would blame us." "Etaṃ panāvuso dhammaṃ" refers to this nature of quarreling and disputing.
21:
"Tañceti" refers to that monk who performs the persuasion. "Thus he should answer" means that instead of saying, "I have established these Suttas in a state of purity," he should answer by showing the very reason for which the persuasion was made. In the phrase "Having heard that Dhamma," "Dhamma" refers to the Sāraṇīya-dhamma (principles of cordiality). In the phrases beginning with "Neither (exalting) oneself," a person who says, "This fire of dispute has risen as high as the Brahma-world; who else but I is capable of extinguishing it?" is said to exalt himself. A person who says, "So many people are wandering about, yet they cannot find an opportunity; there is not even one person capable of extinguishing such a fire," is said to disparage others. That monk does neither of those two. Here, "Dhamma" is the Buddha's explanation, and the persuasion of those monks is the "Anudhamma" (conformity to the Dhamma); thus, he is said to explain that very matter. "Nor is there any fellow-dhamma-practitioner (sahadhammika)" means there is no one else whose argument or counter-argument, spoken with reason, reaches the state of being blameworthy. The rest of the words are clear in meaning.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Kinti Sutta is finished.
## 4. Sāmagāma Sutta Vaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Sāmagāma Sutta)

"Thus have I heard" and so forth refers to the Sāmagāma Sutta. In that sutta, "Sāmagāma" refers to a village so named because of the abundance of sāmāka grass. "Just recently deceased" means he has just now passed away. "Split into two groups" means they have become divided into two parts or two factions. In the context of quarreling and so on, "bhaṇḍana" is the initial dispute; that same dispute, when it escalates through the taking up of sticks and the like, or through the transgression of rules, is called "kalaha." Opposing speech such as "You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya" is called "vivāda." "Stabbing (with words)" means piercing with the spear of the tongue. "My speech is connected with the goal" means my words are associated with benefit. "Your practiced view is overturned" means that your view, which was proficient due to long practice, has retreated upon meeting my argument. "The argument is placed upon you" means I have placed the blame/refutation upon you. "Go to be released from the argument" means taking a food bundle and approaching various people for the sake of being released from the argument...
22:
...wander about seeking further. "Or untangle yourself" means "Or else, release yourself from the argument (blame) I have placed." "If you are able" means if you have the capacity. "Only death" means only the act of dying.

"Among the disciples of Nātaputta" means among the followers of Nātaputta. "Are of a weary nature" means they have a nature of being weary/disgusted, and thus they no longer perform acts like salutation. "Are of a nature devoid of affection" means their love/affection has vanished. "Are of a nature that withdraws" means they have a nature of withdrawing from showing respect to them. Just as one should be weary, dispassionate, and withdrawn in a Dhamma-Vinaya that is badly taught and so forth, so it has arisen in them. "Badly taught" means poorly spoken. "Badly proclaimed" means poorly communicated/understood. "Not leading to peace" means incapable of bringing about the calming of lust and so on. In the phrase "the foundation is broken," here Nātaputta himself was their foundation, like a stupa (thūpa); but he is broken, meaning he is dead. Therefore, it is said "the foundation is broken." "Without a refuge" means being devoid of a refuge because that very Nātaputta is no longer there.

Since this Nātaputta was a resident of Nālandā, why did he pass away in Pāvā? It is said that after hearing the virtues of the Buddha spoken in ten verses by the householder Upāli, who had penetrated the Truth, he vomited hot blood. Then, having become ill, they took him to Pāvā, and he passed away there. While passing away, he thought: "My view does not lead out of suffering and is devoid of essence. We are already ruined; let not the remaining people be those who fill the lower realms. However, if I say 'My teaching does not lead out of suffering,' they will not believe me. What if I do not let two people learn by the same method? They will then dispute with one another after my passing. The Blessed One, depending on that dispute, will deliver a Dhamma discourse; only then will they know the greatness of the Buddha's Dispensation."

Then a disciple approached him and said, "Venerable sir, you are weak; tell me the essence of this Dhamma which is the teacher's standard." He said, "Friend, after my passing, you should take it as 'eternal' (sassata)." Another also approached him, and he made him take it as "annihilation" (uccheda). In this way, instead of making the two people hold a single view, he made many people learn by various methods and then passed away. After performing the funeral rites for Nātaputta, those disciples assembled and asked one another, "Friends, to whom did the teacher tell the essence?" One stood up and said, "He told it to me." When asked, "What did he tell?" he said, "Eternal." Another person refuted that and said, "He told the essence to me." In this way, everyone said, "He told the essence to me, I alone am the leader," thus increasing the dispute among themselves...
23:
Abusing and threatening each other, and even striking one another with hands and feet, they did not travel together on the same path but went their separate ways. Some Nigaṇṭhas disrobed and returned to lay life. However, while the Blessed One was alive, no dispute arose within the Saṅgha of monks. This was because as soon as a cause for dispute arose among those monks, the Teacher would either go himself or have those monks summoned, and he would settle the dispute by teaching one of the principles such as patience, the cultivation of loving-kindness, reflection, non-violence, or the Sāraṇīya-dhammas (virtues of fraternal living). Thus, while he was alive, he was the mainstay of the Saṅgha. Even when he was about to attain Parinibbāna, he did so after establishing the causes for non-dispute. The Four Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa) taught by the Blessed One in the Suttas remain the mainstay and refuge for monks to this day. Similarly, the Four Great Authorities taught in the Khandhaka and the four ways of answering questions taught in the Suttas [also serve as mainstay and refuge]. Therefore, he said: "Ānanda, the Dhamma I have taught and the Vinaya I have prescribed shall be your teacher after my passing."

"Atha kho cundo samaṇuddeso" means this elder was the younger brother of the Marshal of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. Because they called him Cunda the Novice (Samaṇuddesa) even before he became a monk, and continued to call him so even after he became an elder, it is said "Cundo samaṇuddeso". Regarding "upasaṅkami" (approached), why did he approach? It is said that when Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta passed away, people throughout Jambudīpa spoke in various places: "Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta was known as a unique teacher, yet upon his death, such a dispute has arisen among his disciples. The Ascetic Gotama, however, is as prominent in Jambudīpa as the moon and the sun. What kind of dispute will arise among the disciples of the Ascetic Gotama when he attains Parinibbāna?" When the elder heard this talk, he thought: "I will take this matter and report it to the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala); the Teacher, taking this as an occasion, will deliver a discourse." He set out and approached Venerable Ānanda at Sāmagāma. He did not go directly to the Blessed One but approached his preceptor (upajjhāya), Venerable Ānanda. This was because he thought: "My preceptor, Venerable Ānanda, is of great wisdom; he [will report] this news..."
24:
Venerable Ānanda will report this news to the Teacher, and then the Teacher will deliver a Dhamma teaching suitable for that occasion (so thought Venerable Cunda). "Kathāpābhataṃ" means the basis of the talk; the basis is called "pābhata" (a gift or start-up capital). As it is said: "A wise and discerning person, even with small capital (pābhata), can establish himself, just as one blows a small fire into a flame." "Dassanāya" means for the purpose of seeing (visiting). Did this Venerable Cunda not see the Blessed One before? It was not that he had not seen him; he had. This Venerable used to go to pay respects eighteen times a day—nine times during the day and nine times at night. However, even if he wished to go a hundred or a thousand times a day, he would not go without a reason; he would only go taking some question or issue. On that day, wishing to go with Venerable Ānanda, he spoke thus.

"For the harm and suffering of devas and humans" means: how does a dispute arising in the midst of the Saṅgha in a single monastery lead to the harm and suffering of devas and humans? As in the Kosambaka-khandhaka, when two monks fall into a dispute, their pupils in that monastery also dispute. The community of bhikkhunīs who receive their instruction also disputes. Then, their lay supporters dispute. At that time, the guardian deities of the people split into two factions. In that division, the guardian deities of those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī) become dhammavādīs, and the guardian deities of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma (adhammavādī) become adhammavādīs. Then, the terrestrial deities (bhummadevatā) who are friends with those guardian deities also split. In this manner, through a succession, all devas and humans up to the Brahma world—excluding the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka)—split into two factions. Since the adhammavādīs are usually more numerous than the dhammavādīs, people follow the majority. Abandoning the true Dhamma, the majority accept the false doctrine (adhamma). Living and practicing according to adhamma, they are reborn in the woeful planes (apāya). Thus, a dispute arising in the midst of the Saṅgha in a single monastery leads to the harm and suffering of many.

"Abhiññā desitā" refers to the teachings made known by the Buddha through his own direct realization while sitting at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree. "Patissayamānarūpā viharanti" means they live in dependence [upon the teachings]. "Bhagavato accayena" means that at present, they live with reverence, regarding the Blessed One as their chief. [They think:] "Venerable Sir, because of your sublime power and being difficult to approach, [they do not dare] to create a dispute..."
25:
(Venerable Ānanda) submitted that while they currently live respectfully with the Blessed One as their leader, due to the Blessed One’s sharp majesty and the difficulty of approaching him, they are unable to cause disputes; however, after the Blessed One’s passing, they might indeed cause disputes. Wishing to show the grounds where such disputes might arise, the Buddha said, "Whether concerning livelihood or concerning the higher Patimokkha." In that passage, "concerning livelihood" (ajjhājīva) refers to the six training rules prescribed in the Parivāra based on livelihood, such as "A monk claims a superhuman state; he incurs an offense of defeat (pārājika)," and so on. Setting aside those six, all remaining training rules are called the "higher Patimokkha" (adhipātimokkha). The statement "Ānanda, that dispute is trifling" means that a dispute arising from livelihood or the higher Patimokkha is easily abandoned, either through the words of others or by one's own reflection; therefore, it is called "trifling."

Herein, this is the method: In this Dispensation, a certain monk thinks, "It is not possible to obtain any requisites without claiming superhuman states," and so on. For the sake of livelihood, he claims superhuman states, or acts as a messenger, or engages in "indirect talk" (sāmantajappana) by saying, "The monk living in that monastery is an Arahant," and so forth. Or, while not ill, he requests and eats fine foods for himself. Or a nun requests such foods and incurs an offense of confession (pāṭidesanīya). Or any careless monk requests curry and rice, which is a ground for an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Or he lives transgressing one or another of the prescribed rules. His fellow practitioners recognize him thus: "What is the use of these gains to this monk who, having gone forth in the Dispensation, makes a living through wrong livelihood and transgresses the prescribed rules?" By his own nature, he also reflects: "What is the use of these gains to me who, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, makes a living through wrong livelihood and transgresses the prescribed rules?" Having thus reflected, he desists from that wrong livelihood. Because it is easily abandoned in this way, either through the words of others or by one's own reflection, the Blessed One said, "It is trifling."

"Ānanda, whether in the Path or in the Practice," in these words, once the Supramundane Path is reached, what is called "dispute" is entirely stilled; there is no dispute for those who have attained the Path. This was said with reference to the preliminary path (pubbabhāgamagga) and the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapaṭipadā).

Herein, this is the method: People praise a certain monk as being endowed with supramundane states. When disciples such as his co-residents (saddhivihārika) come and pay respects, he asks, "For what purpose have you come?" When they reply, "Venerable sir, we have come to ask about the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to be attended to," he says, "Sit down, I will tell you a meditation subject that can lead to the fruit of Arahantship in a moment." Then, entering his dwelling and sitting down, while that monk attends to his original meditation subject, an illumination (obhāsa) arises. At that time, he perceives, "This illumination is the first path." When a second illumination arises, he perceives, "I have attained the second path." In the same way, he causes the third and fourth illuminations to arise. In this way, the illumination...
26:
Saying, "I will tell you a meditation talk capable of leading to Arahantship in just a moment," he speaks thus: "In this Dispensation, a monk enters his dwelling and, while sitting, attends to his original meditation subject. To him who is thus attending, an illumination arises. This illumination is called the first path. He then produces the second illumination-knowledge, and at that time, the second path is attained. In this way, he also attains the third and fourth paths. By this much, he becomes one who has reached the Path and reached the Fruit." Then those monks come to the conclusion: "One who is not an Arahant is unable to teach meditation in this way; surely this venerable one is an Arahant."

Later, that monk passes away. People from the surrounding alms-villages come and ask, "Venerable sirs, did anyone ask the Elder a question?" The lay devotees also say, "Even before the Elder was ill, he answered questions for us." Those people prepare a flower pavilion and an ornate funeral structure, cover his eyes and face with gold, and make offerings with flowers and perfumes. After celebrating a joyous festival (sādhukīḷana) for seven days, they cremate him, take the bones, and build a stupa (cetiya). Other visiting monks come to the monastery, wash their feet, and ask, "We would like to see the Great Elder. Where is the Great Elder, friends?" They reply, "Venerable sirs, the Elder has attained Parinibbāna." The visitors say, "Friends, the Elder has performed a difficult task in producing the Paths and Fruits. Friends, did you ask him any questions?" They reply, "Venerable sirs, when he taught meditation to the monks, he taught in this manner." The visitors say, "Friends, this illumination is not the Path; it is called an imperfection of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa). You did not know; friends, that Elder was only a worldling (puthujjana)." Those monks, rising up in dispute, say, "Do the monks in the entire monastery and the people in the alms-villages not know, and only you know? From which road did you come? Did you not see the stupa at the monastery gate?" For monks who are in the habit of speaking thus, whether they be a hundred or a thousand, as long as they do not abandon that view, both heaven and the Path are surely obstructed.

Another monk of a similar nature, when teaching meditation, teaches thus: By mere imagination, one places three pans on three hearthstones, puts fire underneath, extracts one's own thirty-two parts and places them in the pans, and by mere imagination, turns them over and over with a rod to roast them. When they are burnt, the resulting ashes should be blown away with the breath from the mouth. By this much, this monk is called one who has shaken off defilements (dhūtapāpa). The rest of the discourse should be expanded according to the previous method.
27:
Another teacher says this: Having set up a large pot by mind alone, and having put whey in it, one should extract one's own thirty-two parts of the body by mind alone, place them in that pot, pour in the whey, and churn it. The mixture being churned dissolves; when it dissolves, foam rises to the top. That foam should be consumed (through the path of insight). By this much, you will be said to have consumed the Deathless (mindfulness of the body). From here on, everything starting with "Atha te bhikkhū" should be understood in detail according to the previous method.

Now, to show the root of such a dispute if it should arise, he spoke the words beginning with "Chayimāni." Therein, "agāravo" means being devoid of respect. "Appatisso" means lack of deference or lack of humble conduct. Here, if a monk, while the Teacher is still alive, does not go to serve him at the three times; or while the Teacher is walking on the walkway without sandals, he walks on the walkway wearing sandals; or while the Teacher walks on a lower walkway, he walks on a higher walkway; or while the Teacher stays on the lower floor, he stays on the upper floor; or in a place where the Teacher can see him, he covers both shoulders, carries an umbrella, wears sandals, or urinates or defecates at a bathing place; or after the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, he does not go to worship at a shrine, and does all the aforementioned disrespectful acts in a prominent place of the shrine as if in the presence of the Teacher; and when other monks say, "Why do you do this? This is not proper; one should feel shame and respect toward the Fully Enlightened One," he remains silent or says, "Why do you keep saying 'Buddha, Buddha'?"—this is called disrespect for the Teacher (satthari agārava).

If a monk, when the announcement for hearing the Dhamma is made, does not go respectfully, does not listen to the Dhamma respectfully, or sits sleeping or talking; does not learn or memorize it respectfully; and when asked, "Why do you show disrespect for the Dhamma?" he remains silent or says, "You keep saying 'Dhamma, Dhamma'; what is this thing called Dhamma?"—this is called disrespect for the Dhamma (dhamme agārava).

If a monk, without being invited by an elder monk, teaches the Dhamma, sits down, or answers questions; or goes, stands, or sits while bumping into senior monks; or uses a cloth strap or a hand strap (āyogapaṭṭa); or covers both shoulders in the midst of the Saṅgha, or carries an umbrella and wears sandals; and even when told, "One should feel shame and respect toward the Saṅgha of monks," he remains silent or says, "You keep saying 'Saṅgha, Saṅgha'; what is the Saṅgha? Is it a herd of deer or a herd of goats?" and so on—this is called disrespect for the Saṅgha (saṅghe agārava). Even showing disrespect to a single monk is considered showing disrespect to the Saṅgha.
28:
Even showing disrespect to a single monk is considered showing disrespect to the Saṅgha. A monk who does not fulfill the three trainings is called one who does not show respect for the training. "Ajjhattaṃ" means within oneself or within one's own group. "Bahiddhā" means in another or in another's group.

Now, to show the legal issues (adhikaraṇa) that arise when a dispute based on these six causes increases, he spoke the words beginning with "Cattārimāni." In that text, they are called "adhikaraṇa" because they must be dealt with by the settlements (samatha) that arise to appease them. Since the dispute itself is a legal issue, it is called "vivādādhikaraṇa" (legal issue arising from dispute). The same method should be understood for the remaining legal issues.

Now, to show the settlements by which that dispute, having reached these four legal issues and increased further, is appeased, he spoke the words beginning with "Satta kho panime." In that text, they are called "adhikaraṇasamatha" because they appease the legal issues. "Uppannuppannānaṃ" means "as they arise." "Adhikaraṇānaṃ" refers to these four legal issues, such as vivādādhikaraṇa. "Samathāya vūpasamāya" means for the sake of harmony and for the sake of appeasement. These seven settlements, from "Sammukhāvinaya should be given..." to "Tiṇavatthāraka," are to be applied.

In this regard, this is the definitive explanation: Among the legal issues, first, the dispute of monks who argue over eighteen grounds, such as "this is Dhamma" or "this is not Dhamma," is called "vivādādhikaraṇa." Accusation, disparagement, and charging based on failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti), or failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatti) is called "anuvādādhikaraṇa." The seven groups of offenses, five mentioned in the Matika and two in the Vibhaṅga, are called "āpattādhikaraṇa." The performance of the four types of formal acts for the Saṅgha, such as the act of announcement (apalokanakamma), is called "kiccādhikaraṇa."

Among those four, "vivādādhikaraṇa" is appeased by two settlements: Sammukhāvinaya and Yebhuyyasikā. A legal issue settled by Sammukhāvinaya alone is settled either in the very monastery where it arose, or on the way while going elsewhere to settle it, or in the monastery where it was handed over to the Saṅgha; if the Saṅgha or a group is unable to settle it there, it is settled by the decision of authorized individuals through the Ubbāhika method in that same monastery. In such a settlement...
29:
In that *Sammukhāvinaya*, there are four types of presence: *Saṅghasammukhatā*, *Dhammasammukhatā*, *Vinayasammukhatā*, and *Puggalasammukhatā*. This kind of presence is called *Sammukhāvinaya*.

Among these four types of presence, the presence through the harmony of the executive Saṅgha is called *Saṅghasammukhatā*. The manifestation of the matter to be settled is called *Dhammasammukhatā*. Settling the matter exactly as it should be settled is called *Vinayasammukhatā*. The presence of both parties involved in the dispute—the one who disputes and the one with whom he disputes—in the matter that is the cause of the dispute is called *Puggalasammukhatā*. In this *vivādādhikaraṇa* (legal question arising from dispute), when it is settled by *ubbāhikā* (referral to a committee), the presence of the Saṅgha (*Saṅghasammukhatā*) is diminished. In the manner already stated, it is first settled by *Sammukhāvinaya* alone.

If it is not settled even in this way, then the bhikkhus appointed by *ubbāhikā* hand it back to the Saṅgha, saying, "We are unable to settle it." Because of this handing over, the Saṅgha appoints a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities as a distributor of voting tickets (*salākaggāhaka*). By means of one of the three ways of taking voting tickets—secretly, openly, or whispering in the ear—the tickets are taken.
