Due to the majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma in the assembled group, the matter is settled as those Dhamma-speakers say. A legal question settled in this way is said to be settled by both *Sammukhāvinaya* and *Yebhuyyasikā*. Among these, *Sammukhāvinaya* is as already described. The performance of the formal act by the majority is called *Yebhuyyasikā*. Thus, a *vivādādhikaraṇa* is settled by two *samathas*.

An *anuvādādhikaraṇa* (legal question arising from accusation) is settled by four *samathas*: *Sammukhāvinaya*, *Sativinaya*, *Amūḷhavinaya*, and *Tassapāpiyasikā*. In a legal question settled by *Sammukhāvinaya* alone, after hearing the words of the accuser and the accused, if there is no offense, it is settled by making both bhikkhus apologize to each other. If there is an offense, it is settled by deciding, "In this case, there is such an offense." Among these four *samathas*, the characteristic of *Sammukhāvinaya* is as already described.

When a bhikkhu who is an Arahant is accused of a groundless fall from virtue and requests *Sativinaya*, the Saṅgha grants him *Sativinaya* by a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements (*ñatticatutthakamma*). At that time, it is said to be settled by both *Sammukhāvinaya* and *Sativinaya*. Once *Sativinaya* has been granted, an accusation by anyone against that person can no longer be raised (is not valid).

When an insane bhikkhu, while in a state of insanity, has committed an improper act unbefitting a monk, and when told by bhikkhus, "Venerable, remember such an offense," he says, "Friends, I did this while I was insane; I do not remember it," even though...
30:
...even though he is being accused by the bhikkhus, he requests *Amūḷhavinaya* so that he may not be accused again. The Saṅgha then grants him *Amūḷhavinaya* by a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements (*ñatticatutthakamma*). At that time, it is settled by both *Sammukhāvinaya* and *Amūḷhavinaya*. Once *Amūḷhavinaya* has been granted, an accusation by anyone against that person based on that insanity can no longer be raised.

When a wicked person, who is prone to evil and who prevaricates (evades one question with another) when accused of a *Pārājika* offense or an offense close to a *Pārājika*, is considered by the Saṅgha thus: "If this person's root is not yet severed, he may practice well and regain restoration to the Saṅgha; if his root is severed, this itself will be his destruction," the Saṅgha performs the formal act of *Tassapāpiyasikā* against him by a formal act consisting of a motion and three announcements (*ñatticatutthakamma*). At that time, it is settled by both *Sammukhāvinaya* and *Tassapāpiyasikā*. Thus, an *anuvādādhikaraṇa* is settled by four *samathas*.

An *āpattādhikaraṇa* (legal question arising from offenses) is settled by three *samathas*: *Sammukhāvinaya*, *Paṭiññātakaraṇa*, and *Tiṇavatthāraka*. For this *āpattādhikaraṇa*, there is no settlement by *Sammukhāvinaya* alone. When a bhikkhu confesses a light offense in the presence of another bhikkhu or in the midst of the Saṅgha or a group, then the *āpattādhikaraṇa* is settled by both *Sammukhāvinaya* and *Paṭiññātakaraṇa*. Among these two, *Sammukhāvinaya* is the presence of the one who confesses and the one who receives the confession. The remaining meaning is as already described. At the time of confession to an individual or a group, the presence of the Saṅgha (*Saṅghasammukhatā*) is diminished. In this confession, when it is acknowledged as "Venerable, I have fallen into such an offense" and "Yes, I see it," the act of saying "Restrain yourself in the future" is called *Paṭiññātakaraṇa*. In the case of a *Saṅghādisesa* offense, the request for *parivāsa* (probation) and so on is the *paṭiññā* (acknowledgment); the granting of *parivāsa* and so on is called *Paṭiññātakaraṇa*.

When quarrelsome bhikkhus on both sides have committed many improper acts unbefitting monks, and when a sense of shame later arises, they see the fault in making each other deal with the offenses, thinking: "If we make each other deal with these offenses, that legal question, because of its harshness, might lead to greater strife." When they then perform the formal act of *Tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass), at that time the *āpattādhikaraṇa* is settled by both *Sammukhāvinaya* and *Tiṇavatthāraka*. In that case, the bhikkhus within the reach of the hand (*hatthapāsa*) do not overturn the act by saying "This act was badly done, it must be done again," without making an open objection such as "I do not approve of that act."
31:
They also fall into sleep. Except for grave offenses (thullavajja—Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa) and those connected with laypeople, they emerge (are purified) from all offenses. Thus, the legal issue of offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa) is settled by three means of settlement (samatha). The legal issue of duties (kiccādhikaraṇa) is settled by only one means of settlement, namely, the verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya).

These four legal issues are settled by these seven means of settlement as appropriate. Therefore, the Buddha said: "For the settlement and calming of legal issues that have arisen, the verdict in the presence should be given... the covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka) should be given." This is just a brief method of decision here; the detailed explanation has already appeared in the Samathakkhandhaka (Cullavagga, 185). Its decision is also stated in the Samantapāsādikā commentary.

In this sutta, the detailed method starting with "Ānanda, here in this Dispensation, monks dispute," should be understood as being taught in summary by this method. Among those terms such as "Dhamma," according to the Suttanta method, first of all, the ten wholesome courses of action are called Dhamma, and the ten unwholesome courses of action are called Adhamma. Likewise, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) such as the four foundations of mindfulness mentioned below are called Dhamma. (However, some) dispute by saying (wrongly) that there are only three foundations of mindfulness, only three right efforts, only three bases of power, six faculties, six powers, eight factors of enlightenment, and nine path factors. Defiled states such as the four kinds of grasping (upādāna) and five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are called Adhamma.

Among those unwholesome states, taking a certain group of Adhamma and thinking, "We will make this Adhamma into Dhamma; by doing so, our lineage of teachers will lead to liberation from the round of rebirth, and we will become famous in the world," they dispute it as Dhamma, saying of that Adhamma, "This is Dhamma." Similarly, taking one among the groups of Dhamma and saying, "This is Adhamma," they dispute it as Adhamma.

According to the Vinaya method, a legal act performed by charging with a true matter, reminding, and in accordance with the acknowledgment is called Dhamma. A legal act performed without charging with a true matter, without reminding, and without acknowledgment is called Adhamma. Regarding those Dhamma and Adhamma in the Vinaya, they dispute Adhamma as Dhamma, saying "This is Dhamma," and they dispute Dhamma as Adhamma, saying "This is Adhamma."

According to the Suttanta method, the subduing of passion, the subduing of hatred, the subduing of delusion, restraint, abandonment, and reflection are called Vinaya. Not subduing passion, etc...
32:
Non-restraint, non-abandonment, and non-reflection are called Avinaya. According to the Vinaya teachings, the perfection of the basis (vatthu-sampatti), the perfection of the motion (ñatti-sampatti), the perfection of the proclamation (anussāvana-sampatti), the perfection of the boundary (sīma-sampatti), and the perfection of the assembly (parisa-sampatti) are called Vinaya. The failure of the basis... the failure of the assembly is called Avinaya. Regarding those Vinaya and Avinaya, they dispute some Avinaya as Vinaya, saying "This is Vinaya." They dispute Vinaya as Avinaya, saying "This is Avinaya."

"The guide of Dhamma should be scrutinized (dhammanetti samanumajjitabbā)" means the rope of Dhamma should be repeatedly handled, rubbed with wisdom, and investigated. That guide of Dhamma is said to have appeared in the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta as "Vaccha, these ten states are unwholesome, these ten states are wholesome." Let it be that guide of Dhamma from the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta, or let it be the Dhamma and Vinaya taught here in this Sāmagāma Sutta. In whatever way it conforms to that guide of Dhamma—"Dhamma is indeed Dhamma, Adhamma is Adhamma, Vinaya is indeed Vinaya, Avinaya is Avinaya"—in that way, according to that conformity, that legal issue should be settled.

By the phrase "of some legal issues" (ekaccānaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ), only the legal issue of disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa) is shown here. However, the verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) is not unavailable in any legal issue (it is available in all). Since that legal issue of disputes is settled by two means of settlement, namely the verdict in the presence and the majority decision (yebhuyyasikā), although it is now the turn for the verdict of innocence (sativinaya) according to the order set in the matrix (mātikā) below, the Buddha did not teach that sativinaya yet. Instead, wishing to show the second means of settlement for the legal issue of disputes itself, he said: "Ānanda, how is the majority decision?" and so on. There, "the greater number" (bahutarā) means exceeding by at least two or three. The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as mentioned below.

Now, starting with the verdict of innocence (sativinaya) which has not been detailed below, in order to detail the remaining means of settlement in order, he said: "Ānanda, how is the verdict of innocence?" and so on. There, "or near a Pārājika" (pārājikasāmantena vā) means there are two kinds: proximity to a group (khandhasāmanta) and proximity to an offense (āpattisāmanta). There, since there are the group of Pārājika offenses, the group of Saṅghādisesa offenses, and the groups of Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, and Dubbhāsita offenses, the group following a preceding offense is called proximity to a group (khandhasāmanta). The Dukkaṭa offense occurring before the first Pārājika, and the Thullaccaya offenses occurring before the remaining Pārājikas, are called proximity to an offense (āpattisāmanta).
33:
Among those two proximities (sāmanta), namely khandhasāmanta and āpattisāmanta, the proximity of a pārājika is called a grave offense (garukāpatti). "Sarata-āyasmā" means "May the venerable one remember." By the phrase "ekaccānaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ," only anuvādādhikaraṇa (legal questions concerning accusations) is shown here.

"Bhāsitaparikkantaṃ" means what is spoken by word and what is undertaken and performed by body. By the phrase "ekaccānaṃ," here too, only anuvādādhikaraṇa is intended. In the case of paṭiññātakaraṇa (procedure by acknowledgement), āpattādhikaraṇa (legal questions concerning offenses) is shown by the word "ekaccānaṃ."

"Davā" means hastily (sahasā). "Ravā" means saying one thing while intending to say another. "Ānanda, thus for that person there is pāpiyasikā" means that the abundance of that person's evil is pāpiyasikā (the procedure for a further misconduct). By this, the basis for the formal act (kamma) is shown. The formal act should be performed only for such a person. The settlement of a legal question (adhikaraṇa) occurs only through the formal act, not through the abundance of the person's evil. Here too, it should be understood that the legal question is only anuvādādhikaraṇa.

In the passage "Ānanda, how is there tiṇavatthāraka (covering with grass)?", this formal act is called tiṇavatthāraka because it is similar to covering (excrement) with grass. Just as when excrement or urine is disturbed, it causes distress due to its foul smell, but when it is well-covered with grass, its smell does not cause distress; in the same way, if a certain āpattādhikaraṇa is settled by going to the very root, it leads to harshness, ferocity, and schism. That āpattādhikaraṇa is settled by this formal act. Because it is settled like foul excrement covered with grass, this formal act is called tiṇavatthāraka due to its similarity to covering with grass. Regarding that tiṇavatthāraka act, only the manner is shown by the words beginning with "Ānanda, when monks in this Dispensation have become quarrelsome." However, the kammavācā (formal procedure) that appears in the Khandhaka Vinaya is the standard (authority) here. In the phrase "excluding thullavajja, excluding what is connected with laypeople"—here, thullavajja refers to the grave faults of pārājika and saṅghādisesa offenses. Gihipaṭisaṃyutta refers to offenses incurred in the low abuse, disparagement, and lawful promises made to laypeople. By the word "adhikaraṇānaṃ," only āpattādhikaraṇa should be understood here. Nothing is said here regarding kiccādhikaraṇa (legal questions concerning obligations). Even if nothing is said, it should be understood that its settlement occurs only through sammukhāvinaya (removal of legal questions in the presence of the parties).
34:
"Ānanda, these six qualities that create conciliation (sāraṇīyadhamma)"—with these words, the discourse begins in the lower part based on disputes, and the sāraṇīyadhammas appear in the upper part. Thus, the teaching proceeds according to the proper sequence (anusaṃdhi). In the Kosambiya Sutta in the lower part, Right View associated with the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) is taught, but in this sutta, it should be understood that Right View associated with the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) is taught. "Aṇu" means having minor faults. "Thūla" means having major faults. The remaining words here are clear.

## The Commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
## 5. Commentary on the Sunakkhatta Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Sunakkhatta Sutta. In that sutta, "aññā" refers to Arahantship. "Byākatā" refers to the declaration made through the four phrases such as "birth is exhausted." "Adhimānena" means declaring attainment through conceit—having the notion of reaching what has not been reached and having the notion of attaining what has not been attained—saying, "We have attained it."

"Sunakkhatta, thus it is for the Tathāgata" means—Sunakkhatta, in the answering of these monks' questions, this matter is not clear to them and is like darkness. Therefore, these monks have the notion of attaining what has not been attained. "Come, I shall teach the Dhamma to them, purifying it and making it clear"—thus it is for the Tathāgata. "However, some here... for him too, there is a change of state" means the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma to those who are practicing. Where there are some worthless men (moghapurisa) who stand in their own desires, the Blessed One sees: "These monks, after learning this question, without knowing will act as if they know, and without reaching will have the notion of reaching, and will wander about boasting in villages and towns. That will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time." Thus, because of those who act according to their own desires, for the sake of those who are practicing, there is a change in the mind that arose thinking, "I shall teach the Dhamma." This was said in reference to that circumstance.

"Lokāmisādhimutto" means one who is strongly intent on the five cords of sensual pleasure which are the baits of the round (vaṭṭāmisa), the baits of sensuality (kāmāmisa), and the baits of the world (lokāmisa); one who leans towards them, values them, and is inclined towards them.
35:
## 
'Tappatirūpī' means resembling sensual pleasures (kāmaguṇa). 'Āneñjapaṭisaṃyuttāya' refers to talk connected with the imperturbable attainments (āneñjasamāpatti). 'Saṃseyya' means one should speak or one might have doubt. 'Āneñjasaṃyojanena hi kho visaṃyutto' refers to one who is not associated with the connection to the imperturbable attainments.

One who is strongly inclined to worldly gain (lokāmisādhimutta) is of such a nature: Indeed, a monk who wears such coarse robes, taking a clay bowl, goes to the borderlands with a few monks like himself. When entering a village for alms, people see them and say, 'The great rag-robe wearers (paṃsukūlika) have arrived,' and respectfully offer gruel, rice, and so on. After the meal, having heard the talk of appreciation (anumodanā), they say, 'Venerable sirs, please enter this very place for alms tomorrow as well.' That monk says, 'Enough, lay devotees, you have already given much today.' Then they say, 'Venerable sirs, if so, please spend the three months of the rains retreat right here,' and having accepted, they ask the way to the monastery and go there. There, they take lodgings and put away their bowls and robes. In the evening, a resident monk asks those guest monks, 'Where did you wander for alms?' When they say, 'In such-and-such a village,' he asks again, 'Was the alms-food plentiful?' They reply, 'Yes, the people have such faith.' He asks, 'Is it only today they are like this, or are they always like this?' They say, 'Those people have faith and are always like this; it is only by depending on those people that this monastery grows and prospers.' Furthermore, those rag-robe wearers repeatedly speak of the virtues of those people. Having spoken during the day, they speak again at night. For a monk established in evil desires (icchācāra) merely by meeting such faithful people, it is as if his head comes out and his belly is split for the sake of gains and offerings. Thus should one inclined to worldly gain be known.

Now, wishing to show the conceited person (adhimānika) who has attained the imperturbable attainments, He spoke the words beginning with 'Ṭhānaṃ khေါ panetaṃ.' 'Āneñjādhimutta' refers to one who is strongly inclined to, leaning towards, honoring, and tending towards the lower six attainments which are free from the moisture of defilements. 'Se pavutte' means that which was spoken. To a conceited person who has obtained the six attainments, the bond of the five cords of sensual pleasure appears like a fallen yellow leaf. Therefore, this was said.

Now, to show the rubbing (nighaṃsa) of a conceited person who has obtained the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), He spoke the words beginning with 'Ṭhānaṃ khေါ panā.' In that text, 'dvedhā bhinnā' refers to a large rock split in the middle. 'Appaṭisandhikā' means that while a small stone the size of a fist can be rejoined by using lac or resin, here it is spoken with reference to a large rock the size of a gabled house. 'Se bhinne' refers to that split. To a person who has obtained the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness, the attainment is like a large rock split in two. Those lower attainments can no longer be rejoined.
36:
## 
For one who has obtained a higher attainment, the lower attainment is like a rock split in two, so the thought 'I will enter that attainment' does not arise. Therefore, this was said.

Now, wishing to show the rubbing of a conceited person who has obtained the attainment of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), He spoke the words beginning with 'Ṭhānaṃ khေါ pana.' In that Pali, 'se vante' means that lower attainment is discarded like vomit. For one who has obtained the eight attainments, the lower attainments appear like vomit, so the thought 'I will enter them again' no longer arises. Therefore, this was said.

Now, wishing to show the rubbing of an Arahant (khīṇāsava), He spoke the words beginning with 'Ṭhānaṃ khေါ pana.' In that Pali, 'se ucchinnamūle' means that person is one whose roots are cut. For one who has obtained a higher attainment, the lower attainment appears like a palm tree cut at the root, so the thought 'I will enter that attainment' no longer arises. Therefore, this was said.

'Ṭhānaṃ khေါ pana' is a separate connection (anusandhi). Although the rubbing of a conceited person and an Arahant who have obtained attainments was told below, the rubbing of a dry-insight (sukkhavipassaka) conceited person and an Arahant has not yet been told. This teaching was begun to show the rubbing of both of them. However, that point is rejected in the Commentary. The reason is that when the rubbing of a conceited person with attainments is told, it is already told for the dry-insight conceited person as well; and when the rubbing of an Arahant with attainments is told, it is already told for the dry-insight Arahant as well. However, this teaching was begun to speak of what is suitable (sappāya) and unsuitable (asappāya) for these two types of monks.

In that regard, there might be an objection: 'Let an object be unsuitable for a worldling (puthujjana), but how is it unsuitable for an Arahant?' Just as it is unsuitable for a worldling, it is also unsuitable for an Arahant. What is called poison is poison whether it is eaten knowingly or unknowingly. Even though one is an Arahant, one should not live unguarded, saying 'I am an Arahant.' An Arahant also ought to live only with diligent effort.

In that Pali, 'samaṇena' refers to the Buddha-Samaṇa. 'Chandarāgabyāpādena' means the fault of poison called ignorance (avijjā) is disturbed and corrupted because of desire-lust and ill-will. 'Asappāyāni' means objects that do not produce growth or welfare. 'Anuddhaṃseyya' means...
37:
It would dry up (wholesome states), it would make them wither. 'Saupādisesaṃ' means remaining with the nature of the poison that has been taken in. In this context, the poison that is taken up is called 'upādi' by the Blessed One. 'Analanca te antarāyāya' means being unable to cause danger to your life. 'Rajosūkaṃ' refers to thorns such as dust and the awns of grain. That ignorance is the very fault of poison. 'Tadubhayena' means due to both the performance of unsuitable actions and the fault of the natural poison. 'Puthuttaṃ' means the state of being great or large.

In the same way, in this context, the fault of the poison of ignorance which has not yet been abandoned should be understood as being like being pierced by an arrow with a residue of poison. The time of being unrestrained in the six sense doors should be understood as being like persisting in unsuitable behavior. Just as one meets death when the fault of the poison in a wound increases, the act of abandoning the training and returning to the low life of a householder should be understood similarly. Just as suffering that is merely enough to cause death, the falling into one or another of the heavy and defiling offenses (āpatti) should be understood. In the case of the wholesome side as well, the comparison between the simile and the thing signified should be understood in this same manner.

In the phrase 'satiyāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ', mindfulness (sati) follows the course of wisdom (paññā). When associated with mundane wisdom, it is mundane mindfulness; when associated with supramundane wisdom, it is supramundane mindfulness. 'Ariyāyetaṃ paññāya' refers to the purified wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā).

Now, wishing to show the power of the Arahant (khīṇāsava), the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'so vata'. In that passage, 'saṃvutakārī' means one who is accustomed to acting with restraint (closing the doors). 'Iti viditvā nirupadhi' means that by knowing thus and abandoning the acquisitions of defilements (kilesupadhi), one becomes free of acquisitions (nirupadhi), meaning one is without grasping. 'Upadhisaṅkhaye vimutto' means liberated by taking Nibbāna, which is the destruction of acquisitions, as an object. 'Upadhismiṃ' refers to the acquisition of sensuality (kāmupadhi). 'Kāyaṃ upasaṃharissati' means he will bring the physical body close (to indulge in it).

This is what is meant: it is impossible for an Arahant, who is liberated by taking Nibbāna—the destruction of craving—as an object, to bring the physical body near or to produce a thought for the sake of indulging in the five cords of sensual pleasure. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, Papañcasūdanī
## The Explanation of the Sunakkhatta Sutta is finished.
38:
## 6. Āneñjasappāyasutta-vaṇṇanā

The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Āneñjasappāya Sutta. In that sutta, "aniccā" (impermanent) means they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. "Kāmā" (sensual pleasures) refers to both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma). "Tucchā" (hollow) means they are empty because they are devoid of any essence of permanence, essence of stability, or essence of self. However, they should not be understood as being non-existent. When one says "tucchamuṭṭhi" (an empty fist), it does not mean that the fist does not exist. If there is nothing inside a fist, that fist is called "tuccha" (empty).

"Musā" means they are destructive. "Mosadhammā" means they have the nature of vanishing. They are not stable like fields, property, gold, and silver appear to be; rather, they perish within a few days like things seen in a dream; they do not remain manifest. Therefore, the Blessed One taught them as "mosadhammā." "Māyākatametaṃ" (this is made of illusion) is like an object shown by magic where water is made to appear as a gem, or a jujube leaf is made to appear as a coin; such deceptive objects appear as such only while one is looking at them (dassanūpacāra), but from the moment one moves beyond that looking, they appear only as they normally are. Similarly, sensual pleasures are called "māyākata" because they appear only for a brief moment. Alternatively, just as a magician deceives by showing water and such as gems and so on, so too sensual pleasures deceive by showing the impermanent and so on as having a permanent nature; thus they are called "māyākata" in the sense of being deceptive.

"Bālalāpanaṃ" (the prattle of fools) is so called because it is the talk and lamentation of fools, such as "my son, my daughter, my gold, my silver." "Diṭṭhadhammikā kāmā" refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure belonging to the human realm. "Samparāyikā" refers to the remaining sensual pleasures belonging to the heavenly realms, excluding those of the human realm. "Diṭṭhadhammikā kāmasaञ्ञā" is the perception that arises in relation to the sensual pleasures of the human realm. "Ubhayametaṃ māradheyyaṃ" means both these sensual pleasures and these perceptions of sensuality are the domain of Māra (māradheyya). Over those who have grasped both of these, Māra exercises his power. With reference to this exercising of power, it is said, "Both of these are the domain of Māra."

In the phrases such as "mārasseva visayo," just as the kingdom of King Coḷa is called Coḷavisaya, the kingdom of King Paṇḍu is called Paṇḍuvisaya, and the kingdom of the Saṃvaras is called Saṃvaravisaya, meaning the place where their power extends, so too Māra exercises his power over those who have grasped these sensual pleasures. With reference to that, it is said, "This is the territory of Māra." Furthermore, Māra goes about scattering the five cords of sensual pleasure like bait (nivāpa) to catch animals. Over those who have taken that bait, Māra exercises his power. With reference to that, it is said, "This is the bait of Māra." And just as a place where elephants and so on exercise their power is called an elephant-range (hatthigocara), a horse-range, or a goat-range...
39:
In this way, those who hold onto these sensual pleasures, Māra can make them follow his will. With reference to this meaning, it is said: "This is the domain (gocara) of Māra."

"Herein" means in these sensual pleasures. "Mānasa" refers to [covetousness, ill-will, and impetuosity] that arise in the mind. In this matter, a question may arise: Let covetousness (abhijjhā), characterized by longing, and impetuosity (sārambha), characterized by excessive action, arise first based on the two kinds of sensual objects (vatthu-kāma and kilesa-kāma); but how does ill-will (byāpāda) arise? People grieve when a cherished object is snatched away or destroyed by others, when it perishes on its own, or when they fear it will be snatched away. Such resentment (āghāta) of the mind is ill-will. Thus, ill-will arises.

"Te va ariyasāvakassa" means "te ariyasāvakassa" (those [defilements] to the noble disciple). The letter "va" is merely an euphonic conjunction (āgama-sandhi). "To one training in this Dispensation" means to one who is still practicing the three trainings (sikkhā) in this Dispensation; those three defilements act as obstacles to him. "Overcoming the world" means overcoming the world of sensual desire (kāma-loka).

"Established by the mind" means being established by the mind that has the jhāna as its object. "Aparitta" (unlimited): Since the sense-sphere mind (kāmāvacara-citta) is called "paritta" (limited), by rejecting it, the lofty (mahaggata) state is called "aparitta". "Pamāṇa" (measure) refers only to the sense-sphere. The fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) are called "appamāṇa" (immeasurable). The name "subhāvita" (well-developed) is not a name for the sense-sphere and so on; it is a name only for the supramundane (lokuttara). Therefore, by the power of this term "subhāvita", all [terms]—aparitta, appamāṇa, and subhāvita—should refer only to the supramundane.

"To one who dwells much in that state" means to one who dwells frequently practicing that very path by restraining sensual pleasures. "The mind is clear in the sphere (āyatana)" means the mind is clear in the cause. What is the cause here? It is either Arahatship, the insight (vipassanā) leading to Arahatship, the fourth jhāna, or the access (upacāra) to the fourth jhāna.

Regarding "when there is clarity (sampasāda)", there are two kinds of clarity: clarity of conviction (adhimokkha-sampasāda) and clarity of attainment (paṭilābha-sampasāda). For one dwelling having initiated insight into Arahatship, when the great elements and so on appear—in whatever manner the great elements appear, the derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) appears, mentality-materiality (nāma-rūpa) appears, causes appear in every way, and insight having the three characteristics as its object appears—the desire "I shall attain Arahatship this very day" remains firm even before it is attained, and one gains conviction (adhimokkha). Or, for one who, having made the third jhāna the basis, performs the preliminary work (parikamma) for the kasiṇa for the sake of the fourth jhāna, and sees the abandonment of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so on—in whatever manner the hindrances are abandoned, the defilements subside, and mindfulness remains firm. Or, when the formations (saṅkhāra) become particularly clear, just as the next world appears to one with the divine eye...
40:
...appears. The occurrence of the mind is concentrated by way of access (upacāra), as if sticking to a sticky mass. The desire "I shall produce the fourth jhāna this very day" remains firm even before it is attained, and one gains conviction. This is called "clarity of conviction" (adhimokkha-sampasāda). When that clarity exists, for the person who attains either Arahatship or the fourth jhāna, his mind is indeed very clear. In this Dispensation, according to the words "the mind is clear in the sphere", the attainment of insight into Arahatship and the attainment of the access to the fourth jhāna should be understood as "clarity of attainment" (paṭilābha-sampasāda). This is because insight is the cause for the resolution of wisdom (Arahatship), and access is the cause for the imperturbable attainment (fourth jhāna).

"Now he enters the imperturbable attainment, or he resolves by wisdom"—here, the meaning should be understood by reversing the terms: "Now he resolves by wisdom, or he enters the imperturbable attainment." This means: when that clarity exists, he now resolves by wisdom, meaning he realizes Arahatship. One who is unable to reach that Arahatship enters the imperturbable attainment. Or, "resolves by wisdom" means developing the path of Arahatship; one who is unable to reach that path of Arahatship enters the imperturbable attainment. One who is unable to develop the path of Arahatship now realizes the Four Truths (through the lower paths). One who is unable to realize them thus enters the imperturbable attainment.

In this matter, there is this method: In this Dispensation, a monk, having made the third jhāna the basis, performs the preliminary work for the kasiṇa for the fourth jhāna. For that monk, the hindrances are abandoned, mindfulness remains firm, and the mind is concentrated by way of access. He discerns materiality and mentality, discerns the causes, and defines insight that has the three characteristics as its object. To that monk, the thought arises: "Through access, the jhāna partaking of distinction (visesabhāgiya) may arise for me; let the state of partaking of distinction be; I shall make this state partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) [Arahatship]." Thus, he increases insight and realizes Arahatship. By this much, his task is said to be completed. But the monk who is unable to realize Arahatship, having a mind that recoils from that Arahatship, does not stop in between but enters the fourth jhāna itself. How? For example, a man takes a spear and pursues [a wild buffalo], thinking "I will kill the wild buffalo." If he can kill that buffalo, he will please all the villagers. But if he cannot, he kills small animals like rabbits and monitor lizards along the way, fills his carrying pole, and returns. It is just like that.
41:
In this context, just as a man holding a spear follows a wild buffalo in the forest, it should be understood that this monk, making the third jhāna the basis, performs the preliminary work for the fourth jhāna. Just as killing the wild buffalo, it should be understood that he develops insight (vipassanā) and realizes the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), thinking: 'For one who observes the abandonment of the hindrances and so forth, the distinction-partaking (visesabhāgiya) jhāna may arise; let the state of distinction-partaking be; I will make it penetration-partaking (nibbedhabhāgiya) [the fruit of Arahantship].' Just as a man unable to kill the buffalo kills small animals like rabbits and iguanas along the way to fill his carrying pole and proceeds, it should be understood that a monk unable to realize the fruit of Arahantship falls back from that and enters the fourth jhāna. The same method applies to the development of the path (magga-bhāvanā) and the realization of the Four Noble Truths.

Now, wishing to show the place of rebirth for one who is unable to realize the fruit of Arahantship, He spoke the words beginning with 'Kāyassa bhedā' (with the breakup of the body). Therein, 'yaṃ' means that because of a certain cause, that consciousness leading to rebirth would reach the imperturbable (āneñja, the fourth jhāna); the meaning is that such a cause exists. Here too, 'taṃ saṃvattanikaṃ' refers to the consciousness leading to rebirth for that monk; it means the resultant rebirth-linking consciousness by which that monk is reborn (nibbattati). 'Āneñjūpagaṃ' means it would reach the nature of the wholesome imperturbable; the meaning is that it would be just like that. Some teachers say it is the wholesome consciousness (kusala-viññāṇa). If the wholesome consciousness, which is the cause of rebirth for that monk, reaches the imperturbable, it would have that same name even at the time of producing its result; this is the meaning. This meaning should be understood by the following method: 'If one performs a meritorious formation, consciousness reaches the meritorious. If one performs a demeritorious formation, consciousness reaches the demeritorious. If one performs an imperturbable formation, consciousness reaches the imperturbable' (SN 12.51). 'Āneñjasappāyā' refers to the practice suitable for the imperturbable, known as the fourth jhāna. It should be understood that this practice is not only suitable for the imperturbable but is also beneficial and suitable for the higher fruit of Arahantship. Thus, in this first imperturbable attainment, falling back by the power of concentration (samādhi) is described.

'Iti paṭisañcikkhati' means that having reached the fourth jhāna, he reflects in this way. Indeed, this monk is wiser than the monk mentioned below; he contemplates by combining both the other monk's meditation subject and his own. 'Tabbahulavihārino' refers to one who dwells frequently performing that same practice by restraining form. Āneñjaṃ...
42:
'Samāpajjati' means entering the imperturbable attainment of the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana). The rest is the same as what was said before. Just as shown here, I will mention only the distinctive points in all other places as well. Thus, in this second imperturbable attainment, falling back by the power of insight (vipassanā) is described. The meaning is that it is described while showing the path of insight with the words 'Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ' (Whatever form...).

'Iti paṭisañcikkhati' means that having reached the Sphere of Infinite Space, he reflects in this way. This monk is wiser than the two monks mentioned below. He contemplates by combining the meditation subjects of those two monks and his own, these three monks together. 'Ubhayametaṃ aniccaṃ' (Both these are impermanent) — in this context, the eight groups are summarized as 'both' by way of the present and the future. 'Nālaṃ abhinandituṃ' means it is not fit to be delighted in by the power of craving and views. In the remaining two phrases, the same method should be understood. 'Tabbahulavihārino' refers to one who dwells frequently performing that same practice by restraining sensual desire and form. 'Āneñjaṃ samāpajjati' means entering the imperturbable attainment of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). In this third imperturbable attainment, falling back by the power of insight is described.

'Iti paṭisañcikkhati' means that having reached the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, he reflects in this way. This monk is wiser than the three monks mentioned below. He contemplates by combining the meditation subjects of those three monks and his own, these four monks together. 'Yatthetā aparisesā nirujjhanti' means that having reached a certain Sphere of Nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), all those perceptions mentioned below cease without remainder. 'Etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītaṃ' means it is peaceful because of the peacefulness of the jhāna factors and the peacefulness of the object; it is sublime (paṇīta) in the sense of being difficult to be satiated with. 'Tabbahulavihārino' refers to one who dwells frequently performing that same practice by restraining those perceptions. In this first section on the Sphere of Nothingness, falling back by the power of concentration is described.

'Iti paṭisañcikkhati' means that having reached the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness itself, he reflects in this way. This monk is wiser than the four monks mentioned below. He contemplates by combining the meditation subjects of those four monks and his own, these five monks together. 'Attena vā attaniyena vā' means it is empty, void, and hollow of the sense of being 'I' or 'what belongs to me'. Thus, here, emptiness with two aspects is shown. 'Tabbahulavihārino' refers to one who dwells frequently performing the practice mentioned below and this practice of emptiness. In this second section on the Sphere of Nothingness, falling back by the power of insight is described.
43:
"Thus he reflects" means that having reached the wholesome jhāna of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, he reflects in this way. This monk possesses greater wisdom than the five monks mentioned below. He contemplates by combining the meditation subjects of those five monks and his own, making six in total. In the passage, "I am not anywhere for anyone in anything, nor is there anything of mine anywhere in anything," the fourfold emptiness (catu-koṭika suññatā) is taught.

How so? "I am not anywhere" means he does not see a self anywhere. "For anyone in anything" means he does not see his own self as something to be brought into the state of being something for another, such as a brother, a friend, or an attendant. It means he does not see the nature of approaching and taking himself to be a brother in the place of a brother, a companion in the place of a companion, or an attendant in the place of an attendant. In the phrase "nor is there anything of mine anywhere," setting aside the word "mine" (mama) for a moment, it means he does not see another's self anywhere. Now, including the word "mine," "nor is there anything of mine in anything" means he does not see another's self as existing in the state of being something of his own concern. It means he does not see the nature of another's self—referred to as a brother in the place of a brother, a companion in the place of a companion, or an attendant in the place of an attendant—as something to be brought into this state of his own concern.

Thus, because this monk does not see a self anywhere, does not see a self to be brought into another's concern, does not see another's self, and does not see another's self to be brought into his own concern, this emptiness should be understood as fourfold emptiness (catu-koṭika suññatā). "One who dwells much in that practice" refers to one who dwells frequently practicing the aforementioned path and this fourfold emptiness. In this third section on the Sphere of Nothingness, the receding (of the mind) is also taught by the power of insight (vipassanā) alone.

"Thus he reflects" means that having reached the jhāna of the Sphere of Nothingness, he reflects in this way. This monk possesses greater wisdom than the six monks mentioned below. He contemplates by combining the meditation subjects of those six monks and his own, making seven in total. "Where these perceptions cease without remainder" means that having reached the jhāna of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, all the aforementioned perceptions cease here. "One who dwells much in that practice" refers to one who dwells frequently practicing that very path by restraining those perceptions. In this section on the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, the receding (of the mind) is taught by the power of concentration (samādhi).

"If it were not, it would not be for me" means if I had not previously exerted effort in the fivefold round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa), then this current fivefold round of resultants (vipāka-vaṭṭa) would not be for me. This round of resultants for me...
44:
...would not be, would not occur. “It will not be” means: if the fivefold round of kamma is not accumulated now. “It will not be for me” means: in the absence of that, the fivefold round of result will not be for me in the future. “What is, what has come to be, that I abandon” means: I abandon the present group of five aggregates that is manifest and has come to be. “Thus he gains equanimity” means that the monk thus gains the equanimity of insight (vipaśyanupekkhā).

“Venerable Sir, would that monk attain final Nibbāna or not?” Why is this asked? The Blessed One has already taught the attainment of Arahantship, the receding, the practice, and the rebirth of a monk who stands based on the third jhāna. Likewise, He taught for those based on the fourth jhāna and so on. However, for a monk who stands based on the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, He said nothing; therefore, the question is asked in reference to that monk. “Apettha” should be resolved as “api ettha.” “He delights in that equanimity” means he greatly delights in that equanimity of insight through the delight of craving and views. The same method applies to the remaining two terms (abhivadati, āsāyati). “Consciousness is dependent on that” means consciousness occurs dependent on insight. “That is his clinging” means that the consciousness of attachment (nikanti-viññāṇa) is called his clinging or grasping in that insight. “With clinging” refers to a monk who has clinging toward insight. “He does not attain final Nibbāna” means that a monk who has attachment to insight in my Dispensation does not attain final Nibbāna. As for a monk who has attachment to monasteries, precincts, or supporters, it goes without saying that they cannot attain the path and fruit. “Where then?” means in what kind of realm or existence? “Clinging, he clings” means the monk taking rebirth clings to existence. “Venerable Sir, that monk is said to cling to the best clinging” means that monk clings to the best and highest existence, which is the realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception; he takes rebirth in that best existence. By this Pali, the rebirth of that monk is taught. Now, to teach his attainment of Arahantship, the words beginning with “Idha Ānanda” are spoken.

“Depending, depending” means depending on various meditative attainments (samāpatti). “The crossing of the flood is declared” means the crossing of the flood is taught. Venerable Ānanda means that the crossing of the flood is taught for a monk based on the third jhāna... and for a monk based on the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.

“Venerable Sir, what is the Noble Liberation (ariya vimokkha)?” What is being asked here? A monk who develops insight based on a meditative attainment and attains Arahantship is like a person crossing a great flood and reaching the other shore by depending on a boat or a raft; he does not struggle. However, a dry-insight monk (sukkhavipassaka), when contemplating the conditioned phenomena and attaining Arahantship, is like a person crossing the flood and reaching the other shore by the strength of his arms; he struggles. Therefore, this is an inquiry about the Arahantship of the dry-insight practitioner. “Noble disciple” (ariya-sāvaka) refers to the noble disciple who is a dry-insight practitioner. Indeed, this noble disciple who is a dry-insight practitioner...
45: ...does not get tired. However, the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka), while contemplating the miscellaneous formations (saṅkhāras) to attain the fruit of Arahantship, gets very tired, like a person crossing to the other shore by cutting through the current with the strength of his arms. Thus, Venerable Ānanda asked, "I ask about the Arahantship of this dry-insight practitioner." "Noble disciple" (ariyasāvaka) refers to the noble disciple who is a dry-insight practitioner. This dry-insight practitioner possesses greater wisdom than the eight monks mentioned earlier. He contemplates by combining the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) of those eight monks and his own, making nine meditation subjects in total. "This is sakkāya, as far as sakkāya extends" means he contemplates that whatever sakkāya exists, known as the round of rebirth in the three planes (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa), all of it is this sakkāya; there is no other sakkāya beyond this. "This is the Deathless (Amata), namely the liberation of the mind through non-clinging (vimokkha)" means he contemplates that whatever is called the liberation of the mind through non-clinging, that fruit of Arahantship is the essence of the Deathless, it is peaceful, it is sublime. Although in other suttas the phrase "anupādā cittassa vimokkho" refers to Nibbāna, in this sutta, it refers to the Arahantship of the dry-insight practitioner. The remaining words are clear in all respects. Specifically, in this sutta, it should be understood that receding (osakkanā) is mentioned in seven instances, rebirth (paṭisandhi) in eight instances, and Arahantship in nine instances. How? For a monk established with the third jhāna as a basis, receding, rebirth, and Arahantship are taught. Likewise for the fourth jhāna and the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). For the three monks established with the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) as a basis, receding, rebirth, and Arahantship are taught. Likewise for the monk established with the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) as a basis. For the one established with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) as a basis, there is no receding; only rebirth and Arahantship are taught. For the dry-insight practitioner, only Arahantship is taught. Thus, it should be understood that receding is taught in seven places, rebirth in eight places, and Arahantship in nine places. By combining these seven instances of receding, eight of rebirth, and nine of Arahantship, this Anāñjasappāya Sutta is well-expounded. ## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, ## the Explanation of the Anāñjasappāya Sutta is finished.
46: ## 7. Explanation of the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta. Therein, "yāva pacchimasopānakalevarā" means up to the plank laid at the head of the first step of the stairs. It is not possible to build a seven-storied palace in a single day. From clearing the ground and erecting the pillars to the final painting work, the gradual process of action (anupubbakiriyā) is evident in the construction of this palace. "Yadidaṃ ajjhayane" means it is also not possible to learn the three Vedas in a single day. It is shown that in the study of these Vedas, only gradual action is evident. "Issatthe" means in the art of weaponry, the skill of hitting a hair's tip (vālavedhī) cannot be mastered in a single day. Through taking the stance, gripping the bow, etc., gradual action is evident in this art of archery as well. "Saṅkhāne" means by calculation (the art of numbers). Wishing to show the gradual process in that art of numbers himself, he said "Thus they are made to count," and so on. In the words "Seyyathāpi brāhmaṇa," the Blessed One, because people who learn arts in external sects become deceitful and crooked, wished to compare his teaching not with external sects but with a noble thoroughbred horse, and thus said "Seyyathāpi," and so on. If a noble thoroughbred horse is trained in a certain skill such as being bridled, it does not transgress that training even for the sake of its life. In the same way, a son of good family who practices rightly in the Dispensation does not transgress the boundary of virtue (sīla). "Mukhādhāne" means placing the bit in the mouth. "Sati-sampajaññāya ca" means for the sake of being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension. There are two types of Arahants: those who habitually dwell in the attainment of the fruit (satatavihārī) and those who do not habitually dwell in it (no-satatavihārī). Between these two, the Arahant who habitually dwells in it can enter the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti) even while performing various construction tasks (navakamma). However, the Arahant who does not habitually dwell in it, being preoccupied with even a small task, is unable to enter the attainment of the fruit. Regarding this inability, there is this story: An Elder Arahant went to live in the forest, taking a novice Arahant with him. In that forest monastery, a dwelling was obtained for the Great Elder, but not for the novice. The Elder, worrying about the novice not having a dwelling, was unable to enter the attainment of the fruit for even a single day. The novice, however, spent the three months of the rainy season delighting in the attainment of the fruit and said, "Venerable Sir, living in the forest is very suitable..."
47:
(Is living in the forest suitable?) he asked the Elder. The Elder replied, "Friend, it is not suitable." In this way, to show that an Arahant of such nature would be able to enter meditative attainments only after reflecting sequentially on these states starting from virtue and so on, the Buddha taught: "Sati-sampajaññāya ca" (And with mindfulness and clear comprehension).

"Yeme bho Gotama" means that while the Blessed One was teaching, the method became clear to the Brahmin Gaṇakamoggallāna: "These individuals do not succeed in the fruit of Arahantship, but these individuals do succeed." To show this, he began to speak in this manner.

"Paramajjadhammesu": What is called "Ajja-dhamma" refers to the teachings of the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa. The meaning is that among those views, the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama alone is the most supreme. The remaining words are clear in every instance.

## Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya
## The Explanation of the Gaṇakamoggallāna Sutta is Finished.

## 8. Gopakamoggallāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta. In that sutta, "Aciraparinibbute bhagavati" (When the Blessed One had not long attained Parinibbāna) refers to the time when the Sangha had arrived at Rājagaha to conduct the Dhamma Council after the distribution of the relics. 

"Rañño pajjotassa āsaṅkamāno" (Apprehensive of King Pajjota): This king named Caṇḍapajjota was a close friend of King Bimbisāra. From the time he sent for the physician Jīvaka to treat him, they became firm friends. When King Caṇḍapajjota heard that "Ajātasattu has killed his father after listening to the words of Devadatta," he spoke in the midst of his assembly: "This Ajātasattu thinks he will rule after killing my dear friend; I will let him know that my friend still has friends." Hearing this, apprehension arose in King Ajātasattu. Therefore, it is said: "Rañño pajjotassa āsaṅkamāno."

"Kammanto" refers to the worksite outside the city for the purpose of repairing the city. 

"Upasaṅkami": Venerable Ānanda approached him thinking, "We are moving about to conduct the Dhamma and Vinaya Council, and this Gopakamoggallāna is influential and a favorite of the king; if he is well-treated, he might provide protection for the Veḷuvana monastery."

"Tehi dhammehi" means by those qualities of the knowledge of omniscience. 

"Sabbena sabbaṃ" means entirely in every aspect. "Sabbathā sabbaṃ" means (it is reflected upon as) entirely in every way.
48:
When King Ajātasattu heard that he was about to kill his own dear friend Bimbisāra to become king, King Caṇḍapajjota said in the midst of the assembly, "I shall let it be known that my friend King Bimbisāra still has friends to rely on." When King Ajātasattu heard those words, he became fearful and terrified. Therefore, the teachers of the Council said, "Being fearful of King Caṇḍapajjota."

While going to the workplace outside the city of Rājagaha for renovations, Venerable Ānanda approached him, thinking, "We are traveling to conduct the Dhamma and Vinaya Council. This brahmin Gopakamoggallāna is powerful and influential, and also intimate with the King. If we honor him, he will protect the Veḷuvana Monastery." (Does he know) everything in every aspect through the qualities of the knowledge of omniscience? He asked, considering, "What is he asking?"

To elaborate on this matter: The six teachers initially went forth from obscure families. These teachers passed away while the Blessed One was still alive. Their disciples also went forth from obscure families. After their teachers passed away, those disciples engaged in great disputes. However, the ascetic Gotama went forth from a noble family. The saying, "When that Venerable One passes away, there will be great disputes among his disciples," spread throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. While the Fully Enlightened One was alive, there were no disputes among the monks. Even if there were, they were settled right then and there.

However, at the time of the Parinibbāna: "Where can an old leaf stand before a storm that can blow away even Mount Sineru, which is 6,800,000 yojanas high? How would the shameless King of Death feel shame before the Teacher who fulfilled the ten perfections and attained the knowledge of omniscience?" Thus, having developed a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the monks became exceedingly united and exceptionally peaceful. He asked, wanting to know, "Why is there such unity?"

"Being recognized" (anusaññāyamāno) means knowing repeatedly, knowing what has been done and what is yet to be done, or reflecting repeatedly.

With the phrase "Is there indeed?" (atthi nu kho), this brahmin Vassakāra also asked the same question that the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna had asked below. He asked, "In this Dhamma and Vinaya which is without a refuge, what is the cause of your unity? What is the support?" "Having the Dhamma as refuge" (dhamma-paṭisaraṇā) indicates that the Dhamma alone is our refuge, the Dhamma alone is our support.

"Proceeds" (pavattati) means existing through mastery and oral recitation. "There is an offense, a transgression" (āpatti hoti vītikkamo) means both falling into an offense and committing a transgression are violations of the Buddha's authority. "We act according to the Dhamma, according to the instruction" (yathādhammaṃ yathānusiṭṭhaṃ kārema) means we act according to how the Dhamma and the instructions are established.

In both phrases "Indeed, the masters do not make us act; the Dhamma makes us act" (na kira no bhavanto kārenti dhammo no kāreti), the word "no" is merely a particle. Therefore, the meaning here is: "It is not that you sirs make us act, but the Dhamma itself makes us act."

"Indeed" (taggha) is a particle meaning "certainly." The question "Where is the Master Ānanda?" was not asked because he did not know the Elder was staying at Veḷuvana; he knew. He asked because he wanted to praise himself, as he himself was providing protection for Veḷuvana. One day, Vassakāra the brahmin saw the Elder Mahākaccāna descending from Gijjhakūṭa Mountain and (insulted him by saying), "This monk looks just like a monkey."
49:
The Brahmin Vassakāra had provided protection for the Veluvana Grove; therefore, wishing to exalt himself, he asked the question. Why did that Brahmin provide protection there? It is said that one day, seeing the Elder Mahākaccāyana descending from Gijjhakūṭa Hill, he said, "This one is like a monkey." When the Blessed One heard those words, he said, "If he asks for forgiveness, it is well. If he does not, he will be reborn as a monkey with a tail like a plow-head in this Veluvana Grove." When the Brahmin heard this, he thought, "The words of the recluse Gotama are never ambiguous; in the future, when I become a monkey, this will be my foraging ground." Thus, he had various trees planted in Veluvana and provided protection. Later, after passing away, he was reborn as a monkey in that very grove. When called by the name "Vassakāra," he would come and stand nearby. The word "taggha" is an indeclinable particle meaning "certainly" in all instances. The statement "Certainly, O Ānanda" was made because the Elder knew he was being exalted by the Brahmin in the midst of the assembly, and thinking, "I too shall exalt the Elder," he spoke thus.

In saying, "Not so, O Brahmins," the Elder thought: "The Fully Enlightened One has taught both praised jhāna and unpraised jhāna. But this Brahmin misrepresents the matter by saying the Buddha praises all jhāna. It is not right to look to his face [seek his favor] or to be concerned about protecting one's alms-food; I shall answer the question directly." Thus he began to speak. "Antaraṃ karitvā" means having made it internal. By the words, "Brahmin, that Blessed One praised such a jhāna," the jhāna that encompasses all is spoken of in this sutta.

Regarding the phrase "Which we...", it is said that this Brahmin Gopakamoggallāna was envious of the Brahmin Vassakāra. Therefore, although he expected that the question asked by Vassakāra would not be answered, upon realizing it had been answered, he became displeased, thinking: "He answered the question asked by Vassakāra in detail, repeatedly mentioning his name. But the question asked by me, he answered only partially, as if pressing down with the tip of a staff." Thus he spoke. The meaning of the remaining words is clear and easy to understand in every respect.

## The Commentary on the Gopakamoggallāna Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
50:
## 9. Commentary on the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta
This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta. Therein, "tadahu" means on that day, on that date. It is called "uposatha" because they dwell here fully [in virtue]. "Upavasanti" means they dwell endowed with virtue or by fasting.

To extract the specific meanings of this term "uposatha": In passages such as "Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the uposatha," the recitation of the Pātimokkha is called uposatha. In passages such as "Visākhā, the uposatha endowed with eight factors is observed," virtue (sīla) is called uposatha. In passages such as "For the pure, it is always the Phagguna; for the pure, it is always the uposatha," fasting (upavāsa) is called uposatha. In passages such as "The Naga King named Uposatha," a designation or name is called uposatha. In passages such as "Monks, on that uposatha day, residences with monks...," the day on which the observance should be kept is called uposatha. In this sutta as well, that very uposatha day is intended. That uposatha day is of three kinds: the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth. Therefore, to exclude the other two days, it is said "pannarase" (on the fifteenth). Thus it is said, "It is called uposatha because they dwell fully on this day." "Puṇṇā" means full or complete due to the fullness of the month. The word "mā" refers to the moon; since it is full on this night, it is called "puṇṇamā". Thus the meaning of these two words "puṇṇāya puṇṇamāyā" should be understood.

"Desaṃ" means the cause. Why did the Blessed One, instead of teaching the monk while he was standing, have him sit down, saying, "Therefore, monk, sit in your own seat and ask"? It is said that this unnamed monk was the senior of a group of sixty monks practicing meditation. He took those sixty monks and lived in the forest. They took meditation subjects from him and strove and exerted themselves. They grasped the great elements (mahābhūta), the derived materiality (upādārūpa), and insight (vipassanā) characterized by the causes, characteristics, and objects of mind and matter. Then, when they came to attend to their teacher and sat down after paying homage, the Elder questioned them on the grasping of the great elements and so on. They could answer everything, but when asked questions regarding the paths and fruits (magga-phala), they were unable to answer. Then the Elder thought: "There is no decline in my instruction to these monks, and they live with stirred-up energy. They are not negligent even for the time it takes a cock to drink water. Yet, they are unable to produce the paths and fruits. I do not know their inclinations; they must be those who can only be disciplined by the Buddha. I will take them to the Teacher, and the Teacher will teach them the Dhamma according to their temperaments." Thus, he took those monks and came to the Teacher.
51:
The Blessed One, in the evening, having taken the water brought by the Venerable Ānanda and having bathed his body, sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the precinct of the Migāramātupāsāda (Visākhā’s mansion). The Saṅgha of monks also sat surrounding the Blessed One.

At that time, the sun was setting and the moon was rising. The Blessed One sat in the center. There was no light from the moon, nor light from the sun. Overpowering the radiance of the moon and sun, the six-colored twin Buddha-rays shone forth, appearing in clusters and radiating throughout all directions. This should be understood in detail according to the method previously mentioned. This is called the 'Ground of Praise for Appearance' (vaṇṇabhūmi). Here, the capacity of the Dhamma-preacher is the measure; he should explain as much as he is able. It should not be said that it is poorly spoken. While the assembly was thus seated together, the Venerable Ānanda rose and requested the Blessed One for the opportunity to ask a question.

Then the Blessed One thought: "If this Ānanda asks while standing, the other monks will think, 'Our teacher has stood up,' and they too will stand. If this happens, it will be an act of disrespect toward the Tathāgata. If the monks remain sitting while their teacher asks while standing, it will be an act of disrespect toward the teacher. In that case, they will not be able to receive the Dhamma teaching with a concentrated mind. Only when the teacher, Ānanda, is seated will those monks also remain seated. Only then will they be able to receive the Dhamma teaching with a concentrated mind." For this reason, the Blessed One did not speak to the standing Ānanda but made him sit down.

The words "Venerable Sir, these things..." were spoken as if asking out of doubt. However, the Venerable Ānanda, having contemplated the arising and passing away of the five aggregates and having attained the fruit of Arahantship, was a great khīṇāsava (one whose taints are destroyed) and had no doubt. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to ask as if one does not know, even though one knows. For if one asks as if one knows, the respondent, thinking "This person already knows," might only explain a portion. But if one asks as if one does not know, the respondent will bring reasons from various texts and explain clearly. Some people, though they do not know, ask as if they do. How could the Venerable Ānanda ever do such a thing? It should be understood that he was asking as if he did not know, while in fact he knew.

"Chandamūlaka" means rooted in craving (taṇhā). "May I be of such an appearance" means if one wishes to be of a fair complexion, one might long, "May I be like the color of yellow orpiment or like the color of realgar." If one wishes to be of a dark complexion, one might long, "May I be like the color of a blue lotus, the color of collyrium, or the color of a jasmine flower." "May I have such a feeling" means longing to have a wholesome feeling or a pleasant feeling. The same method should be understood for the aggregates of perception and so on.
52:
One longs. If one wishes to be of a dark complexion (as a king, brahmin, etc.), one longs, "If only I were like the color of a blue lotus, or the color of collyrium, or the color of a flax flower, how good it would be!" "One of such feeling" means longing for a wholesome feeling or a pleasant feeling. The same method applies to other aggregates such as perception. This is because there is no such thing as longing for the past; even if one longs, one cannot obtain that past aggregate. Nor can it happen in the present (as one longs). Indeed, a fair person cannot become a dark person in the present just by longing, nor can a dark person become fair, nor a tall person become short, nor a short person become tall. However, for one who gives gifts or undertakes virtue and longs, "In the future, may I be a khattiya (noble) or a brahmin," that longing will be fulfilled. Therefore, the Blessed One took only the future aggregate.

"Khandhādhivacana" (designation of aggregates) is a question asking: "By how much meaning does the designation of the aggregates occur?"

In the phrase "Mahābhūta hetu" (the great elements are the cause), in passages such as "the three wholesome roots (hetu)," the term "hetu" is used in the sense of cause. Ignorance (avijjā) is called a "common cause" (sādhāraṇa-hetu) because it is associated with all formations such as meritorious formations. Wholesome and unwholesome actions are "supreme causes" (uttama-hetu) in giving their respective results. Here, however, "causal condition" (paccaya-hetu) is intended. Therein, the great element of the earth element is both the cause and the condition for the designation and the discernment through wisdom of the other three elements and derived matter (upādā-rūpa). The application should be understood in the same way for the remaining terms.

"Phassa" (contact) means that according to the teaching, "Monks, one who has made contact feels, one who has made contact perceives, one who has made contact intends," contact is both the cause and the condition for the designation of the three aggregates (feeling, perception, and formations). In the term "viññāṇakkhandhassa" (of the aggregate of consciousness), first, along with the rebirth-consciousness, for beings in the womb, thirty types of matter and the three associated aggregates arise in the upper limit. That mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) is both the cause and the condition for the designation of the rebirth-consciousness. In the eye-door, the eye-sensitivity and the visible object are called "materiality" (rūpa), and the three associated aggregates are called "mentality" (nāma). That mentality-materiality is both the cause and the condition for the designation of the eye-consciousness. The same method applies to the remaining types of consciousness.

"Venerable Sir, how is it?"—these words were spoken by the wanderer (paribbājaka) wishing to ask about the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) in terms of its extent. "Sakkāyadiṭṭhi does not occur"—these words were spoken by the wanderer wishing to ask about the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa/Nirvana).
53:
By the phrase "Ayaṃ rūpe assādo" (This is the gratification in form), both the penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha) and the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) are taught. By the phrase "Ayaṃ rūpe ādīnavo" (This is the danger in form), both the penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha) and the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) are taught. By the phrase "Idaṃ rūpe nissaraṇaṃ" (This is the escape from form), both the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha) and the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) are taught. In these three truths, there are states such as right view and so on; this collection of states is the truth of the path (magga-sacca), known as the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

"Bahiddhā" (externally) refers to the body of another which possesses consciousness. By the word "sabbanimittesu" (in all signs), it also includes inanimate matter (anindriyabaddha). Alternatively, by the phrase "saviññāṇake kāye" (in the body with consciousness), both one's own body and the bodies of others are taken; and by taking "bahiddhā" and "sabbanimitta," inanimate matter is included.

"Anattakatāni" means deeds done by standing in [the view of] non-self. "Kamatthānaṃ phusissanti" (In what self will they touch [the result]?) is said by one who falls into the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi), thinking, "In what kind of self will they reside to show the result?" "Taṇhādhipateyyena" means by a mind governed by craving. "Tatra tatra" means in those various states. "Saṭṭhimattānaṃ" (about sixty) refers to these sixty bhikkhus who, giving up their original meditation subject and contemplating a new meditation subject, attained Arahatship in that very seat without breaking their cross-legged posture. The remaining words are clear in all places.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta is finished.

## 10. Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta Vaṇṇanā

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Cūḷapuṇṇama Sutta (The Lesser Discourse on the Full Moon). Therein, "tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ" (silent, silent) means that in whichever direction he looked, there was only silence. "Anuviloketvā" (having looked around) means having opened the eyes adorned with the five types of sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa) and looking here and there, seeing that there was not even the slightest movement of hands or feet. "Asappurisa" means a bad person. "No hetaṃ, bhante" (Not so, venerable sir) was said because, just as a blind man cannot know another blind man, that bad person cannot know another bad person. In this same way, the meaning should be understood in the subsequent sections. "Assaddhamma-samannāgato" means being endowed with evil states. "Asappurisa-bhatti" means having devotion to or associating with bad persons.
54: "Asappurisacintī" means one who is habituated to thinking the thoughts of a bad person. "Asappurisamantī" means one who consults in the manner of bad persons. "Asappurisavāco" means one who speaks the speech of bad persons. "Asappurisakammanto" means one who performs the deeds of bad persons. "Asappurisadiṭṭhi" means one who is endowed with the view of bad persons. "Asappurisadānaṃ" means the gift given by bad persons. "Tyāssa mittā" means those who are endowed with states such as lack of shame (ahirika) and so on are the friends of that bad person. Thinking to harm oneself means thinking for one's own suffering thus: "I will kill living beings, I will take what is not given, I will engage in sexual misconduct, I will undertake and practice the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusala-kammapatha)." Thinking to harm others means thinking for the suffering of others thus: "Such and such a person kills such and such a living being, takes the property of such and such a person that is not given, and undertakes and practices the ten courses of unwholesome action; I will command him to do so." Thinking to harm both means thinking for the suffering of both thus: "I will take such and such persons and we all will undertake and practice the ten courses of unwholesome action."##In the phrases such as "consulting to harm oneself," one who consults saying, "I will undertake and practice the ten courses of unwholesome action," is said to consult to harm himself. One who consults saying, "I will make such and such a person undertake the ten courses of unwholesome action," is said to consult to harm others. One who consults with another saying, "We both together will undertake and practice the ten courses of unwholesome action," is said to consult to harm both.##Giving a gift disrespectfully (asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ deti) means showing no respect to either the gift or the recipient. Not respecting the gift means giving food that is defective, such as poorly cooked rice, and not making it pleasing. Not respecting the recipient means giving the gift after making the recipient sit anywhere at all without sweeping the sitting place, and placing whatever support (such as a bowl-rest) is available. "Asahatthā" (not with one's own hand) means not giving with one's own hand but having it given by slaves, workers, and so on. Giving without care (acittīkatvā) means giving without showing respect to either the gift or the recipient as mentioned above. Giving as if discarding (apaviddhaṃ) means giving with a desire to be rid of it, like throwing a snake into an anthill. Giving without a view of the future result (anāgamanadiṭṭhika) means giving without longing for the fruit of the action.
55:
In that context, 'upapajjati' (is reborn) does not mean that one is reborn in hell because of giving gifts (dāna). Rather, because that person holds a bad view and has adopted a wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), he is reborn in hell because of that wrong view. The bright side (sukka-pakkha) should be understood by the method opposite to the dark side already mentioned. The greatness of devas (deva-mahattatā) refers to the devas of the six sensual heavens. The greatness of humans (manussa-mahattatā) refers to the prosperity of the three [noble] families. The rest is clear in all respects. This sutta, however, is taught solely by the power of the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
