## 2. Anupada Vagga
## 1. Commentary on Anupada Sutta
The discourse beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Anupada Sutta. In that sutta, 'etadavoca' refers to the Buddha speaking words of praise regarding the virtues of the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, because he is worthy of praise through methods such as 'paṇḍito' (wise). Why did he speak so? Among the remaining elders, the virtue of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna as being of great psychic power is well-known; the Elder Mahākassapa as a proponent of dhutaṅga practices; the Elder Anuruddha as possessing the divine eye; the Elder Upāli as a bearer of the Vinaya; the Elder Revata as a meditator delighting in jhāna; and the Elder Ānanda as one of great learning. Thus, the respective virtues of those various elders are well-known, but the virtues of the Elder Sāriputta are not well-known. Why? Because the virtues of a wise person are not easy to know without being spoken of. Therefore, the Buddha, intending to 'preach the virtues of Sāriputta,' awaited the assembly of a compatible audience. It is not appropriate to speak of virtues in the presence of incompatible persons, for when virtues are spoken of, they tend to look for faults and speak ill. On this day, seeing that a compatible assembly for the Elder had gathered, the Teacher, desiring to preach his virtues, began this teaching.

In that context, 'paṇḍita' (wise) means one is called wise because of these four reasons: skill in the elements (dhātu), skill in the sense bases (āyatana), skill in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and skill in what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna). In the terms such as 'mahāpañño' (of great wisdom), it means one endowed with great wisdom and so forth.

The distinction of great wisdom and so forth is as follows—among those, what is great wisdom (mahāpaññā)? It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha); it is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha), the aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha). It is called great wisdom because it comprehends the great instances of what is possible and impossible, the great meditative attainments (vihārasamāpatti), the great Noble Truths, the great foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the right efforts (sammappadhāna), the bases of power (iddhipāda), the great faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the great Noble Path, the great fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), the great direct knowledges (abhiññā), and the great ultimate reality, Nibbāna.
57:
What is wide wisdom (puthupaññā)? It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various diverse aggregates. It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various diverse elements, in various diverse sense bases, in various diverse meanings, in various diverse instances of dependent origination, in various diverse natures of emptiness (suññata) and the unfindable (anupalabbha), in various diverse meanings (attha), phenomena (dhamma), language (nirutti), and eloquence (paṭibhāna), in various diverse aggregates of virtue, in various diverse aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, in various diverse instances of what is possible and impossible, in various diverse meditative attainments, in various diverse Noble Truths, in various diverse foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, in various diverse Noble Paths, in fruits of recluseship, in direct knowledges, and because knowledge occurs in the ultimate reality, Nibbāna, having transcended various diverse phenomena common to worldlings.

What is joyous wisdom (hāsapaññā)? Here, some person, being full of joy, full of zest, full of satisfaction, and full of gladness, fulfills virtue, fulfills the restraint of the sense faculties, practices moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, and fulfills the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—this is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy and full of gladness, one penetrates what is possible and impossible; being full of joy, one fulfills meditative attainments—this is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy, one penetrates the Noble Truths. One develops the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Path—this is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy, one realizes the fruits of recluseship and penetrates the direct knowledges—this is called joyous wisdom. Being full of joy, zest, satisfaction, and gladness, one realizes the ultimate reality, Nibbāna—this is called joyous wisdom.

What is swift wisdom (javanapaññā)? Whatever form (rūpa)—past, future, or present... whether far or near—one quickly penetrates and knows all form as impermanent; this is called swift wisdom. One quickly penetrates as suffering... one quickly penetrates as non-self; this is called swift wisdom. All feeling (vedanā)... all consciousness (viññāṇa)—past, future, or present... one quickly penetrates and knows all consciousness as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; this is called swift wisdom. The eye... aging and death—past, future, or present—one quickly penetrates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; this is called swift wisdom. Having weighed, judged, clarified, and made clear that form—past, future, or present—is impermanent in the sense of being subject to destruction, suffering in the sense of being fearful, and non-self in the sense of being coreless, one quickly penetrates and knows Nibbāna, which is the cessation of form; this is called swift wisdom. Feeling, perception, mental formations,
58:
It is called 'swift wisdom' (javana-paññā) because it swiftly penetrates and knows Nibbāna, the cessation of aging and death, by making manifest the states of the past, future, and present—consciousness, the eye, and so forth, up to aging and death—as impermanent, in the sense of being subject to exhaustion, and so forth. It is called 'swift wisdom' because it swiftly penetrates and knows Nibbāna, the cessation of aging and death, by weighing, judging, clarifying, and making manifest the states of the past, future, and present—materiality... consciousness, the eye... up to aging and death—as impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.

What is 'sharp wisdom' (tikkha-paññā)? It is called 'sharp wisdom' because it swiftly cuts through the defilements. It does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought; it does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill-will, an arisen thought of cruelty, nor any evil unwholesome states that repeatedly arise. It is called 'sharp wisdom' because it does not tolerate but abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence arisen greed, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, disparaging, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, stubbornness, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, heedlessness, all defilements, all misconduct, all volitional formations, and all kamma leading to rebirth. The attainment, realization, and seeing through wisdom of the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical insights, and the six higher knowledges in a single sitting is called 'sharp wisdom.'

What is 'penetrative wisdom' (nibbedhika-paññā)? Here, a certain person is full of agitation, full of dread, full of dissatisfaction, full of discontent, and full of aversion towards all formations; being outward-facing, they do not delight in all formations. It is called 'penetrative wisdom' because it penetrates and breaks through the mass of greed that was never before penetrated or broken through. It is called 'penetrative wisdom' because it penetrates and breaks through the mass of hatred, the mass of delusion, anger, resentment... and so forth, up to all kamma leading to rebirth, which were never before penetrated or broken through.

'Insight into states one by one' (anupada-dhamma-vipassanā) means contemplating insight into dhammas in successive order, either by the power of meditative attainments or by the power of jhāna factors. Contemplating in this way, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera reached Arahantship in half a month. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, however, reached it in seven days. Even so, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera was much greater in wisdom. For the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera reached Arahantship after striving for seven days, contemplating only a portion, like one pressing down on the investigative practice of disciples with the tip of a staff. The Venerable Sāriputta Thera, excluding the investigative path of the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, investigated the investigative path of disciples without remainder. Investigating in this way, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera strove for half a month, and upon reaching Arahantship, he realized: 'Except for the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, there will be no other disciple who is able to reach the distinction of wisdom that I have attained.'
59:
He realized: 'Except for the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, there will be no other disciple who is able to reach the distinction of wisdom that I have attained.' For example, just as a man, thinking 'I will take a bamboo staff,' sees a large, tangled bamboo thicket and, thinking 'If I cut through the tangle, it will cause me delay,' reaches his hand into the middle, cuts a bamboo staff that he happens to reach at the base and the tip, and goes away. Although that man goes first, he does not obtain a bamboo staff that has pith or is straight. Another man, seeing such a bamboo thicket, thinks, 'If I only take the bamboo staff I happen to reach, I will not obtain one that has pith or is straight.' He then girds his loins, cuts the bamboo thicket with a large knife, selects bamboo staves that have pith and are straight, and goes away. Although this man goes later, he obtains bamboo staves that have pith and are straight. In this way, the fulfillment of this simile should be understood regarding the striving of these two elders.

Thus, having strove for half a month, the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, while standing and fanning the Buddha as the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being preached to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, at the entrance of the Boar's Cave (Sūkarakhata-leṇa), sent forth his knowledge according to the sequence of the teaching. On the fifteenth day from his ordination, he reached the summit of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, penetrating sixty-seven kinds of knowledge and attaining sixteen-fold wisdom.

'Monks, this is Sāriputta's insight into states one by one'—it is called 'insight into states one by one' because he contemplates insight into states one by one. In that insight into states one by one, the following sequential investigation occurred for the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. This was said now with reference to those various groups of insight.

'In the first jhāna' means those states within the attainment of the first jhāna. 'For him, those states' means for that Venerable Sāriputta, those states. 'Were defined one by one' means they were defined, delimited, known, and understood in successive order. How? When the Elder was looking at those states, he knew: 'Initial application (vitakka), characterized by directing the mind onto the object, occurs.' Likewise, sustained application (vicāra), characterized by examining the object; rapture (pīti), characterized by pervading; bliss (sukha), characterized by pleasantness; one-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā), characterized by non-distraction; contact (phassa), characterized by touching; feeling (vedanā), characterized by experiencing the flavor of the object; perception (saññā), characterized by noting the object; volition (cetanā), characterized by mental urge; consciousness (viññāṇa), characterized by cognizing; desire (chanda), characterized by the wish to act; decision (adhimokkha), characterized by resolve; characterized by upholding...
60:
Energy (vīriya) has the characteristic of supporting; mindfulness (sati) has the characteristic of establishing; equanimity (upekkhā) has the characteristic of neutrality; and attention (manasikāra), which has the characteristic of directing the mind toward the object, occurs—thus he knows. Knowing thus, he defines applied thought (vitakka) according to its nature in the sense of placing [the mind] on the object... he defines attention (manasikāra) according to its nature in the sense of reflecting on the object. Therefore, [the Buddha] said: "Those states were defined by him one by one as they occurred."

"They arise known" means they arise being clearly manifest even as they are arising. "They remain known" means they remain being clearly manifest even as they are present. "They disappear known" means they disappear being clearly manifest even as they are ceasing. Here, however, one must be free from [the fallacies of] self-cognition (taññāṇatā) and multiplicity of knowledge (ñāṇabahutā). Just as it is impossible to touch the tip of a finger with that same finger-tip, so it is impossible to know the arising, presence, or dissolution of a mind with that very same mind. Thus, first, one must be free from self-cognition. If two minds were to arise simultaneously, it might be possible to know the arising, presence, or dissolution of one mind with the other mind. But there is no such thing as two contacts, feelings, perceptions, volitions, or minds arising together; they arise only one by one. Thus, one must be free from the multiplicity of knowledge. If this is so, how is it that for the Great Elder [Sāriputta], sixteen states were clearly known within the attainment? It is because the base (vatthu) and the object (ārammaṇa) had been comprehended. For the Elder had comprehended both the base and the object; therefore, when he adverted to the arising of those states, the arising (uppāda) became manifest; when he adverted to the presence, the presence (ṭhī) became manifest; when he adverted to the breaking, the dissolution (bhaṅga) became manifest. Therefore, it was said: "They arise known, they remain known, they disappear known."

By the phrase "they come into being without having been," he sees the rise (udaya). By the phrase "having been, they vanish," he sees the fall (vaya). "Anupāya" means occurring without approaching through the power of lust. "Anapāya" means occurring without departing through the power of aversion. "Anissita" means unsupported by the supports of craving and views. "Appaṭibaddha" means unfettered by desire and lust. "Vippamutta" means released from sensual lust. "Visamyutta" means detached from the four yogas or from all defilements. "Vimariyādīkata" means made without boundaries [by the absence of boundary-making defilements]. He dwells with such a mind.
61: In that context (regarding 'vimariyādīkatena' etc.), there are two kinds of boundaries (mariyādā): the boundary of defilements and the boundary of objects. If lust and other defilements had arisen in the Venerable Sāriputta regarding the sixteen states occurring within the attainment, he would have made a boundary of defilements. However, since not even one of those defilements arose in him, there is no boundary of defilements. If, while he was adverting to the sixteen states occurring within the attainment, some states did not come into the range [of his mind], then he would have had a boundary of objects. But since there was no state that did not come into the range for him while adverting to those sixteen states, there is also no boundary of objects. There are another two boundaries: the boundary of suppression (vikkhamphana) and the boundary of eradication (samuccheda). Among these, the boundary of eradication will be discussed later. Here, however, the boundary of suppression is intended. Because he has removed the opposing states and is without boundaries, he dwells with a mind free from the defilements and objects that create boundaries. "Uttari nissaraṇaṃ" (further escape) means there is an escape (the second jhāna) beyond this (the first jhāna). Although in other Suttas the term "uttari nissaraṇaṃ" refers to Nibbāna, in this Sutta, it should be understood as the specific [jhāna] occurring immediately after. "Tabbahulīkārā" means because of making that knowledge frequent. "Atthitvevassa hoti" means it occurs more firmly to that Elder that [those states] exist. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining sections as well. In the second section, it is called "sampasāda" (tranquillity) because of the sense of making clear. He defines it according to its nature. In the fourth section, "upekkhā" (equanimity) is just the equanimity of feeling (vedanūpekkhā) in the place of pleasure. "Passaddhattā cetaso anābhogo" (the mind's non-adverting due to tranquility) means: where there is the mind's adverting in those jhānas as "this is indeed pleasant," this [third jhāna] is called "gross" because of that adverting. Thus, because of tranquility, it means the non-adverting of the mind, or the absence of that adverting. "Satipārisuddhi" (purity of mindfulness) is just purified mindfulness. Equanimity is also the equanimity of purity (pārisuddhi-upekkhā). "Sato vuṭṭhahati" (he emerges mindful) means he emerges from the attainment being endowed with mindfulness and knowing clearly with wisdom. "Te dhamme samanupassati" (he contemplates those states): since the insight into states one by one (anupada-dhamma-vipassanā) in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception belongs only to the Buddhas and not to the disciples, he said this to show the insight by groups (kalāpa-vipassanā) here.
62:
"And seeing with wisdom, his taints are exhausted" means that by seeing the Four Noble Truths with the wisdom of the Path, the four taints are exhausted. For the Elder Sāriputta, there are instances where he reached Arahantship by yoking serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā), and there are instances where he entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). In this sutta, the instance of reaching Arahantship is taken. However, it is said that because of his mastery through practice, he would enter cessation again and again in later times.

In that regard, at the time when the attainment of cessation is primary for him, the turn for cessation arrives, and the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) becomes hidden. At the time when the attainment of fruition is primary, the turn for the attainment of fruition arrives, and the attainment of cessation becomes hidden. However, the Elders residing in Jambudīpa say: "The Elder Sāriputta, having yoked serenity and insight, realized the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) and entered cessation; emerging from cessation, he reached Arahantship."

"Te dhamme" refers to the material phenomena produced by the three causes occurring within the attainment, or the states occurring in the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception below. For those states also are phenomena to be contemplated with insight in this section. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said to show that he contemplates those states also with insight.

"Vasippatto" means he has reached mastery through practice. "Pāramippatto" means he has reached completion. In the terms beginning with "Orasa" (breast-born), the Elder is called "Orasa" because he was born from hearing the sound of the teaching produced in the Blessed One's breast. He is called "Mukhato jāta" (born from the mouth) because he was born from hearing the sound manifested through the mouth. Because he was born of the Dhamma, he is "Dhammaja"; because he was created by the Dhamma, he is "Dhammanimmita". Because he takes the inheritance of the supramundane Dhamma, he is "Dhamma-dāyāda"; because he does not take the material inheritance, he is "No āmisadāyāda". The rest of the words are clear in every instance.

## The Explanation of the Anupada Sutta is Finished.

## 2. Chabbisodhana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Chabbisodhana Sutta. In that sutta, among the terms beginning with "Khīṇā jāti" (birth is exhausted), Arahantship is declared by even a single term, or by two. Here, however, the declaration of Arahantship comes by four terms. In "Diṭṭhe diṭṭhavādī" (one who speaks of what is seen as seen) and so forth, the intention by which one says "I have seen" according to the convention of the Noble Ones is called "Diṭṭhe diṭṭhavādī". In the remaining terms such as "Suta" (heard) and so forth, it should be understood in this same way. "Anudhamma" is the natural characteristic of this phenomenon. "Abhinanditabbaṃ" means it is not merely to be delighted in, but rather that all respect should be paid to that Arahant who has attained Parinibbāna. By the term "Uttariṃ pi", it is shown that if the questioning monk is not satisfied with the person's answer, he should ask this question further. In the three sections following this one, it is the same way. "Abalaṃ" means a state that is weak or without core. "Virāgaṃ" means a state characterized by dispassion. "Anassāsikaṃ" means a state devoid of relief. "Upāyūpādāna" are names for craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). Indeed, craving and views attach to the states belonging to the three planes...
63:
The intention by which one says 'I have seen' regarding a seen object is called 'diṭṭhe diṭṭhavādī' (speaking of the seen as seen). In the remaining terms such as 'suta' (heard), etc., the method is the same. 'Ayaṃ anudhamma' means this is the inherent nature of this phenomenon. 'Abhinanditabbaṃ' means not only should one rejoice, but indeed, all forms of respect should be paid to that Arahant who has attained Parinibbāna. 'Uttariṃ pañho' means it is shown that if one is not satisfied with that person's explanation, this question should be asked further. In the three sections that follow, the method is the same.

'Abalaṃ' means weak or without essence. 'Virāguṇaṃ' means a phenomenon characterized by fading away. 'Anassāsikaṃ' means a phenomenon devoid of relief (or breath). 'Upāyupādāna' is a name for craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). Craving and views are called 'upāya' because they approach the phenomena occurring in the three planes, and 'upādāna' because they cling. 'Cetaso adhiṭṭhānābhinivesānusaya' is also a name for that same craving and views. Because the mind stays and is established in the phenomena of the 'existing body' (sakkāya) through craving and views, craving and views are called 'cetaso adhiṭṭhāna' (the mind's foundation). Because the mind enters into them firmly through these, they are called 'abhinivesa' (insistence). Because the mind lies latent in them through these very things, they are called 'anusaya' (latent tendencies). In the terms beginning with 'khayā virāgā,' the meaning is 'through destruction, through dispassion.' All these are merely synonyms for one another.

'Pathavīdhātu' (earth element) is the element of support. 'Āpodhātu' (water element) is the element of cohesion. 'Tejodhātu' (fire element) is the element of ripening. 'Vāyodhātu' (air element) is the element of distension. 'Ākāsadhātu' (space element) is the element that is untouched. 'Viññāṇadhātu' (consciousness element) is the element of cognizing. 'Na anattato upagacchanti' means not approaching in terms of a 'self' (atta) or as 'I,' as a constituent of a self. 'Na ca pathavīdhātunissitaṃ' refers to the remaining three great elements, derived matter (upādā-rūpa), and the mental aggregates (nāma-khandha). Since these phenomena have a material base and are dependent on the earth element, in one sense they are indeed dependent on the earth element. Therefore, by saying 'not dependent on the earth element,' it is meant that one does not approach the remaining material and mental phenomena as a self. In the phrase 'dependent on the space element' (ākāsadhātu-nissita), by way of inseparability, all primary matter, derived matter, and the mental aggregates dependent on that matter are said to be dependent on the space element. Thus, here too, both matter and mind are included. In the phrase 'dependent on the consciousness element' (viññāṇadhātu-nissita), the three co-nascent aggregates and the matter produced by consciousness are dependent on the consciousness element; thus, both matter and mind are included.

In the phrase 'rūpe cakkhuviññāṇe cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbesu dhammesu,' the visible forms that appeared at the eye-door and ceased in the past, those that will appear and cease in the future, and those that appear and cease in the present are called 'rūpa.' 'Cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabba-dhamma' refers to the visible forms that cease without reaching the eye-door in all three periods of time: past, future, and present. When this was stated collectively, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: 'If one distinguishes two types (objects that appear and those that do not) in this eye-door section, how will one handle the section on desire (chanda) above? Such a meaning of objects reaching or not reaching the eye is not found in the world.'
64:
All forms that have entered the range of the eye-door and ceased in the past, those that will enter the range of the eye-door and cease in the future, and those that enter the range of the eye-door and cease in the present, are called 'form' (rūpa). Regarding those forms that cease without entering the range of the eye-door in the past, future, or present—when it was said that all such forms are included in 'dhammas to be known by eye-consciousness' (cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbadhamma), Elder Tipitaka Cūḷābhaya said: "Divide this into two parts at this point; how will you handle the section on desire (chandavāra) above? This (attaining an object that does not appear) is not possible." Therefore, whether it comes into focus or not in the three periods of time, all such form is simply the base of form (rūpāyatana). However, the three aggregates—the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations—associated with eye-consciousness should be understood as 'dhammas to be known by eye-consciousness.' The meaning here is: "Among the dhammas to be known by insight-wisdom together with eye-consciousness."

'Desire' (chanda) means the desire of craving. 'Lust' (rāga) is that same desire of craving in the sense of attachment. 'Delight' (nandī) is that same desire of craving in the sense of rejoicing. 'Craving' (taṇhā) is that same craving in the sense of longing. The same method applies to the remaining doors. In the phrase 'I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency of conceit,' 'I-making' is conceit (māna), 'mine-making' is craving (taṇhā), and that same conceit is the 'underlying tendency of conceit' (mānānusaya). Why was 'knowledge of the destruction of taints' (āsavānaṃ khayañāṇa) mentioned without mentioning the supernormal knowledge of past lives and the divine eye? Because monks do not ask about mundane states, they only ask about supramundane states; therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to answer only the question asked, spoke thus. This sutta is called the Ekavissajjita Sutta; it is also named the Chabbisodhana Sutta. In this sutta, these six categories are purified: the four modes of expression, the five aggregates, the six elements, the six internal and external bases, one's own conscious body, and the conscious bodies of others; therefore, it is called 'Chabbisodhanīya.' However, the Elders living on the other side of the ocean consider one's own and others' conscious bodies as one, and together with the four nutriments, they speak of six categories.

These six categories should be investigated according to the Vinaya-niddesa method: "What have you attained? By what means have you attained? When did you attain? Where did you attain? Which defilements have you abandoned? Of which states are you a possessor?"

Here, "What have you attained?" (kiṃ te adhigataṃ) is a question about attainment (adhigama); it asks which among the jhānas, liberations (vimokkha), etc., or the Path of Stream-entry, etc., have you attained. "By what means have you attained?" (kinti te adhigataṃ) is a question about the method (upāya). The meaning here is: Did you attain by making the mark of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa) the priority, or one of the marks of suffering or non-self? Or did you attain by means of concentration...
65:
...by attending, or by attending through the power of insight (vipassanā)? Likewise, did you attend to materiality (rūpa), or to mentality (arūpa)? Did you attend to the internal (ajjhatta), or to the external (bahiddhā)? Thus it should be asked. "When did you attain?" (kadā te adhigataṃ) is a question about time. It means: At what time—morning, midday, etc.—did you attain?

"Where did you attain?" (kattha te adhigataṃ) is a question about the location. It means: In what location—at the place for the night, the place for the day, at the foot of a tree, in a pavilion, or in which monastery—did you attain? By the phrase "Which defilements have you abandoned?" (katame te kilesā pahīnā), one asks about the abandoned defilements. It means: Which of your defilements, to be abandoned by which Path, have been abandoned?

"Of which states are you a possessor?" (katamesaṃ tvaṃ dhammānaṃ lābhī) is a question about the states acquired. It means: Which states among the first Path, etc., are you a possessor of?

Therefore, even now, if any monk declares the attainment of a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), he should not be honored merely by that declaration. Rather, for the sake of investigation, he should be asked about these six points: "What have you attained? Have you attained a jhāna, or one of the states such as the liberations (vimokkha)?" For the state attained by someone is clear to that person. If he says, "I have attained such-and-such a state," then he should be asked, "How did you attain it?" He should be asked: Among the marks of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa), etc., which did you make the priority? Among the thirty-eight objects, or among the states distinguished as materiality, mentality, internal, external, etc., through which door did you attend and attain? For the manner of attending that someone has is clear to that person.

If he says, "I have such-and-such a manner of attending; I attained in this way," then he should be asked, "When did you attain? Was it in the morning, or at some other time such as midday?" For the time of one's own attainment is always clear to everyone. If he says, "I attained at such-and-such a time," then he should be asked, "Where did you attain? Was it at the place for the day, or at some other location such as the place for the night?" For the location of one's own attainment is always clear to everyone. If he says, "I attained at such-and-such a location," then he should be asked, "Which defilements have you abandoned? Have you abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by the first Path, or those to be abandoned by the second Path, etc.?" For the defilements abandoned by the Path one has attained are clear to everyone.
66:
If he says, "I have abandoned such and such defilements," then he should be asked, "Which states have you attained? Is it the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), or one of the paths such as once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga), and so on?" This is because the state attained by oneself is always clear to all. If he says, "I have attained such and such states," his words should not be believed based on that alone. Monks who are learned and skilled in learning and inquiry are able to investigate these six points. This monk's practice leading to [the Noble Path] should be investigated. If that practice is not pure, it should be rejected, saying, "By such a practice, the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) cannot be attained."

If, however, his practice leading to it is pure, and it is evident that "for a long time he has been diligent in the threefold training, devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and dwells with a mind like the palm of a hand in the open sky," then that monk's answer accords and agrees with his practice. It is like the saying, "Just as the water of the Ganges accords and agrees with the water of the Yamunā, even so, the practice leading to Nibbāna well-prescribed by the Blessed One for his disciples accords and agrees with Nibbāna and the practice" (DN 2.296).

Nevertheless, honor and offerings should not yet be made based merely on this agreement. Why? Because even some worldlings (puthujjana) may have a practice similar to that of an Arahant (khīṇāsava). Therefore, that monk should be frightened by various means. For an Arahant, even if a thunderbolt falls upon his head, there is no fear, trembling, or hair-standing on end. For a worldling, however, fear, trembling, and hair-standing on end can occur even due to a slight cause.

In this regard, there are these stories: It is said that Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, being unable to test a certain alms-gathering monk (piṇḍapātika), gave a signal to a young monk. That young monk dived into the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River where the alms-gathering monk was bathing and grabbed his feet. Thinking it was a crocodile, the alms-gathering monk made a loud cry; at that time, they knew he was a worldling. During the time of King Candamukha Tissa, however, an Arahant elder who was the Sangha-elder at the Mahāvihāra stayed only in the monastery because of weak eyesight. The king, thinking "I will test the elder," approached quietly while the monks had gone for alms and grabbed his feet like a snake. The elder remained motionless like a stone pillar and asked, "Who is there?"
67:
The elder said, "Great King, I am Tissa." The king asked, "Tissa, does the [fragrance of virtue] smell sweet?" Thus, for an Arahant, there is no such thing as fear.

However, some worldlings are also very brave and fearless. Such a person should be tested with an alluring object. King Vasabha, wishing to test a certain elder, invited him to sit in the palace and sat near him crushing jujube fruit to make a drink (badara-sāḷava). Saliva moved in the great elder's mouth; then the elder's status as a worldling became clear. Indeed, for an Arahant, craving for taste (rasataṇhā) is well-abandoned; there is no attachment even to divine tastes. Therefore, having tested him by these means, if fear, trembling, hair-standing on end, or craving for taste arises in that monk, he should be dismissed, saying, "You are not an Arahant." But if he sits like a lion, without fear, trembling, or alarm, and does not produce attachment even to divine objects, then this monk is one whose declaration is accomplished and is worthy of the honor and offerings sent from various directions by kings, royal ministers, and others.

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī
## The Explanation of the Chabbisodhana Sutta is finished.
## 3. The Explanation of the Sappurisa Dhamma Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ," etc., is the Sappurisa Dhamma Sutta. In that sutta, "sappurisa-dhamma" means the qualities of good people. "Asappurisa-dhamma" means the qualities of bad people. Having thus set out the table of contents (mātikā), just as a man skilled in the road leaves the left path and takes the right path, speaking first of the path to be abandoned, even so, the Blessed One, wishing to first teach the states to be abandoned, said, "Monks, what is the quality of a bad person?" and so on. In that text, "uccākula" (high birth) means the Khattiya clan or the Brāhmaṇa clan. Only these two clans are called "high birth." "So tattha pujjo" means that monk is worthy of honor among those monks. "Antaraṃ karitvā" means having placed inside (having considered).

"Mahākula" (great birth) means the Khattiya clan, the Brāhmaṇa clan, or the Vessa clan. Only these three clans are called "great birth." "Mahābhogakula" means...
68: Mahābhogakula refers to families endowed with great wealth. Uḷārabhogakula refers to families endowed with noble wealth. In these two terms, all four types of families can be included. This is because a person born into any family can become one with great wealth or extensive wealth due to the power of their past merit. Yasassī means being endowed with a retinue. Appaññāta refers to those who are obscure, like arrows shot in the night, not being prominent in the midst of the Saṅgha and so on. Appesakkha means those with few followers. Āraññika refers to one who has undertaken the forest-dweller’s ascetic practice. The same method applies to the remaining ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). Although only nine ascetic practices appear in the Pali text of this sutta, in detail there are thirteen. Everything that should be said regarding these ascetic practices has been stated in every aspect in the 'Description of Ascetic Practices' (Dhutaṅganiddesa) of the Visuddhimagga. In the term 'atammayatā', 'tammayatā' refers to craving (taṇhā); thus, 'atammayatā' means the absence of craving. 'Atammayataññeva antaraṃ karitvā' means either by making the absence of craving the cause or by producing it within the mind. In the section on cessation (nirodhavāra), since only Non-returners (anāgāmī) and Arahants can enter that attainment (samāpatti), and worldlings (puthujjana) do not have that attainment, the section on the unworthy person (asappurisavāra) is omitted. One does not conceive any person through the three types of conceiving (maññanā). One does not conceive in any place. One does not conceive that person by means of any object. The remaining words are clear in all places. ## The commentary on the Sappurisadhamma Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. ## 4. Commentary on the Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta. In that sutta, 'tañca aññamaññaṃ kāyasamācāraṃ' means: 'I speak of one kind of bodily conduct to be associated with and another kind of bodily conduct not to be associated with.' It means: 'I do not say that bodily conduct to be associated with is, for some reason, not to be associated with; nor do I say that bodily conduct not to be associated with is, for some reason, to be associated with.' The same method should be understood for verbal conduct (vacīsamācāra) and so on.
69:
Thus, the Blessed One, having laid down the matrix (mātikā) with seven terms, concluded the teaching without analyzing it in detail. Why did he conclude it thus? It was to give the opportunity to the Elder Sāriputta.

In mental conduct (manosamācāra), wrong view and right view are not taken as separate factors by way of the section on the acquisition of view (diṭṭhipaṭilābhavāra).

In the section on the arising of thought (cittuppādavāra), covetousness (abhijjhā) and so on, which have not yet reached the course of action (kammapatha), should be understood.

In the section on the acquisition of perception (saññāpāṭilābhavāra), terms such as "perception accompanied by covetousness" were spoken to show the perception of sensual desire (kāmasaññā) and so on.

"Sabyābajjha" means being with suffering. "Apariniṭṭhitabhāvāya" means because of the state of existences not being finished. Here, there are four kinds of individual existences (attabhāva) that are with suffering. If a worldling (puthujjana) cannot finish existence with that individual existence, for him, from the moment of rebirth-linking, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, and he is said to bring about an individual existence that is with suffering. Likewise for Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners.

Let alone worldlings and others, how does a Non-returner bring about an individual existence with suffering, and how do unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline for that Non-returner? When a Non-returner is reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), upon seeing the gardens, mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees, he utters an inspired utterance (udāna): "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!" In a Non-returner, greed for existence (bhavalobha) and craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) are not yet abandoned. Because of that unabandoned craving, unwholesome states are said to increase and wholesome states are said to decline, and while bringing about an individual existence with suffering, he should be understood as one whose existence is not yet finished.

"Abyābajjha" means the absence of suffering. This point should also be understood by way of the four types of persons. If a worldling can finish existence with that individual existence and does not take rebirth again, for him, from the moment of taking rebirth, unwholesome states decline and only wholesome states increase, and while bringing about an individual existence without suffering, he is called one whose existence is finished. Likewise for Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners.

Let alone Stream-enterers and others, how does a worldling bring about an individual existence without suffering, and how do the decline of unwholesome states and so on occur for him? If a worldling is a person in his final existence (pacchimabhavika), he is capable of finishing existence with that individual existence.
70: Just like Aṅgulimāla, who killed a thousand people minus one, the individual existence (attabhāva) of such a person (a worldling in their final birth) is indeed free from affliction and indeed brings existence to an end. Only unwholesome states decline, and only insight (vipassanā) is made to dwell within (like carrying a fetus). Regarding the terms such as 'cognizable by the eye' (cakkhuviññeyya), because lust and so on arise in some people toward that very form, they delight in it and enjoy it; and by delighting and enjoying, they reach ruin and destruction. In others, lust and so on do not arise; they become disenchanted and dispassionate; and by being disenchanted and dispassionate, they reach the peace of Nibbāna. Therefore, the Blessed One did not say, 'that form and each other.' This method is the same in all places. 'Thus the meaning should be understood in detail'—in this context, who understands the meaning of this sutta spoken by the Blessed One, and who does not? Those who learn the Pali and the Commentary of this sutta but do not act accordingly, and do not practice the aforementioned conformable practice (anulomapaṭipadā), are said to be those who do not understand. However, those who act according to what is stated in that sutta and practice the aforementioned conformable practice are said to be those who understand. Even so, let it be for the benefit and happiness of those who are still subject to rebirth for a long time; but how is it for those who are no longer subject to rebirth? Those who are no longer subject to rebirth are extinguished like fires without fuel; even after the passing of a hundred thousand aeons, there is no more suffering for them. Thus, it is certainly for their benefit and happiness for a long time. The remaining text is clear in all places. ## The commentary on the Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. ## 5. Commentary on the Bahudhātuka Sutta The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Bahudhātuka Sutta. In that sutta, among the terms such as 'bhayāni' (fears), 'bhaya' means mental terror. 'Upaddava' (misfortune) means the state of being unsettled. 'Upasagga' (affliction) means the state of being beset or the state of clinging here and there. Their distinctness should be understood thus: Thieves relying on uneven places such as mountains send word to the inhabitants of a district, saying, 'On such and such a day, we will attack your village.' That news...
71:
In the passages beginning with "bhayāni," the meaning should be understood in the following manner. Fear (bhaya) is mental terror (cittutrāsa). Misfortune (upaddava) is the state of being unsettled (anekkaggatākāra). Adversity (upasagga) is the state of being afflicted (upasaṭṭhākāra) and the state of clinging (lagganākāra) to various ruined animate and inanimate objects. The distinction between fear, misfortune, and adversity should be understood thus: Bandits relying on uneven places such as mountains send a message to the inhabitants of the countryside, saying, "We bandits will destroy your village on such and such a day." From the time they hear that news, they fall into fear and terror. This fear and terror is called mental terror (cittutrāsa). Thinking, "These bandits are angry and might bring about our ruin," they take their essential wealth and enter the forest along with their two-footed and four-footed animals, and sleep on the ground in various parts of the forest. Being bitten by gadflies, mosquitoes, and so on, they enter thickets and tread on stumps and thorns. The state of being scattered while wandering in this way is called the state of being unsettled (anekkaggatā).

Thereafter, while they are wandering, if the bandits do not come on the appointed day, they say, "That message must have been empty; let us enter the village," and they enter the village with their belongings. Then, knowing that they have entered, the bandits surround the village, set fire to the gates, kill the people, plunder all the wealth, and leave. Those who remain among the people after the slaughter extinguish the fire and sit in the shadows of granaries or walls, clinging to the ruined animate and inanimate objects, repeatedly grieving over their lost wealth. This repeated grieving is called the state of being afflicted or the state of clinging (upasaṭṭhākāra, lagganākāra).

"Naḷāgārā" refers to houses covered with reeds. In these houses, the structures remaining after the roofing and walls are made of wood. The same method applies to grass houses (tiṇāgāra). "Bālatော uppajjanti" means that dangers and so on arise only depending on the fool. To explain this further: A foolish, unwise man, desiring kingship, the position of viceroy, or another high office, takes a few widows' sons or great scoundrels like himself and says, "Come, I will make you rulers." Relying on mountain thickets and forest thickets, he attacks the outlying villages, making his banditry known, and gradually attacks towns and the countryside. The villagers abandon their homes and flee to other places, seeking safety. The monks and nuns who live depending on those villagers also abandon their dwellings and flee. In every place they go, almsfood and lodgings are difficult to obtain. Thus, danger truly comes to the four assemblies. Among the monks, two foolish monks start a dispute with each other and begin accusations. Thus, a great quarrel arises, like that of the monks living in Kosambī. Danger truly comes to the four assemblies. In this way, various dangers arise. It should be understood that all those dangers arise because of the fool.

"Etadavoca" means that the Blessed One finished the Dhamma teaching without bringing it to a conclusion. Thinking, "It would be good if I (Elder Ānanda) were to ask the One of Ten Powers and complete this teaching through His Omniscient Knowledge," he spoke these words. Among the eighteen elements, one element is included in matter along with the portion of the dhamma-element called subtle matter and Nibbāna. Among the eighteen elements, seventeen elements are included in mind along with the portion of the dhamma-element called the fifty-two mental factors. Thus, it is taught that the eighteen elements are included in mind and matter. All eighteen elements, by way of the aggregates, become the five aggregates. The five aggregates, excluding craving, are called the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The craving that produces that Truth of Suffering is called the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The cause of the non-arising of both the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin is called the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). The practice of the Eightfold Path that knows the Truth of Cessation is called the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). In this way, the meditation on the Four Noble Truths for a certain...
72:
Venerable Ānanda thought, "It would be good if I were to ask the Blessed One and make the completion of the Blessed One's teaching through His omniscience alone," and spoke these words: "To what extent, Bhante..." and so on.

Among the eighteen elements (dhātu), grasping eleven elements as materiality (rūpa) and grasping seven and a half elements as mentality (arūpa) is taught; thus, only the grasping of materiality and mentality is taught. All elements, by way of the aggregates, become the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā). These five aggregates are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); the craving (taṇhā) that gives rise to them is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca); the non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca); the practice that knows the Truth of Cessation is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Thus, the meditation on the Four Truths is taught to a certain monk, leading him to the final goal and pinnacle. This is the summary here; the details of these elements have already been taught in the Visuddhimagga. "Knows and sees" refers to the Path (magga) together with Insight (vipassanā).

The earth element (pathavī-dhātu) and others are taught to show that the body, together with consciousness, is empty (suññato) and non-self (nissattato). These six elements should also be filled by the previously mentioned eighteen elements. One who fills them should do so by extracting from the consciousness element (viññāṇa-dhātu). This consciousness element is of six kinds by way of eye-consciousness and so on. Among those six, when the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇa-dhātu) is grasped, its base, the eye element (cakkhu-dhātu), and its object, the form element (rūpa-dhātu)—these two elements—are also grasped. This method is the same in all cases. When the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇa-dhātu) is grasped, the mind element (mano-dhātu) by way of its preceding and succeeding states, and the dhamma element (dhamma-dhātu) by way of its object—these two elements—are also grasped. Thus, among these eighteen elements, grasping eleven elements as materiality, as in the previous method, is taught to a certain monk, leading him to the final goal and pinnacle.

In the "pleasant element" (sukha-dhātu) and so on, it is called the pleasant element because it is pleasant and also an element in the sense of being non-self and empty. This method is the same in all terms. Here also, the first four elements are taken by way of opposites, and the last two by way of similarity. Due to its unmanifest nature, the neutral element (upekkhā-dhātu) is similar to the ignorance element (avijjā-dhātu). Here also, when the pleasant and painful elements are grasped, the body-consciousness element (kāyaviññāṇa-dhātu) is also grasped; when the remaining four elements are grasped, the mind-consciousness element is also grasped. These six elements should also be filled only by the eighteen elements mentioned below. One who fills them should do so by extracting from the neutral element. Thus, among these eighteen elements, eleven elements...
73:
"Grasping materiality"—this statement is also taught to a certain monk, leading him to the final goal and pinnacle, just as in the previous method.

The meaning of the sense element (kāma-dhātu) and so on should be understood according to the method taught regarding sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) and so on in the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta (M. Ni. 1.206). In the Abhidhamma (Vibhaṅga 182) also, the details of these elements have already appeared in the manner of: "Therein, what is the sense element? It is the thought (takka), the applied thought (vitakka) associated with sensual pleasures," and so on. These six elements should also be completed only by the eighteen elements mentioned below. The practitioner of insight (vipassanā-yogī) who completes them should do so by extracting from the sense element. Thus, among these eighteen elements, the eleventh element, which is a part of the dhamma element called the 16 kinds of subtle materiality (sukhuma-rūpa), is taught as "grasping materiality" to a certain monk, leading him to the final goal and pinnacle, just as in the previous method.

Among the sense element and so on, the five sense-sphere aggregates (kāmāvacarakkhandhā) are called the sense element (kāma-dhātu); the five fine-material sphere aggregates (rūpāvacarakkhandhā) are called the fine-material element (rūpa-dhātu); the four immaterial sphere aggregates (arūpāvacarakkhandhā) are called the immaterial element (arūpa-dhātu). In the Abhidhamma, however, the details of these elements have already appeared in the manner of: "Therein, what is the sense element? Making the Avīci hell the lower limit," and so on. These three elements should also be completed only by the eighteen elements mentioned below. The practitioner of insight who completes them should do so by extracting from the sense element. Thus, among these eighteen elements, the eleventh element, which is a part of the dhamma element called the 16 kinds of subtle materiality, is taught as "grasping materiality" to a certain monk, leading him to the final goal and pinnacle, just as in the previous method.

"Conditioned" (saṅkhata) means that which is produced by the meeting of causes, and it is a designation for the five aggregates. "Unconditioned" (asaṅkhata) means not conditioned by causes; it is a designation for Nibbāna. These two elements should also be completed only by the eighteen elements mentioned below. The practitioner of insight who completes them should do so by extracting from the conditioned element. Thus, among these eighteen elements, the eleventh element, which is a part of the dhamma element called the 16 kinds of subtle materiality, is taught as "grasping materiality" to a certain monk, leading him to the final goal and pinnacle, just as in the previous method.

"Internal and external" (ajjhattika-bāhira) refers to internal things and external things. Here, there are the six internal bases (ajjhattikāyatana) such as the eye and so on, and the six external bases (bāhirāyatana) such as forms and so on. In this section on the bases (āyatana-vāra) as well, "knows and sees" refers to the Path together with Insight.

The statement "When this is, that is" and so on has already been explained in detail in the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta.
74:
"Aṭṭhāna" means the rejection of a cause (hetu). "Anavakāsa" means the rejection of a condition (paccaya). By both these terms, the Buddha rejects the cause. Because a cause exists in dependence on its effect, it is called "ṭhāna" (ground/basis) and "avakāsa" (opportunity/occasion) for its own result. "Yaṃ" means "by which cause." "Diṭṭhisampanna" refers to a Noble Disciple (ariyasāvaka), a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) who is endowed with the wisdom of the Path. "Kañci saṅkhāraṃ" means even a single conditioned thing among those belonging to the four planes. "Niccato upagaccheyya" means to perceive it as permanent. "Netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati" means this cause does not exist, it is not possible. "Yaṃ puthujjano" means "by which cause a worldling." "Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati" means this cause exists. It means that a worldling, through eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi), might take some conditioned thing among those belonging to the three planes as permanent. However, conditioned things belonging to the fourth plane, due to their intense power, do not become objects of wrong view or other unwholesome states, just as flies cannot land on an iron ball that has been heated all day. In this manner, the meaning should also be understood in phrases such as "viewing any conditioned thing as pleasant (sukha)," and so on.

"Sukhato upagaccheyya" is spoken with reference to the attachment to pleasure through the power of self-view (attadiṭṭhi), such as "After death, the self is exclusively happy and free from disease." However, with a mind dissociated from wrong view, a Noble Disciple—oppressed by the heat of defilements and seeking to allay that heat—might approach some conditioned thing as pleasant, like a rogue elephant restrained by a bamboo-mantra, or like a brahmin desiring purity approaching foul dung. In the section on self (attavāra), the Buddha said "kañci dhammaṃ" (any phenomenon) instead of "saṅkhāra" to include designations (paññatti) such as kasinas. Here too, it should be understood in terms of the four planes for the Noble Disciple and the three planes for the worldling. In all sections, it is appropriate to define the scope for the Noble Disciple in terms of the three planes as well. This is because whatever a worldling grasps, from that very thing the Noble Disciple unties the grasp. Whatever a worldling takes as permanent, pleasant, or self, the Noble Disciple, taking it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, unties that grasp.

In the words "mātaraṃ" (mother) and so on, "mātā" refers to the biological mother, "pitā" to the biological father, and "arahā" to an Arahant who is a human being. If it is asked, "Would a Noble Disciple deprive another being of life?"—this too is an impossibility. Even if a Noble Disciple has gone to another life and does not yet know their status as a Noble One, if someone were to say, "Kill this small insect and take the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch over the entire universe," even then, that Noble Disciple would not deprive that insect of life. Furthermore, if that person were to say, "If you do not kill this insect, I will cut off your head," the Noble Disciple would rather have their own head cut off, but they would not kill that creature. ...
75:
If someone were to say to a Noble Disciple who does not yet know their status as a Noble One (having been reborn in another life), "Kill this small insect (ant) and take the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) over the entire universe," that Noble Disciple would never deprive that insect of life. Furthermore, if that person were to say, "If you do not kill this creature, we will cut off your head," they would only desire their own head to be cut off; they would not kill that creature. This is spoken to show the great fault of the state of a worldling and to demonstrate the power (bala) (such as faith and energy) of a Noble Disciple. The meaning here is: the state of a worldling is blameworthy, for a worldling might even commit heinous crimes (ānantariya) such as matricide. A Noble Disciple, however, possesses great power, as they do not commit such deeds. "Duṭṭhacitto" means having a malicious mind with the intent to kill. "Lohitaṃ uppādeyya" (causing blood to flow) means causing even as much blood as a small fly might drink to be shed from the body of a living Buddha. "Saṃghaṃ bhindeyya" (splitting the Sangha) means causing a schism in a Sangha that shares the same communion and stays within the same boundary, through five means. It is said: "Upāli, the Sangha is split by five means: by a legal act (kamma), by recitation (uddesa), by assertion (vohāra), by proclamation (anussāvana), and by taking voting tickets (salākaggāha)."

Among those five, "kammena" means by one of the four types of legal acts, such as an act of proposal (apalokana). "Uddesena" means by one of the five types of Pātimokkha recitations. "Voharanto" means speaking, pointing out the eighteen grounds for schism, such as asserting non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and so on, through various occurrences. "Anussāvanena" means whispering in the ear and persuading in this manner: "Do you not know that I am one who has gone forth from a high family and am very learned? It is proper for you to even think that one like me would uphold the Teacher's Dispensation, even if it were non-Dhamma or non-Vinaya. Is Avīci hell as cool as a forest of blue lotuses to me? Do I not fear the states of misery?" and so on. "Salākaggāhena" means, after persuading them thus and making their minds firm and unwavering, saying "Take this voting ticket" and having them take the tickets.

In this context, only the legal act (kamma) or the recitation (uddesa) is the standard (the actual split), while assertion, proclamation, and taking voting tickets are the preliminary stages. For even if one speaks by pointing out the eighteen grounds, persuades them to create a preference, and has them take voting tickets, the Sangha is not yet split. Only when four or more monks, having taken the voting tickets, perform a separate legal act or recitation, is it then called a split in the Sangha. Thus, the Buddha has made clear the five heinous crimes, such as matricide, which a worldling may commit but a Noble Disciple does not, through this sequence of words.
76:
They perform a separate act (kamma) or a separate recitation (uddesa); at that time, the Saṅgha is said to be divided. It is impossible for a person endowed with the Path-knowledge (magga-paññā) to divide the Saṅgha. By this explanation, the five heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma), such as matricide (mātughāta), which are committed only by worldlings (puthujjana) and not by noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka), have been shown. To clarify those kammas:

The decision should be understood by way of kamma, door (dvāra), duration of the aeon (kappa-ṭṭhiti), and likewise by the commonality of result, etc.

Among those decisions, I shall first speak by way of kamma—here, when a human being takes the life of a human mother or father, even if their gender has changed, that person's kamma is an ānantariya-kamma. Even if one intends to prevent the result of that ānantariya-kamma by filling the entire universe with golden stupas the size of the Great Stupa, or by giving a great offering (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha of monks sitting throughout the entire universe, or by following the Blessed One without letting go of the corner of his double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi), one will surely be reborn in hell upon the dissolution of the body.

However, if a human kills a mother or father who has become an animal, or if an animal kills a human parent, or if an animal kills its own animal parent, that kamma does not constitute an ānantariya-kamma. Nevertheless, it is a heavy (bhāriya) kamma and stands close to being an ānantariya-kamma. This problem is discussed in terms of those of human birth.

In this regard, the fourfold case of the sheep (eḷaka-catukka), the fourfold case of the battle (saṅgāma-catukka), and the fourfold case of the thief (cora-catukka) should be explained. Even with the intention 'I will kill a sheep,' if one kills a human mother or father who is in the place of a sheep, one incurs the ānantariya-kamma. However, if one kills a sheep with the intention of killing a sheep or with the intention of killing a parent, one does not incur the ānantariya-kamma. If one kills a parent with the intention of killing a parent, one certainly incurs it. The same method applies to the other two fourfold cases. Just as with parents, these fourfold cases should also be understood regarding Arahants.

Only by killing a human Arahant does one incur the ānantariya-kamma, not by killing an Arahant who is a yakkha. However, that kamma is heavy and is just like an ānantariya-kamma. Even if a human Arahant was struck with a weapon or given poison while still a worldling, if he dies from that injury after attaining Arahantship, it is indeed the murder of an Arahant (arahantaghāta). An offering given while one was a worldling is considered given to a worldling, even if the recipient consumes it after becoming an Arahant.
77:
For one who kills noble persons (ariya-puggala) other than Arahants, there is no ānantariya-kamma. However, that kamma is a grave offense and is similar to ānantariya-kamma.

Regarding the act of wounding a Buddha (lohituppāda), because the body of the Tathāgata cannot be destroyed, no one can cause blood to flow by cutting the skin through another's effort. However, blood may collect in one place only within the body. The splinter that broke off from the great rock hurled by Devadatta also struck the Blessed One's foot; the foot suffered internal bruising as if struck by an axe. For one who acts thus, it is an ānantariya-kamma. Jīvaka, however, according to the Blessed One's wish, cut the skin with a small knife to remove the bad blood from that spot and provided relief. For one who acts thus, it is only a meritorious kamma (puñña-kamma).

If it is asked, 'What happens to those who, after the Tathāgata has attained Parinibbāna, destroy a stupa, cut the Bodhi tree, or attempt to destroy a relic?' It is a heavy kamma similar to ānantariya-kamma. It is permissible to cut a Bodhi branch that is pressing against a stupa or an image containing relics. Even if birds perched on that Bodhi branch drop excrement on the stupa, it is indeed permissible to cut it. This is because a bodily-relic shrine (sarīra-cetiya) is more noble than a use-relic shrine (paribhoga-cetiya). It is also permissible to cut and remove a Bodhi root that is piercing the foundation of a stupa. However, one is not allowed to cut a Bodhi branch that is pressing against a Bodhi-house (bodhighara) just to protect that house. This is because the house exists for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house. The same method applies to an altar-house (āsana-ghara). However, if relics are enshrined in that altar-house, it is permissible to cut a Bodhi branch to protect that house. It is certainly permissible to cut a branch that saps the nutrients or a decaying part to care for the Bodhi tree; this is meritorious, just like attending to the physical body of the Blessed One.

Regarding the crime of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabhedaka-kamma), for one who—before the monks within the boundary (sīmā) have assembled—takes a separate group and performs the act of speaking divisive words, persuading them, or taking voting tickets (salāka-gāha), or performs a separate formal act (kamma) or recites a separate recitation (uddesa), there is both a schism and the ānantariya-kamma. However, for one who performs the act thinking 'it is permissible' with the perception of harmony (samagga-saññā), there is only a schism but not the ānantariya-kamma. Likewise, it is not an ānantariya-kamma in an assembly of fewer than nine. At the minimum limit, among nine persons, he who [divides] the Saṅgha...
78:
For the monk who causes a schism in the Saṅgha, it is an ānantariya-kamma (an action with immediate retribution). For the unrighteous persons (adhammavādī) who follow that monk, it is a kamma of great fault. For the righteous persons (dhammavādī), however, there is no fault.

Regarding that kamma of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabhedaka-kamma), there is this Sutta passage stating that a schism in the Saṅgha occurs only when there are nine monks: "Upāli, on one side there are four monks, and on the other side there are four monks. The ninth monk announces, distributes voting slips (salāka), and says, 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction; accept this view, approve of this view.' Upāli, such an act is called both a rift in the Saṅgha (saṅgharāji) and a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda). Upāli, whether there are nine monks or more than nine, it is both a rift in the Saṅgha and a schism in the Saṅgha" (as taught in the Cūḷavagga Pāḷi). Among these five ānantariya-kammas, saṅghabhedaka-kamma is a verbal action (vacī-kamma), while the remaining four are bodily actions (kāya-kamma). Thus, the decision should be understood by way of action (kamma).

In terms of the doors (dvāra), all these ānantariya-kammas arise from both the body-door (kāya-dvāra) and the speech-door (vacī-dvāra). Among these five ānantariya-kammas, the first four, though arising from the speech-door by way of command (āṇattika) and effort through knowledge (vijjāmaya-payoga), fulfill only the body-door. For one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha through hand gestures, although it arises from the body-door, it fulfills only the speech-door. Thus, the decision should also be understood by way of the doors.

In terms of lasting for an aeon (kappaṭṭhitiya), among these five kammas, only saṅghabhedaka-kamma lasts for an entire aeon. Whether one causes a schism at the beginning of the world-cycle or in the middle, he is released from hell only when the world-cycle ends. If one causes a schism today knowing that "the world will end tomorrow," he will be released tomorrow, having suffered in hell for only one day. However, such an occurrence does not exist. The remaining four kammas are merely ānantariya-kammas and do not last for an entire aeon. Thus, the decision should also be understood by way of kappaṭṭhitiya.

In terms of the result (pāka), if a person has committed all five of these ānantariya-kammas, only the saṅghabhedaka-kamma will yield the result of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). The remaining four kammas fall into the category of lapsed action (ahosi-kamma), such as "it was a kamma, but there is no result of the kamma." If there is no saṅghabhedaka-kamma, the lohituppādaka-kamma (wounding a Buddha) yields the rebirth-linking result. In its absence, the arahantaghātaka-kamma (killing an Arahant) yields it. In its absence, if the father is virtuous and the mother is immoral (or if the mother is virtuous but not as much as the father), the pitughātaka-kamma (patricide) yields the rebirth-linking result. If one has killed both parents, and they are equal in virtue or immorality, then only the mātughātaka-kamma (matricide), by the power of rebirth-linking...
79:
(If one kills both parents, only the mātughātaka-kamma) yields the result. This is because a mother is one who performs what is difficult for her sons and is of great benefit to them. Thus, in these ānantariya-kammas, the clear decision should be understood by way of the result (pāka).

Regarding "sādhāraṇādīhi," the first four ānantariya-kammas are common (sādhāraṇa) to all laypeople and monastics. However, as for saṅghabhedaka-kamma, according to the words: "Upāli, a bhikkhunī does not cause a schism in the Saṅgha, nor does a sikkhamānā, a sāmaṇera, a sāmaṇerī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā. Upāli, only a monk who is of normal status (pakatatta), who belongs to the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka), and who stays within the same boundary (samānasīmā) causes a schism in the Saṅgha," it occurs only to a monk of the described type and not to anyone else. Therefore, it is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) kamma. By the word "ādi" (etc.), it should be understood that all these ānantariya-kammas are accompanied by painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) and are associated with hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). Thus, the decision should also be understood here by way of commonality and so forth.

"Aññaṃ satthāraṃ" means that there is no possibility for one to think, "This teacher of mine is unable to perform the duties of a teacher," and thus take another sect-founder (titthakara) in another life, saying, "This person is my teacher."

"Ekissā lokadhātuyā" means it occurs in a ten-thousandfold world system. There are three fields (khetta): the field of birth (jāti-khetta), the field of authority (āṇā-khetta), and the field of range (visaya-khetta). Among these three, the field of birth is the ten-thousandfold world system. Indeed, that world system trembles at the time the Tathāgata descends into his mother's womb, at the time of his birth, at the time of his enlightenment, at the time of his preaching the Dhammacakka, at the time of his relinquishing the life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra), and at the time of his Parinibbāna. The hundred-billion world systems are called the field of authority. The power and authority of the Āṭānāṭiya, Mora, Dhajagga, and Ratana Parittas, etc., prevail in this field. There is no limit to the field of range. For the Buddhas, according to the words: "As far as there is knowledge, so far is there the knowable (neyya); as far as there is the knowable, so far is there knowledge; knowledge has the knowable as its limit, and the knowable has knowledge as its limit," there is no such thing as a non-object (something unknowable).

Among these three fields, there is no Sutta (scripture) stating that Buddhas arise in another world system while excluding this world system; there are only Suttas stating that they do not arise. Among the three Pitakas—Vinaya Piṭaka, Suttanta Piṭaka, and Abhidhamma Piṭaka—and the three Councils—the Council of Elder Mahākassapa, the Council of Elder Yasa, and the Council of Elder Moggaliputtatissa—within the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) included in these three Councils...
80:
There is no discourse (Sutta) stating that Buddhas arise in other universes excluding this one; however, there is a discourse stating that they do not arise [elsewhere].

'Apubbaṃ acarimaṃ' means neither before nor after. It means that they do not arise simultaneously, but they arise either before or after [one another]. In this context, the period from the time the Bodhisatta sat on the Throne of Enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka) thinking, 'I shall not rise until I attain Enlightenment (Bodhi),' until the taking of conception in the mother's womb, is not to be regarded as 'before'. This is because, by the shaking of the ten thousand universes upon the Bodhisatta's conception, the field [of authority] is already claimed, and the arising of another Buddha is already prevented. The period from the time of Final Nirvana (Parinibbāna) as long as a relic (dhātu) even the size of a mustard seed remains, is not to be regarded as 'after'. As long as the relics remain, the Buddhas are indeed still present. Therefore, during this interval, the arising of another Buddha is already prevented. However, when the disappearance of the relics (Dhātu-parinibbāna) occurs, the arising of another Buddha is no longer prevented.

There are three types of disappearance (antaradhāna): the disappearance of learning (Pariyatti-antaradhāna), the disappearance of realization (Paṭivedha-antaradhāna), and the disappearance of practice (Paṭipatti-antaradhāna). Among them, Pariyatti refers to the Three Piṭakas. Paṭivedha refers to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Paṭipatti refers to the practice (paṭipadā). Among these three, Paṭivedha and Paṭipatti may or may not exist. For at one time, monks who possessed realization were so numerous that a monk who was a worldling (puthujjana) had to be pointed out with a finger. Even on this island [of Sri Lanka], there was once a time when there was no such thing as a worldling monk. Those who fulfill the practice also are sometimes many and sometimes few. Thus, while Paṭivedha and Paṭipatti may or may not exist, Pariyatti is the standard for the endurance of the Dispensation (Sāsana).

A wise person, having heard the Three Piṭakas, can fulfill both [realization and practice]. For example, our Bodhisatta, after developing the five mundane superknowledges and the seven attainments under the ascetic Āḷāra, asked about the preliminary work (parikamma) for the attainment of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. Āḷāra said, 'I do not know.' Then, having gone to the ascetic Udaka and compared his attained distinction, he asked about the preliminary work for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, and Udaka explained it. Immediately upon hearing those words, the Great Being (Mahāsatta) accomplished that Dhamma. In the same way, a wise monk, having heard the Pariyatti, can fulfill both. Therefore, as long as Pariyatti remains, the Sāsana remains.
81:
When the Pariyatti Sāsana disappears, first the Abhidhamma Piṭaka perishes. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the Paṭṭhāna disappears first, and finally, in due order, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī disappears. Even when the Dhammasaṅgaṇī has disappeared, as long as the other two Piṭakas remain, the Sāsana is still considered to remain. When the Suttanta Piṭaka disappears, first the Aṅguttara Nikāya disappears, starting from the Book of the Elevens down to the Book of the Ones. After that, the Saṃyutta Nikāya disappears, starting from the Cakkapeyyāla down to the Oghataraṇa Sutta. After that, the Majjhima Nikāya disappears, starting from the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta down to the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. After that, the Dīgha Nikāya disappears, starting from the Dasuttara Sutta down to the Brahmajāla Sutta. Even if the questioning of one or two verses (gāthā) reaches a long duration, it can no longer bear the Sāsana. It becomes like the questions of Sabhiya and the questions of Āḷavaka. These verses, it is said, belonged to the time of Kassapa Buddha and could not bear the Sāsana in the intervening period.

Even when two Piṭakas have disappeared, as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka remains, the Sāsana remains. When the Parivāra and Khandhaka have disappeared, if the Ubhatovibhaṅga remains, the Sāsana is still considered to remain. When the Ubhatovibhaṅga has disappeared, if the Mātikā (Pātimokkha) remains, the Sāsana is still considered to remain. When the Mātikā has disappeared, if the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the novice ordination (pabbajjā), and the higher ordination (upasampadā) remain, the Sāsana remains. The outward appearance [of a monk] may last for a long time, but the lineage of white-robed recluses from the time of Kassapa Buddha could not bear the Sāsana. From the time of the realization of the truth by the last person and the failure of virtue (sīla) by the last person, the Sāsana is said to have declined. From that time on, the arising of another Buddha is no longer prevented.

There are three types of Final Nirvana (Parinibbāna): the Final Nirvana of defilements (Kilesa-parinibbāna), the Final Nirvana of the aggregates (Khandha-parinibbāna), and the Final Nirvana of the relics (Dhātu-parinibbāna). Among these three, Kilesa-parinibbāna occurred at the Throne of Enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka), Khandha-parinibbāna occurred at Kusinārā, and Dhātu-parinibbāna will occur in the future. At the time of the decline of the Sāsana, the relics in this island of Tambapaṇṇi will gather and go to the Mahācetiya. From the Mahācetiya, they will go to the Rājāyatana Cetiya in Nāgadīpa, and from there to the Mahābodhi Throne. Relics from the dragon realm, the deva realm, and the brahma realm will also go only to the Mahābodhi Throne. Not even a relic the size of a mustard seed will perish in the interval. All the relics, having massed together at the Mahābodhi Throne like a great mass of gold, will become a single solid block and emit six-colored rays. Those rays will pervade the ten thousand world-systems. At that time, the deities living in the ten thousand universes will gather and, reflecting, 'Today our Teacher, the Buddha, attains Final Nirvana; today the Sāsana declines; this sight is the last we shall see,' they will weep with a compassion even greater than on the day the Buddha attained Final Nirvana. Except for the Non-returner (Anāgāmī) and Arahant deities, the remaining deities will be unable to restrain themselves. The fire element (tejo-dhātu) will arise from the relics and rise upwards as far as the Brahma world. As long as there is a relic the size of a mustard seed, a single continuous flame will exist. When the relics are exhausted, the flame will cease. Thus, when the relics disappear in due order, the Sāsana is said to have disappeared. (This Sāsana will continue to exist) as long as it has not disappeared.
