82: Due to this pervasiveness, the deities dwelling in the ten thousand world systems will gather and, reflecting, 'Today our Teacher, the Exalted Buddha, attains Parinibbāna; today the Sasana declines; this is now our final sight [of him],' they will show even greater compassion and lamentation than on the day the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) attained Parinibbāna. Except for the deities who are Anāgāmīs and Arahants, the remaining deities will be unable to remain composed in their natural state. Among the relics, the fire element (tejo-dhātu) will arise and ascend as far as the Brahma realm. As long as a relic even the size of a mustard seed remains, there will be a single flame; when the relics are exhausted, it will cease. Having shown such great power, when the relics disappear, the Sasana is said to have disappeared. As long as it has not disappeared in this way, it is called 'not the last' (acarima). Thus, the occurrence of two Buddhas arising simultaneously is impossible. Why do they not arise simultaneously? Because it would not be extraordinary. Indeed, Buddhas are extraordinary human beings. As it is said: 'Monks, there is one person who, when arising in the world, arises as an extraordinary human being. Who is that one person? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened Buddha.' (A. Ni. 1.171-174). If two, four, eight, or sixteen Buddhas were to arise at once, they would not be extraordinary. Just as in a single monastery, if there are two stupas, the offerings and honor do not become grand and extensive, and because monks are numerous, they are not seen as extraordinary; so too would it be with Buddhas. Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. It is also because there would be no distinction in the teaching. Indeed, the Dhamma consisting of the Satipaṭṭhāna and so forth, which one Buddha teaches, would have to be taught by another even if he arose. Then it would not be extraordinary; but when only one Buddha teaches the Dhamma, the teaching is extraordinary. It is also to prevent disputes. If many Buddhas were to arise, the disciples of many teachers might dispute like this: 'Our Buddha is inspiring; our Buddha has a sweet voice, is highly supported, and is meritorious.' Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. Furthermore, this reason was explained in detail by the Elder Nagasena when questioned by King Milinda. For it is said in that Milindapañhā: 'In that regard, venerable Nagasena, this was also spoken by the Blessed One: "Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that in a single world system, two Arahants..."'
83: "...Fully Enlightened Buddhas should arise simultaneously; this is impossible.' 'Venerable Nagasena, all Tathāgatas teach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma); when speaking, they speak of the Four Noble Truths; when training, they train in the three trainings; when exhorting, they exhort in the practice of heedfulness (appamāda). Venerable Nagasena, if all Tathāgatas have the same teaching, the same speech, the same training, and the same exhortation, for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise at the same moment? By the arising of even one Buddha, this world becomes filled with light. If a second Buddha were to arise, this world would become even more filled with light through the radiance of those two. When exhorting, two Tathāgatas could exhort with ease, and when instructing, they could instruct with ease. Tell me the reason for this, so that I may be free from doubt.' 'Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha; it supports the virtue of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system could not support him; it would shake, tremble, bend, sink, scatter, perish, and be utterly destroyed; it could not remain stable. Great King, for example, suppose there were a boat that could support only one person. If one person boards, that boat can travel smoothly. Then, if a second person, similar in age, complexion, years, stature, and physical build, were to come and board that boat—Great King, would that boat support the weight of both?' 'No, venerable sir. It would shake, tremble, bend, perish, and sink into the water.' 'Even so, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha; it supports the virtue of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system could not support him; it would shake... [pe]... it could not remain stable. Or again, Great King, suppose a man were to eat as much food as he desired, filling himself up to the throat. When he is satiated, satisfied, full, without gaps, heavy, and as stiff as an unbending rod, if he were to eat that same amount of food again—Great King, would that man be at ease?' 'No, venerable sir. He would not be at ease; having eaten once, he would have to vomit it out.' 'Even so, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha... [pe]... it could not reach stability.' 'Venerable Nagasena, how is it? Does the earth shake because of the weight of the noble Dhamma?' 'Great King, suppose there were two carts in this world, fully loaded with jewels up to the top. If one were to take the jewels from one cart and pour them into the other—Great King, would that cart support the jewels of two carts?' 'No, venerable sir. The rim of that cart would shake, the spokes would break, the frame would fall, and the axle would break.' 'What do you think, Great King? Is it because of the weight of the noble jewels...'
84:
Great King, if that man (who is already full) were to eat that much food again, would he be happy? "No, Bhante Nāgasena, it is not possible; he would die just by eating once more." Even so, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can bear only one Buddha... it cannot reach the state (of bearing two Buddhas).

"Bhante Nāgasena, does the earth shake because of the weight of the sublime Dhamma?" Great King, in this world, there might be two carts filled to the brim with jewels. If one were to take jewels from one cart and pour them into the other, Great King, would that cart be able to bear the weight of the jewels of both carts? "No, Bhante Nāgasena, its hub would shake, its spokes would break, its rim would fall off, and its axle would break." Great King, does the cart break because the weight of jewels is too great? "Yes, Bhante." Even so, Great King, the earth shakes because of the weight of the sublime Dhamma.

Great King, this reason is stated to demonstrate the power of the Buddha. Listen further to another suitable reason why two Rightly Self-Awakened Ones do not arise at the same time. Great King, if two Rightly Self-Awakened Ones were to arise at the same time, a dispute would arise among their followers, saying 'Your Buddha, our Buddha,' and they would split into two factions. Just as, Great King, the followers of two powerful ministers might split into factions and dispute, saying 'Your minister, our minister,' even so, Great King, if two Rightly Self-Awakened Ones were to arise at the same time, the followers would split into two factions and dispute, saying 'Your Buddha, our Buddha.' This is the first reason why two Rightly Self-Awakened Ones do not arise at the same time.

Great King, listen to another even more excellent reason. If two Rightly Self-Awakened Ones were to arise at the same time, the statement 'The Buddha is the Foremost (Agga)' would be false. The statement 'The Buddha is the Eldest (Jeṭṭha)' would be false. The statements 'The Buddha is the Best (Seṭṭha), the Most Distinguished (Visiṭṭha), the Supreme (Uttama), the Most Sublime (Pavara), the Peerless (Asama), the Equal to the Peerless (Asamasama), the Matchless (Appaṭisama), the Incomparable (Appaṭibhāga), the Unique Person (Appaṭipuggala)' would all be false. Great King, you should accept this reason by its meaning. Furthermore, Great King, it is the nature of Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world. This is because the qualities of the Omniscient Buddhas are so great. Great King, listen to another reason. Whatever is great is usually unique. Great King, the earth is great, and there is only one earth. The ocean is great, and there is only one ocean. Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, is great, and there is only one such mountain. The sky is great, and there is only one sky. Sakka is great, and there is only one Sakka. Brahma is great...
85:
Great King, accept the reason by its meaning, the reason why two Rightly Self-Awakened Ones do not arise at the same time.

Furthermore, Great King, it is the natural way of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world. For what reason? Because of the greatness of the qualities of an Omniscient Buddha. Great King, listen to another reason: whatever is great in the world is unique. Great King, the earth is great, and it is only one. The ocean is great, and it is only one. Mount Sineru is great, and it is only one. The sky is great, and it is only one. Sakka is great, and he is only one. Māra is great, and he is only one. Brahma is great, and he is only one. Even so, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, is great, and He is the only one in the world. In the world system where they arise, there is no room for another. Therefore, Great King, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, arises as the only one in the world. "Bhante Nāgasena, the problem has been well explained with similes and reasons," (the King said).

"Ekissā lokadhātuyā" means in a single universe (Cakkavāḷa). By this term, the ten thousand universes are also included below; those ten thousand universes should also be defined by a single universe. Indeed, when Buddhas arise, they arise only in this universe. When the place of arising is restricted, it is already restricted that they do not arise in universes other than this one.

"Apubbaṃ acarimaṃ"—in this text, the time before the appearance of the Wheel Treasure is called "pubba" (before), and the time after the disappearance of that Wheel Treasure is called "carima" (after). Regarding that disappearance, the Wheel Treasure disappears for two reasons: either due to the death of the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) or due to his renunciation. When it disappears, it vanishes on the seventh day after the death or renunciation. After those seven days have passed, the appearance of another Universal Monarch is not prohibited.

Why do two Universal Monarchs not arise simultaneously in a single universe? It is to cut off disputes, to maintain the sense of wonder, and because of the great power of the Wheel Treasure. If two Universal Monarchs were to appear, disputes would arise, saying "Our king is greater, our king is greater." Also, having one Universal Monarch on each island would not be a cause for wonder...
86:
The reason why two Wheel-turning Monarchs cannot arise in a single world system is as follows: The great power of the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana), which is capable of granting sovereignty over the four great islands along with their two thousand surrounding small islands, would decline if there were two Wheel-turning Monarchs. Thus, to cut off disputes, to maintain the quality of being a wonder, and because of the great power of the Wheel-treasure, two Wheel-turning Monarchs do not arise simultaneously in a single world system.

'It is impossible for a woman to be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha'—regarding this point, let alone the state of Buddhahood, which is capable of delivering beings from the world by producing qualities such as omniscience, even the mere aspiration (paṇidhāna) for Buddhahood cannot be fulfilled by a woman.

'Being human, being male, the cause (possession of roots), the sight of a Teacher,
Renunciation, the attainment of qualities, dedication, and strong desire—
Through the combination of these eight factors, the aspiration (abhinīhāra) succeeds.' (Bv. 2.59)

For these are the causes for the perfection of the aspiration. Thus, for a woman who is unable to even fulfill the aspiration, how could there be the state of Buddhahood? Therefore, it is said, 'It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a woman should be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.' Because a heap of merit perfected in every way produces a physical existence (attabhāva) that is perfected in every way, only a male becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.

Regarding the points such as 'It is impossible for a woman to be a Wheel-turning Monarch'—this is stated because a woman does not fulfill the marks due to the absence of features such as the male organ being ensheathed, because the possession of the Seven Treasures cannot be fulfilled due to the absence of the Woman-treasure, and because she does not possess a physical existence superior to all humans. Since the three positions such as that of Sakka are noble and the female gender is inferior, those positions like Sakka are also prohibited for her.

Is it not the case that just as there is no female gender in the Brahma world, there is also no male gender? Therefore, should it not also be said that 'a man can perform the role of a Brahma' is incorrect? It is not that it should not be said; it should indeed be said. Why? Because a man from here can be reborn there. By 'the state of a Brahma,' the state of a Great Brahma (Mahā-brahmā) is intended. A woman, having developed jhāna here, upon passing away, can be reborn into the company of the Brahma-pārisajja, but not as a Great Brahma. However, it cannot be said that a man cannot be born in that Mahā-brahmā realm. Although both genders are absent there, Brahmas have only a male appearance, not a female appearance. Therefore, this statement is well-spoken.
87: Regarding the terms such as "kāya-duccaritassa" (of bodily misconduct), just as seeds of the neem (nimbabīja) or the sponge gourd (kosātakibīja) do not produce sweet fruit but only produce unpleasant and non-sweet fruit, similarly, bodily misconduct and the like do not produce sweet results (vipāka) but only produce unpleasant results. Just as seeds of sugarcane or sālī rice produce only sweet and delicious fruit and do not produce unpleasant or bitter fruit, similarly, bodily good conduct and the like produce only sweet results and do not produce unpleasant results. It has also been said: "According to the seed that is sown, so is the fruit that is reaped. The doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil." Therefore, it is said: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that for one who has committed bodily misconduct (there should be a good result)," and so on. Regarding the terms such as "kāya-duccarita-samangī" (one possessed of bodily misconduct), "possession" (samangī) is of five kinds: possession by accumulation (āyūhana-samangitā), possession by volition (cetanā-samangitā), possession by kamma (kamma-samangitā), possession by result (vipāka-samangitā), and possession by appearance (upaṭṭhāna-samangitā). Among these five, the moment of striving and accumulating wholesome or unwholesome kamma is called "possession by accumulation." "Possession by volition" is the same. As long as beings have not reached the fruit of Arahantship, they are called "possessed of kamma" (kamma-samangī) with reference to the kamma accumulated in the past that is capable of yielding results; this is "possession by kamma." "Possession by result" should be understood only at the moment the result is given. As long as beings have not reached the fruit of Arahantship, when they pass away from various realms, for those about to be born in hell, hell appears through signs such as flames of fire or iron cauldrons (lohakumbhī); for those about to enter a womb (gabbhaseyyaka), the mother's womb appears; for those about to be born among devas, the deva world appears through signs such as wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha) or celestial mansions. Thus, the sign of rebirth (paṭisandhi-nimitta) appears. This state of being inseparable from the appearance of the sign of rebirth is called "possession by appearance." Only this "possession by appearance" is unstable (changeable); the other types of possession are stable. Even after the sign of hell has appeared, the sign of the deva world can appear; even after the sign of the deva world has appeared, the sign of hell can appear; even after the sign of the human world has appeared, the sign of the animal realm can appear; and even after the sign of the animal realm has appeared, the sign of the human world can appear. In this regard, there is this story: At the Acela Monastery at the foot of Sona Mountain, there was a Dhamma preacher named Elder Soṇa. His father was a man who made a living by hunting with dogs. Although the Elder tried to restrain him, he could not establish him in restraint. Thinking, "May my father not perish," he ordained him as a monk in his old age, even though the father was unwilling. ...
88:
The man named "Jaraka" was ordained in his old age against his will. While he was lying on his sickbed due to illness, hell appeared to him. Large dogs from the foot of Soṇagiri mountain approached and surrounded him as if they wanted to bite and eat him. Terrified by this great danger, he cried out, "Dear Soṇa, stop them! Dear Soṇa, stop them!" When asked, "Great Elder, what should I stop?", he replied, "Dear, do you not see?" and explained the situation. The Elder Soṇa thought, "How can the father of one like me be reborn in hell? I shall be his refuge." He then had the novices bring various kinds of flowers and arranged for offerings of floor-coverings and seats at the stupa courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard. He carried his father on a couch to the stupa courtyard, sat him up on the couch, and said, "Great Elder, this offering is made for your benefit. Say, 'This is my humble gift to the Blessed One,' and pay homage to the Blessed One to gladden your mind." When the Great Elder saw the offering and acted accordingly, his mind became clear. At that very moment, the deva world appeared before him. It was as if the Nandana Grove, Cittalatā Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, celestial mansions, and divine dancers stood surrounding him. He said, "Move aside, move aside, Soṇa!" When asked, "Great Elder, what is this?", he replied, "Dear, these are your mothers coming." The Elder thought, "Heaven has appeared to the Great Elder." It should be understood that this attainment of manifestation (upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā) is unstable. Among these attainments, it is spoken of as "one endowed with bodily misconduct," etc., by the power of the volition of karma exerted in this Dispensation.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the Venerable Ānanda thought, "The Blessed One has reflected well on the entire sutta from the beginning and taught it so gloriously, yet He has not yet given a name to the sutta He taught. I will ask Him for a name." He then addressed the Blessed One in this way. In the words "Therefore, you..." etc., the connection of meaning is: Ānanda, because in this Dhamma discourse, many elements have been analyzed as "Ānanda, these eighteen elements, these six elements," therefore, you should remember this Dhamma discourse as the "Bahudhātuka Sutta." Furthermore, because in this sutta, by the power of elements, bases, dependent origination, and possible and impossible causes, there are four rounds (parivaṭṭa)...
89:
...has been taught; therefore, remember this discourse also as the Catu-parivaṭṭa Sutta. Just as the reflection of a face is clear to one looking into a mirror, so too are the meanings of these elements and so forth clear to one who looks into and contemplates this Dhamma teaching; therefore, remember this discourse also as the Dhammādāsa Sutta. Just as warriors who crush the enemy's army raise the sound of the battle-drums, enter the enemy's ranks, crush the foes, and achieve their victory; in the same way, yogis who crush the army of defilements raise insight (vipassanā) as taught in this discourse, crush the defilements, and achieve their victory, which is the fruit of Arahantship; therefore, remember this discourse also as the Amatadundubhi Sutta. Just as brave warriors on the battlefield take up the five kinds of weapons, destroy the enemy's army, and achieve victory; in the same way, yogis take up the weapon of insight taught in this discourse, destroy the army of defilements, and achieve the victory of Arahantship; therefore, remember this discourse also as the Anuttaro Saṅgāmavijayo Sutta.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Bahudhātuka Sutta is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Isigili Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Isigili Sutta. In that sutta, the phrase "aññāva samaññā ahosi" means that at the time when the name 'Isigili' arose for Mount Isigili, Mount Vebhāra was not known as Vebhāra, but had another name. "Aññā paññatti" is a synonym for the preceding phrase "aññā samaññā". The same method should be understood for the remaining terms.

At that time, it is said that the Blessed One, having emerged from meditative attainment in the evening, came out of the Fragrant Cell (Gandhakuṭi) and sat surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at a place where the five mountains were clearly visible, and he explained these five mountains in order. In doing so, although the Blessed One had no personal need for the mountains, when explaining these mountains in order, the reason for Isigili being called 'Isigili' had to be told. When that was told, the names of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas, who were the sons of Queen Padumavatī, and the aspiration of Padumavatī would also have to be told; therefore, the Blessed One explained the sequence of these five mountains.
90:
It means that they are seen entering, but once they have entered, they are seen no more. Having wandered for alms in a suitable place and finished their meal, they return and enter the mountain by splitting it in two, as if opening the great twin doors of a shrine's inner chamber. Having created places for the night and places for the day, they dwell within that mountain; therefore, He said, "These sages (isī)." "These sages" refers to these Paccekabuddha sages.

When did those Paccekabuddhas dwell within that mountain? It is said that in the past, before the appearance of the Tathāgata, a certain noble daughter living in a small village near Bārāṇasī was guarding a field. She offered a single lotus flower along with five hundred portions of puffed rice to a Paccekabuddha and prayed for five hundred sons. At that very moment, five hundred hunters also offered delicious meat and prayed, "May we become the sons of this woman." After living out her lifespan, she was reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from there, she was conceived in a lotus calyx in the Jātassara lake. A certain hermit saw her and raised her. As she wandered about, lotus flowers sprang up from the earth at every step she took. A forest-dweller saw this and informed the King of Bārāṇasī. The King had her brought to him and made her his chief queen. She became pregnant, and Prince Mahāpaduma dwelt in his mother's womb, while the remaining five hundred princes were born dependent on the impurities of the womb. When they reached maturity, while playing in the lotus pond in the royal garden, they sat upon individual lotus flowers and, by contemplating decay and dissolution (khaya-vaya), they attained the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. This was their verse of declaration:

"The lotus born in the lake, together with its leaves,
Well-bloomed and frequented by swarms of bees,
Having realized it is subject to impermanence,
One should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn."

At that time, those Paccekabuddhas dwelt there, and thus the name "Isigili" (Sage-swallower) arose for that mountain.

Regarding "Ye sattasārā," He mentioned the names of thirteen Paccekabuddhas: Ariṭṭha, Upariṭṭha, Tagarasikhī, Yasassī, Sudassana, Piyadassī, Gandhāra, Piṇḍola, Upāsabha, Nīta, Tatha, Sutavā, and Bhāvitatta. Now, wishing to show the names of these and other Paccekabuddhas in verse form, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Ye sattasārā." In that text, "Sattasārā" means they are the essence because they are endowed with the essence of beings, such as mindfulness and virtue. "Anīghā" means those who are free from suffering. "Nirāsā" means those who are free from craving. "Dve Jālī" refers to the two Paccekabuddhas named Cūḷajālī and Mahājālī. "Santacitta" is also the name of a single Paccekabuddha. In the passage "Passī jahi upadhidukkhamūlaṃ," there is a Paccekabuddha named Passī; the phrase "abandoned upadhi, the root of suffering" is a praise (thuti) of that Paccekabuddha.
91:
The Teacher spoke the words beginning with "Sattasārā." Therein, "Sattasārā" means those who are the essence of beings (endowed with the essence of mindfulness, virtue, etc.). "Anīghā" means those without suffering. "Nirāsā" means those without craving.

"Dve Jālino" refers to the two named Cūḷajālī and Mahājālī. The name "Santacitto" is also the name of a single Paccekabuddha. In the passage "Passī jahi upadhidukkhamūlaṃ," there is a Paccekabuddha named Passī; the statement that he abandoned upadhi, the root of suffering, is a praise (thuti) of him. "Aparājito" is also the name of a single Paccekabuddha.

There are these five individuals: Satthā, Pavattā, Sarabhaṅga, Lomahaṃsa, and Uccaṅgamāya. There are also these three individuals: Asita, Anāsava, and Manomaya. "Mānacchido ca Bandhumā" refers to one Paccekabuddha named Bandhumā; he is called "Mānacchida" because he has cut off pride. "Tadādhimutto" is also a name.

There are these three individuals: Ketumbharāga, Mātaṅga, and Ariya. "Athaccuto" refers to Atha and Accuta. There are these two individuals: Accutagāmabyāmaṅka. There are only these two: Khemābhirata and Sorata.

"Sayho anomanikkamo" refers to the Buddha named Sayha; he is called "Anomanikkama" because of his undiminished exertion. "Ānando nando upanando dvādasa" means there are four named Ānanda, four named Nanda, and four named Upananda, making twelve in total. "Bhāradvājo antimadehadhārī" refers to the Buddha named Bhāradvāja. The phrase "Antimadehadhārī" (bearer of the final body) is a praise.

"Taṇhacchido" is a praise of the Paccekabuddha Sikharī. "Vītarāgo" is a praise of the Paccekabuddha named Maṅgala. "Usabhacchidā jāliniṃ dukkhamūlaṃ" means the Buddha named Usabha cut the net of craving (jālinī), which is the root of suffering. "Santaṃ padaṃ ajjhagamopanīto" means the Buddha named Upanīta reached the peaceful state (Nibbāna). "Vītarāgo" is also the name of a single Paccekabuddha. "Suvimuttacitto" is a praise of the Paccekabuddha named Kaṇha.

"Ete ca anye ca" means these Paccekabuddhas mentioned in the Pali text and other Paccekabuddhas not mentioned in the Pali text who share the same names as those in the Pali. Indeed, among these five hundred Paccekabuddhas, there were those with identical names, such as two, three, ten, or twelve, just like the Ānandas and others. Thus, using only the names that appear in the Pali text, [He spoke] the names of all Paccekabuddhas...
92:
"They are spoken" means that after this specific enumeration, instead of speaking separately, he says, "These Paccekabuddhas and others." The rest of the text is clear in all places.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Isigili Sutta is finished.
## 7. Explanation of the Mahācattārīsaka Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahācattārīsaka Sutta. In that sutta, "ariya" (noble) refers to the faultless supramundane Dhamma; for only the faultless Dhamma is called "ariya." "Sammāsamādhi" (right concentration) refers to the concentration associated with the Path (maggasamādhi). "Saupanisa" (with its causes) means occurring together with its causal conditions. "Saparikkhāra" (with its requisites) means occurring together with its followers.

"Parikkhata" (encompassed) has the meaning of being surrounded by followers. "Right view is the precursor" means that two kinds of right view, namely, insight right view (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi) and path right view (magga-sammādiṭṭhi), are the precursors (the leaders). Insight right view investigates the formations belonging to the three planes of existence by way of impermanence and so forth. Path right view, however, at the conclusion of the investigation, arises while utterly uprooting and calming the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) that has gained a footing, like pouring a thousand pots of cold water over the head.

Just as a farmer, when working the field, first cuts down the trees in the forest and later sets them on fire, and that fire completely burns the previously cut trees without remainder; in the same way, insight right view first investigates formations by way of impermanence and so forth, and path right view arises while utterly uprooting those formations investigated by insight, by way of their non-recurrence. In this sutta, both these kinds of right view are intended.

"He knows it as wrong view" means that he knows wrong view by taking it as an object through the penetration of characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. He knows right view by way of its function and by way of non-delusion. "He has right view" means that such knowing is called his right view.

"I speak of two kinds" means he speaks of two portions (mundane and supramundane). "Puññabhāgiya" (sharing in merit) means belonging to the portion of merit. "Upadhivepakka" (ripening in the essentials of existence) means giving the result (vipāka) known as the aggregates (upadhi).

In the terms "paññā" (wisdom) and "paññindriya" (wisdom faculty) and so forth, it is called "paññā" because it shows and makes known the door to the Deathless by analyzing and distinguishing. It is called "paññindriya" because it exercises lordship (indatta) in that sense. Because of ignorance...
93:
It is called the power of wisdom (paññābala) because it is unshakable. It is called the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) because, having reached the state of an enlightenment factor, it investigates the four noble truths. It is called right view (sammādiṭṭhi) because it is a beautiful and praised vision due to the attainment of the Path. It is called a path factor (maggaṅga) because it is a limb of the Noble Path. "So" refers to that bhikkhu. "Pahānāya" means for the purpose of abandoning. "Upasampadāya" means for the purpose of attaining. Right effort (sammāvāyāma) is the wholesome effort that leads out of saṃsāra. "Sato" means being endowed with mindfulness. "Anuparihāventi anuparivattanti" means that they surround it, being both conascent (sahajāta) and pre-nascent (purejāta). Here, right effort and right mindfulness surround supramundane right view as conascent factors, like a sword-bearer and an umbrella-bearer standing on the same chariot attending a king. Insight right view, however, surrounds it as a pre-nascent factor, like infantrymen in front of a chariot. From the second section onwards, it should be understood that the three factors beginning with right intention are also only conascent attendants.

"He knows it as wrong intention" means he knows wrong intention by taking it as an object through the penetration of characteristics as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. He knows right intention by way of its path-function and by way of non-delusion. In the subsequent factors such as right speech and so forth, the application should be understood in this same way. Sensual intention and so forth have already been mentioned in the Dvedhāvitakka Sutta.

In the terms "takka" and so forth, it is called "takka" (reasoning) by way of thinking. That same factor is called "vitakka" (applied thought) by expanding the word with the prefix "vi," and it is called "saṅkappa" (intention) by way of intending. It is called "appanā" (absorption) because it fixes the mind on the object by being one-pointed. It is called "byappanā" (fixed absorption) by expanding the word with the prefix "vi." "Cetaso abhiniropanā" means the directing of the mind onto the object. When vitakka is present, vitakka directs the mind onto the object. But when vitakka is absent, the mind ascends to the object by its own nature, like a well-born and well-known man entering the king's palace. For an unknown man, there is a need for a messenger or a doorkeeper. But all the king's great ministers know a well-known man of good birth, so he enters and leaves by his own nature. This should be understood according to this analogy. It is called verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra) because it prepares and conditions speech. Here, only mundane vitakka conditions speech, not supramundane vitakka. Even though it does not condition speech, its name remains "vacīsaṅkhāra." "Sammāsaṅkappaṃ anuparihāventi" means they surround supramundane right intention. In this surrounding, the three...
94:
The three types of Right Intention, starting with the intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa), are obtained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage (of the Path). At the moment of the Path, however, a single Right Intention arises, fulfilling the factor of the Path while completely cutting off and uprooting sensual intention and so forth; it receives three names by way of renunciation intention and so forth. The same method should be understood for Right Speech and so forth that follow.

In terms such as 'abstinence from false speech' (musāvādā veramaṇī), both abstinence (virati) and volition (cetanā) are appropriate. In terms such as 'ārati', it is called 'ārati' because of abstaining far from verbal misconduct. It is called 'virati' because of abstaining by being devoid of those verbal misconducts. It is called 'paṭivirati' because of abstaining by turning back from those various misconducts. Alternatively, these are just names for the nature of abstaining, with the words expanded by the power of prefixes (upasagga). It is called 'veramaṇī' because it destroys enmity (vera, unwholesome kamma). This too is a synonym for abstaining. In terms such as 'abstinence from taking life' (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī), both volition and abstinence are also appropriate.

In terms such as 'kuhanā' (scheming), it is called 'kuhanā' because it makes the world wonder through the three bases of scheming. It is called 'lapanā' (persuading) because of speaking with the desire for gain, honor, and renown. It is called 'nemittika' because of the habit of giving hints to obtain requisites, and the state of such people is called 'nemittikatā' (hinting). It is called 'nippesika' because of the habit of belittling or pressuring for the sake of gain and honor, and the state of such people is called 'nippesikatā' (belittling). It is called 'lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanā' because of seeking the gain of others with one's own gain, and the state of such people is called 'lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā' (pursuing gain with gain). This is only a brief explanation here. In detail, these terms like 'kuhanā' have been explained in the Sīlaniddesa of the Visuddhimagga, citing the Pāḷi and Commentaries.

In the phrase 'for the abandoning of wrong livelihood' (micchā-ājīvassa pahānāya), it is not only the wrong livelihood mentioned in the Pāḷi text, but also the volitions of the seven courses of action (kammapatha), such as taking life, which arise for the sake of livelihood, that are also wrong livelihood. The abstinence (virati) that arises while completely cutting off and uprooting those seven volitions and fulfilling the Path factor is called Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva).

'Sammādiṭṭhissa' means for a person established in Right View associated with the Path. 'Sammāsaṅkappo pahoti' means Right Intention associated with the Path arises; for a person established in Right View associated with the Fruition, Right Intention associated with the Fruition also arises. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms.
95:
In the phrase 'sammāñāṇassa sammāvimutti', for a person established in Path Right Concentration, Right Knowledge that reviews the Path arises; for a person established in Fruition Right Concentration, Right Knowledge that reviews the Fruition arises. For a person established in Right Knowledge that reviews the Path, Path Right Liberation arises; for a person established in Right Knowledge that reviews the Fruition, Fruition Right Liberation arises. This is the meaning. Here, it is stated that, setting aside the eight factors of Fruition, it is appropriate to treat reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) as Right Knowledge and Fruition (phala) as Right Liberation.

In these sections beginning with 'Monks, for one with Right View, wrong view is worn away,' the Elders who are reciters of the other Nikāyas say that Fruition is being taught; however, the Elders who are reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya say that the Path is being taught in the context of the ten things that lead to wearing away (nijjaravatthu). Therein, it should be known as Right View because of the sense of seeing the Four Noble Truths; as Right Knowledge because of the sense of making known what has been known; and as Right Liberation because of the sense of being released into that object.

'Twenty wholesome factors' (vīsati kusalapakkha) refers to the ten factors starting with Right View and the ten factors taught by the method 'due to Right View, many wholesome states arise,' thus making twenty wholesome factors. 'Twenty unwholesome factors' (vīsati akusalapakkha) should be known as the ten factors starting with wrong view taught by the method 'wrong view is worn away' and the ten factors taught by the method 'due to wrong view, many evil states arise,' thus making twenty unwholesome factors. It is called 'Mahācattārīsaka' (The Great Forty) because it shows the forty factors—both the noble wholesome factors and the unwholesome factors—which give great results.

In this sutta, five types of Right View are taught: Insight Right View (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi), Right View of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-sammādiṭṭhi), Path Right View (magga-sammādiṭṭhi), Fruition Right View (phala-sammādiṭṭhi), and Reviewing Right View (paccavekkhaṇā-sammādiṭṭhi). Among those five, the Right View taught by the method 'one understands wrong view as wrong view' is called Insight Right View. The Right View taught by the method 'there is the result of giving' is called Right View of the ownership of kamma. In the passage 'Monks, for one with Right View, Right Intention arises,' both Path Right View and Fruition Right View are taught. In the passage 'Right Knowledge arises,' it should be understood that Reviewing Right View is taught.
96:
Reviling Right View means that one who says, 'This so-called Right View is not beautiful,' or 'This so-called Right View is not good,' is said to revile Right View. 'Okkala' refers to the inhabitants of the Okkala region. 'Vassabhañño' refers to two individuals named Vassa and Bhañña. 'Ahetukavāda' (the doctrine of non-causality) refers to those who hold views such as 'There is no cause or condition for the purification of beings.' 'Akiriyavāda' (the doctrine of non-action) refers to those who reject action, holding views such as 'Even if one does evil, it is not considered as having been done.' 'Natthikavāda' (the doctrine of nihilism) refers to those who hold views such as 'There is no fruit in giving or offerings.' These people become fixed and established in these three views.

As to how the result becomes fixed in those views—a certain person, having adopted such a view, sits during the night or day, reciting and investigating it. For him, wrong mindfulness (*micchā-sati*) becomes established on that object, thinking: 'There is no cause, no condition; even if one acts, no evil is done; there is no fruit in giving; upon the breakup of the body, one is annihilated.' The mind becomes concentrated, and the impulsion-moments (*javana*) run. During the first impulsion-moment, he can still be cured; likewise in the second and so on. However, at the seventh impulsion-moment, he becomes incurable even by the Buddhas; he does not turn back, becoming like the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇḍaka.

Among those views, some enter into one view, some into two, and some into all three. Such a person becomes one of fixed wrong view (*niyata-micchādiṭṭhi*) and reaches the state of being obstructed from the path to heaven and the path to liberation. He is incapable of going even to heaven immediately after that life, let alone to liberation. This being is like a stump in the round of rebirths (*vaṭṭakhāṇu*), a 'guardian of the earth.' Generally, for such a person, there is no rising up from existence. Vassa and Bhañña were also such persons. 'Nindābyārosaupārambhabhayā' means out of fear of being reviled, fear of being offended or oppressed, and fear of being blamed. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## 8. Explanation of the Ānāpānassati Sutta
'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth: this is the Ānāpānassati Sutta. In that sutta, 'aññehi ca' (and with others) means that, setting aside the ten great elders mentioned in the Pāḷi, together with other well-known and very learned disciple-monks, the assembly of monks at that time was very grand and immeasurable in number. 'Ovādānusāsanī' means instructing and admonishing by supporting them with the two kinds of hospitality—material hospitality and Dhamma hospitality—and by giving meditation subjects...
97:
(He dwelt) together with many disciples. At that time, the assembly of monks was grand and of immeasurable number.

'They instruct, they admonish repeatedly' means they instruct and admonish by supporting them with the two kinds of hospitality—material hospitality and Dhamma hospitality—and by giving meditation subjects, instructing, and repeatedly admonishing. In the phrase 'te ca', the letter 'ca' is merely a grammatical conjunction (*āgamasandhi*). 'They know a grand distinction following a previous one' means they know a subsequent distinction, such as the preliminary work for kasiṇa meditation, which is more excellent and grander than a previous distinction such as the fulfillment of virtue.

'Āraddho' means satisfied (pleased). 'For the sake of attaining the unattained' means for the purpose of reaching the fruit of Arahantship which has not yet been reached. The same meaning should be understood for the remaining two phrases. 'The full moon day of the fourth month, Komudī' refers to the full moon day of the latter Kattika, the end of the four months. That month is called 'Komudī' because the white water lilies (*kumuda*) bloom then, and it is called 'Cātumāsinī' because it is the end of the four months of the rainy season. 'I shall wait' means that after performing the Pavāraṇā today, until that Kattika full moon arrives, I shall stay right here without going anywhere else. Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to allow the favor of Pavāraṇā to the monks, spoke in this way.

The favor of Pavāraṇā (*pavāraṇā-saṅgaha*) is given by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (*ñattidutiya-kamma*). To whom is it given, and to whom is it not given? Firstly, it is not given to a foolish worldling who does not practice. Likewise, it is not given to those who are already practicing insight (*vipassanā*) or to the noble disciples (*ariya-sāvaka*). However, it is given to a monk whose tranquillity (*samatha*) or insight is still tender (immature). At that time, the Blessed One, investigating the mental behavior of the monks and knowing the immaturity of their tranquillity and insight, thought: 'If I were to perform the Pavāraṇā today, the monks who have completed the rains retreat in various regions would flock here to Sāvatthī. Then, these monks (with immature practice) would not be able to achieve distinction because the senior monks would have taken up the lodgings. If I were to set out on a journey, it would be difficult for these monks to find a place to stay. But if I do not perform the Pavāraṇā, the monks will not flock to Sāvatthī, and I myself will not set out on a journey. In this way, the dwelling place of these monks will be free from disturbance. Staying comfortably in their respective places, they will be able to strengthen their tranquillity and insight and achieve distinction.' Having thought thus, he did not perform the Pavāraṇā on that day, but decided to perform it on the Kattika full moon day, and addressed the monks...
98: The Blessed One allowed the support through the Pavāraṇā invitation (pavāraṇā-saṅgaha). When such support through Pavāraṇā is obtained, if the teachers and preceptors of a monk living in dependence (nissaya) depart for another place, that monk, thinking, 'If a suitable teacher who can give dependence arrives, I will take dependence from him,' is allowed to stay until the last month of the summer (the full moon of Āsāḷha). Even if senior monks of sixty years' standing arrive, they are not permitted to take that monk's lodgings. This support through Pavāraṇā, even if given to one individual, is considered as given to all monks. 'They descend to Sāvatthī' means that upon hearing in various places that the Blessed One had granted the support through Pavāraṇā, they stayed for a full month according to their inclination, performed the Uposatha on the full moon day of Kattika, and then descended (to Sāvatthī); this was said with reference to that. In the phrase 'before and after' (pubbenāpara), practicing the tender stages of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) and making them strong is called the 'distinction occurring before.' Thereafter, contemplating conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) with a concentrated mind, some realized the Fruit of Stream-entry... and some realized Arahantship. This is called the 'great distinction occurring after.' 'Alaṃ' means it is suitable. 'Counts of yojanas' (yojana-gaṇanāni) means one yojana is just one yojana, ten yojanas are just ten yojanas; any number beyond that is called 'yojana-gaṇanāni.' Here, even a hundred yojanas or a thousand yojanas are intended. 'Even with a bag of provisions' (puṭosena pi) means a bag of provisions is called 'puṭosa.' The meaning is that it is indeed suitable to approach even while carrying that bag of provisions. There is also a variant reading 'puṭaṃsena,' which means one who has a bag on the shoulder; thus it means even while carrying a bag of provisions on the shoulder. Now, to show that there are monks in this Dispensation endowed with such conduct, He said 'There are, monks' (santi, bhikkhave) and so forth. Therein, 'the four foundations of mindfulness' and so forth were spoken to show the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) undertaken by those monks. Therein, the thirty-seven qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), both mundane and supramundane, were taught. For those monks who develop the Path at that moment, they are supramundane. For those who are still striving in insight, they are mundane. In the phrase 'application to the development of the perception of impermanence' (anicca-saññā-bhāvanā-anuyoga), insight is taught by way of perception (saññā). Since among this group of monks, by the power of the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) meditation...
99:
Among these monks, there are many who are firmly established in the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-kammaṭṭhāna). Therefore, having briefly spoken of the other meditation subjects, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Ānāpānasati, bhikkhave," wishing to explain mindfulness of breathing in detail. Since this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing has been explained in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga, the meaning of the Pali text and the method of its development (bhāvanā) should be understood exactly as stated in that work.

"Kāyanyataraṃ" (one of the bodies) means one of the four bodies such as the earth-body (pathavīkāya); it means the wind-body (vāyokāya). Alternatively, the twenty-five material groups starting from the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) up to nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) are called the "material body" (rūpakāya). Among these material groups, mindfulness of breathing is included in the sense-base of touch (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), and thus it is one among the bodies; for this reason, it was spoken of in this way. "Tasmātiha" means because one repeatedly contemplates either the wind-body, which is one among the four bodies, or mindfulness of breathing, which is one among the twenty-five material groups of the material body; therefore, one is called "a contemplator of the body in the body" (kāye kāyānupassī). In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sentences.

"Vedanānyataraṃ" (one of the feelings) is spoken with reference to pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā), which is one among the three feelings. "Sādhukaṃ manasikāraṃ" (thorough attention) refers to the excellent attention that arises by way of experiencing rapture (pīti-paṭisaṃveditā), etc. If it is asked, "Is attention (manasikāra) pleasant feeling?" No, it is not. However, this is taught as a heading of the teaching (desanāsīsa). Just as in the passage "devoted to the development of the perception of impermanence" (aniccasaññābhāvanānuyoga-manuyuttā), wisdom (paññā) is spoken of by the name of perception (saññā), so too here, feeling (vedanā) should be understood as being spoken of by the name of attention (manasikāra). In the first phrase of this tetrad (catukka), feeling is spoken of with rapture (pīti) as the heading; in the second phrase, feeling is spoken of by its own nature as "bliss" (sukhaṃ).

In the two phrases regarding mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra), because of the statement "Perception and feeling are mental; these things are mental formations bound to the mind," and because of the statement "Excluding initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra), all states associated with the mind are included in mental formations," feeling is spoken of by the name of mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra). Including all of that under the name of attention, it is said here as "thorough attention" (sādhukaṃ manasikāraṃ).

Even so, if it is said that "Because this feeling is not the object, contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā) is not appropriate," it is not that it is inappropriate; it is indeed appropriate. For in the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna, it is explained: "Having made that particular object such as pleasure the basis, feeling itself feels; however, based on the occurrence of that feeling, there is merely the conventional expression 'I feel.'"
100:
It is stated thus. Furthermore, in the explanation of the meaning of the terms beginning with 'experiencing rapture' (pītipaṭisaṃvedī), the answer to this problem has already been explained (by me, the commentator). This statement is explained in the Visuddhimagga as follows:

'Rapture is clearly experienced (felt) in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion. How is rapture clearly experienced by way of the object? One enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture (the first and second jhānas) in succession; for that person, at the moment of attainment, because of the attainment of the jhāna, rapture is clearly experienced by way of the object, since the object is experienced. How is rapture clearly experienced by way of non-delusion? Having entered the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and having emerged, one contemplates the rapture associated with the jhāna by way of its passing away and vanishing; for that person, at the moment of insight, because of the penetration of the characteristics, rapture is clearly experienced by way of non-delusion. This was also stated (by the Venerable Sāriputta) in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "For one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by virtue of a long inhalation, mindfulness is established; with that mindfulness and with that knowledge, that rapture is clearly experienced." In this very way, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning.'

Just as rapture, pleasure, and mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra) are clearly experienced by way of the object through the attainment of jhāna, so too this yogi, through the attainment of attention called feeling associated with jhāna, clearly experiences feeling by way of the object. Therefore, this statement: 'At that time, a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings' is well-stated.

In the passage, 'Monks, I do not say (that there is the development of mindfulness of breathing) for one who is unmindful and lacks clear comprehension,' this is the intended meaning: Because a monk proceeding in the manner beginning with 'experiencing the mind, I shall breathe in,' even if he takes the sign of inhalation and exhalation as the object, he proceeds by establishing mindfulness and clear comprehension in the object of that mind; therefore, he is indeed one who contemplates the mind in the mind. Indeed, for one who is unmindful and lacks clear comprehension, there is no development of mindfulness of breathing. Therefore, by virtue of clearly experiencing the mind by way of the object, etc., the statement 'At that time, a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind' is well-stated. Having seen with wisdom the abandoning of those covetousness and grief, he is one who looks on with equanimity. Here, by 'covetousness' (abhijjhā), the hindrance of sensual desire is meant, and by virtue of 'grief' (domanassa)...
101:
...the hindrance of ill-will is shown. This tetrad is stated solely by virtue of insight (vipassanā). Contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) is sixfold by virtue of the section on hindrances and so on. In that contemplation of phenomena, the section on hindrances is the beginning. In that section on hindrances, these two hindrances (sensual desire and ill-will) are the beginning. Thus, to show the beginning of the contemplation of phenomena, it is said: 'of covetousness and grief' (abhijjhā-domanassānaṃ). By 'abandoning' (pahāna), the knowledge of abandoning, which is the abandoning of the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence, is intended. 'Having seen that with wisdom' means seeing that knowledge of abandoning—known as the contemplation of impermanence, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment—with subsequent insight wisdom, and that with further insight wisdom; thus it shows the succession of insight. 'He is one who looks on with equanimity' (ajjhupekkhitā hoti) is of two kinds: looking on with equanimity at insight preceded by serenity (samatha), and looking on with equanimity at the manifestation as a whole. In such looking on with equanimity, there is looking on with equanimity at conascent (sahajāta) states and looking on with equanimity at the object; here, looking on with equanimity at the object (ārammaṇa-ajjhupekkhanā) is intended.

Therefore, monks, because a monk proceeding in the manner beginning with 'contemplating impermanence, I shall breathe in' sees with wisdom and looks on with equanimity not only at the phenomena such as hindrances, but also at the knowledge of abandoning those phenomena mentioned under the heading of covetousness and grief, it should be understood that 'At that time, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.'

'Investigates' (pavicinati) means investigating and contemplating by virtue of impermanence and so on. The other two terms (dhamma-vicaya, parivīmaṃsa) are synonyms for this term. 'Unworldly' (nirāmisa) means free from defilements. 'Subsides' (passambhati) means that both body and mind become calm due to the subsiding of bodily and mental distress. 'Is concentrated' (samādhiyati) means it is well-established, as if reaching absorption (appanā). 'He is one who looks on with equanimity' means he looks on with equanimity by way of looking on with equanimity at conascent states.

Thus, for a monk who grasps the body in fourteen ways, the mindfulness in that body is the mindfulness enlightenment factor (sati-sambojjhaṅga). The knowledge associated with mindfulness is the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga). The bodily and mental energy associated with that is the energy enlightenment factor (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga). Rapture, tranquility, and one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā) are also enlightenment factors. The neutral mode of these six enlightenment factors, characterized by neither retreating nor overreaching, is the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga). Just as a charioteer, when the horses are running evenly, does not prick them with a goad saying 'this one is lagging,' nor pulls the reins saying 'this one is running too fast,' but merely remains in a state of watching, even so, the neutral mode of these six enlightenment factors, characterized by neither retreating nor overreaching, is called the equanimity enlightenment factor. What is stated by this much? The insight enlightenment factors, which occur in a single mind-moment and have various functions and characteristics, are stated.
102:
The words beginning with "vivekanissita" are just as previously explained. In this context, the mindfulness that grasps the in-breaths and out-breaths is mundane. Mundane in-breaths and out-breaths fulfill the mundane foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Mundane foundations of mindfulness fulfill the supramundane factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). Supramundane factors of enlightenment fulfill the fruit of knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti), which is Nibbāna. Thus, it should be understood that where mundane factors of enlightenment appear, mundane foundations of mindfulness are taught, and where supramundane factors of enlightenment appear, supramundane foundations of mindfulness are taught. However, the Elder said: "In other suttas it may be so, but in this sutta, as it appears above, mundane in-breaths and out-breaths fulfill the mundane foundations of mindfulness; mundane foundations of mindfulness fulfill the mundane factors of enlightenment; mundane factors of enlightenment fulfill the supramundane fruit of knowledge and liberation, Nibbāna. In this context, by the term 'vijjā-vimutti', the fruit of knowledge and liberation, Nibbāna, is intended."

## the Explanation of the Āနāpānassati Sutta is finished.
## 9. Explanation of the Kāyagatāsati Sutta

153-4. The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Kāyagatāsati Sutta. In that sutta, "gehasita" refers to states based on the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Sarasaṅkappa" refers to thoughts that run towards various objects. They are called "sarā" because they run; the meaning is "running". "Ajjhattameva" means staying only within the internal sphere which is one's own object. "Kāyagatāsati" refers to both the mindfulness that grasps the in-breaths and out-breaths, and the mindfulness associated with insight that has the in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. When it is said "grasping the body" (kāyapariiggāhika), it refers to calm (samatha); when it is said "having the body as object" (kāyārammaṇa), it refers to insight (vipassanā). By both, both calm and insight are taught. By the words "Puna caparaṃ... pe... evampi, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāyagatāsatiṃ bhာveti", the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) is taught in fourteen ways within the foundations of mindfulness. "Antogadhāvassa" means they have entered into the meditation of that bhikkhu. "Vijjābhāgiya" means, in this context, they are called 'partaking of knowledge' because they associate with the eight kinds of knowledge by way of association (sampayoga). Alternatively, they are called 'partaking of knowledge' because they exist in the portion of knowledge, the category of knowledge.
103:
In the term *vijjābhāgiya*, there are eight kinds of knowledge: insight knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), mind-made power (*manomayiddhi*), and the six higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). According to the first meaning mentioned, the mental states (*citta-cetasika*) associated with these eight knowledges are also called *vijjābhāgiya* (states partaking of knowledge). According to the latter meaning, one of those eight is called *vijjā* (knowledge), and the remaining seven are called *vijjābhāgiya*. Thus, both the eight knowledges and the mental factors associated with knowledge should be understood as *vijjābhāgiya*.

Regarding the phrase "pervaded with the mind" (*cetasa phuṭo*), there are two types of pervading: pervading with the water element (*āpo-pharaṇa*) and pervading with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu-pharaṇa*). Among them, entering the water-kasina and pervading with the counterpart sign of the water-kasina is called *āpo-pharaṇa*. In the Great Ocean thus pervaded, all the small rivers flowing into the ocean are as if they have entered within. Developing the light-kasina and seeing the entire ocean with the divine eye-knowledge is called *dibba-cakkhu-pharaṇa*. In the Great Ocean thus pervaded, all the small rivers flowing into the ocean are likewise as if they have entered within.

"*Otāra*" refers to an opening or gap for the arising of defilements. "*Ārammaṇa*" refers to the cause for the arising of defilements. "*Labhetha otāraṃ*" means that [defilements] might gain access, or might penetrate through to the end. "*Nikkhepana*" is the place of putting down.

Thus, after comparing a person who has not developed mindfulness of the body to a heap of wet clay and so on, the phrase beginning with "*seyyathāpi*" is spoken to compare a person who has developed mindfulness of the body to a heartwood plank and so on. In that phrase, "*aggaḷaphalaka*" means a door-panel.

"*Kākapeyya*" (crow-drinkable) means [a pond so full of water] that a crow sitting on the rim can drink without bending its neck. "*Abhiññā-sacchikaraṇīyassa*" means inclining the mind toward a state that is to be realized through higher knowledge. "*Sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti*" means reaching the state of direct witnessing. "*Sati sati āyatane*" means "when there is a cause." What is the cause here? Higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) itself is the cause. "*Āḷibandhā*" means bound by embankments.

"*Yānikatāya*" means mindfulness of the body that is made like a well-fitted vehicle. "*Vatthukatāya*" means mindfulness of the body that is made into a foundation. "*Anuṭṭhitāya*" means mindfulness of the body that is practiced repeatedly. "*Paricitāya*" means mindfulness of the body that is familiarized. "*Susamāraddhāya*" means mindfulness of the body that is well-undertaken and well-upheld. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Kāyagatāsati Sutta is finished.
104:
## 10. Commentary on the Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta

'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth—this is the Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta. In that sutta, 'saṅkhārupapatti' means only the arising of volitional formations, not the arising of a being or a person. Alternatively, it means the arising of the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) that reach existence due to volitional formations of merit (puññābhisaṅkhāra).

'Saddhāya samannāgato' refers to the arising of the five mundane qualities starting with faith (saddhā). 'Dahati' and 'adhiṭṭhāti' mean to establish. 'Saṅkhārā ca vihārā ca' refers to these same five qualities, such as faith, together with the aspiration (patthanā). 'Tatrupapattiyā' means for the sake of arising in that place through rebirth. 'Ayaṃ maggo ayaṃ paṭipadā' also refers to those same five qualities together with the aspiration.

If a person possesses the five qualities but lacks the aspiration, his destination (gati) is not fixed. If a person has the aspiration but lacks the five qualities, his destination is also not fixed. Only when a person possesses both does the destination become fixed. For example, just as a stick thrown into the sky is not certain to fall on its tip, its middle, or its base, the taking of rebirth by beings is likewise uncertain. Therefore, one should perform meritorious deeds and make an aspiration for a specific existence.

'Āmaṇḍa' refers to a wood-apple (āmalaka). Just as everything is clearly visible to a man with pure vision, the thousandfold world system, along with the beings born there, is clearly visible to that Brahmā. This method should be understood in all instances.

'Subha' means beautiful. 'Jātimā' means endowed with excellent quality. 'Suparikammakato' means well-prepared by polishing and so forth. 'Paṇḍukambale nikkhitto' is like a beryl gem placed on a crimson rug.

'Satasahasso' refers to a Brahmā who can pervade a hundred thousand world systems with light. 'Nikkha' is an ornament made of gold weighing five suvaṇṇas. An ornament made of gold weighing less than a nikkha cannot withstand polishing. Gold that exceeds that weight can withstand polishing but does not look beautiful and appears coarse. Only when made with the exact weight of a nikkha can it withstand polishing and also be beautiful. 'Jambonada' refers to the gold that arises in the places where the Jambu fruits fall from the branches of the Great Jambu tree into the rivers flowing on both sides. The river water [carries] those gold sprouts...
105:
...when carried in due course by the river water, they enter the great ocean. With reference to that, it is called 'Jambonada' (Jambu-river gold). 'Dakkhakammāraputtaukkāmukhasukusalasampahaṭṭha' refers to gold that has been refined and made radiant in a furnace by a skilled and very expert goldsmith. 'Ukkāmukhe' means in a furnace. 'Sampahaṭṭha' means that which has been washed, rubbed, and polished (finished). In the Vatthūpama Sutta and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the purification of raw lumps (piṇḍasodhana) is taught. In this sutta, however, the purification of finished articles (katabhaṇḍasodhana) is taught.

In the phrase 'pervading and resolving' (pharitvā adhimuccitvā) mentioned in all sections, pervasion (pharaṇa) is of five kinds: pervasion of mind (cetopharaṇa), pervasion of kasina (kasiṇapharaṇa), pervasion of the divine eye (dibbacakkhupharaṇa), pervasion of light (ālokapharaṇa), and pervasion of body-radiance (sarīrapharaṇa). Among these five, 'pervasion of mind' means knowing the minds of beings in a thousandfold world system. 'Pervasion of kasina' means spreading the kasina in a thousandfold world system. 'Pervasion of the divine eye' means increasing light and viewing a thousandfold world system with the eye of higher knowledge (abhiññā). 'Pervasion of light' is the same as this pervasion of the divine eye. 'Pervasion of body-radiance' means spreading body-radiance in a thousandfold world system. In all places, these five kinds of pervasion should be explained without omission.

However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said, 'It appears like the pervasion of kasina in the gem simile, and like the pervasion of body-radiance in the nikkha simile.' This was rejected, stating that there is no such commentary as the Elder's view, and that pervasion of body-radiance is not possible at all times; thus, it should be explained by keeping these four kinds of pervasion intact. The word 'adhimuccati' is merely a synonym for the word 'pharaṇa'; or else, 'pharati' means spreading and 'adhimuccati' means knowing.

Regarding the terms such as 'Ābhā', there are no separate deities named 'Ābhā'; the three types of deities starting with Parittābhā are called 'Ābhā', and those starting with Parittasubha and Subhakiṇha are called 'Subhā'. The sections on Vehapphala and so forth are already clear.

May one develop these five qualities and be reborn in the sense-sphere realms. If it is asked, 'How does one reach rebirth in the Brahmā world and the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya)?'—these five qualities are virtue (sīla). That person, established in this virtue, performs the preliminary work for kasina, develops various meditative attainments (samāpatti), and is reborn in the fine-material Brahmā world. [Developing] formless jhanas...
106:
...having produced [formless jhanas], he is born in the formless Brahmā world. Having developed insight (vipassanā) with the meditative attainments as the proximate cause, and having realized the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), he is born in the five Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa). By developing the higher paths, he reaches the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya).

## The Commentary on the Second Chapter (Vagga) is finished.
107:
## 3. Suññata Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Cūḷasuññata Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Thus have I heard" (Evaṃ me sutaṃ) is the Cūḷasuññata Sutta. Regarding the words "At one time this" (Ekamidaṃ) in that sutta: It is said that the Elder [Ānanda], after performing his duties for the Blessed One, went to his own place for the day's rest. Having set a time limit, he entered and dwelt in the Suññata-phala-samāpatti (Attainment of the Fruit of Emptiness) taking Nibbāna as the object, and emerged at the designated time. At that moment, the formations (saṅkhāra) appeared to him as empty. A desire arose in that Elder to hear a discourse related to emptiness.

Then this thought occurred to him: "It is not appropriate to go directly to the Blessed One and say, 'Venerable Sir, please preach the Suññatā-kathā (Discourse on Emptiness) to me,' as if striking one burden against another (competing in strength). If I remind the Blessed One of a single statement He made while staying near the Nagaraka market town, the Blessed One will preach the Suññatā-kathā to me." Thus, wishing to remind the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), he spoke the words beginning with "At one time this."

In that context, "idaṃ" is merely a particle. Regarding the request "Is this so, Venerable Sir?" (Kaccimetaṃ bhante): How could the Elder, who was capable of learning and retaining sixty thousand words after hearing just one verse, not be able to retain the single phrase "suññatā-vihārena" (by the dwelling of emptiness)? In truth, one who wishes to hear the Dhamma should not ask as if they already know when they do. Wishing to hear the Suññatā-kathā explained clearly and in detail, he spoke as if he did not know. Some people act as if they know when they do not. How could the Elder practice such deceit? Even in matters he already knew, he spoke the words beginning with "Is this so" to show respect to the Blessed One.

"Formerly too" (Pubbe pi) refers to the time he stayed near the Nagaraka market town during the early period of the Enlightenment. "Now too" (Etarahi pi) refers to the present time. After the Blessed One spoke thus, He thought: "Ānanda wishes to hear the Suññatā-kathā. Some can listen but cannot memorize. Some can listen and memorize but cannot preach. Ānanda, however, is capable of all three: listening, memorizing, and preaching. Therefore, I shall preach the Suññatā-kathā." Thinking thus, He spoke the words beginning with "Just as" (Seyyathāpi). In those words, "empty of elephants, cattle, horses, and mares" (suñño hatthigavāssavaḷavena) means: In that (Migāramātu) palace, there might be elephants and so on made of wood, clay, or paintings. There might also be those made with intricate painting as in the dwellings of Vessavaṇa or King Mandhātu, or gold and silver present in the form of jeweled windows, doors, couches, and stools.
108:
There is also gold and silver kept for repairing old and decayed parts. There are also women and men who come for listening to the Dhamma or asking questions, etc., represented by wooden figures and so on. Therefore, that palace is not empty of those. This was said referring to the absence of elephants and so on that are bound by faculties and possessed of consciousness, the absence of gold and silver that can be used at any desired moment, and the absence of women and men who reside there permanently.

"Dependent on the Saṅgha of monks" (Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṭicca) means that even when the monks have entered for alms, the palace is not empty because of the monks who receive the monastery meals, the sick monks, the attendants of the sick, the designated monks (uddesa), and those busy with robe-making (cīvarakamma). Thus, because monks are always present, He spoke in this way. "Singleness" (Ekattatā) means the state of being one, or having one kind of non-emptiness. It means there is one state of non-emptiness. "Without attending to" (Amanasikaritvā) means without making it in the mind, without reflecting, and without contemplating repeatedly. "Perception of village" (Gāmasaññā) is the perception of "village" that arises either through the continuity of the grasped aggregates (upādinnaka-khandha) or through the power of defilements. The same method applies to the perception of man (manussa-saññā). "Dependent on the perception of forest, he attends to singleness" means he attends to the perception of forest alone, thinking, "This is a forest, this is a tree, this is a mountain, this is a dark green woodland." "Enters into" (Pakkhandati) means he descends into. "Becomes confident" (Adhimuccati) means he resolves and attends to it in this way. "Whatever distresses there might be" (Ye assu darathā) means the distresses of the process (pavatta-daratha) or the distresses of defilements (kilesa-daratha) that would arise dependent on the perception of village are not present here in this perception of forest. The same method applies to the second phrase. "There is only this" (Atthi cevāyaṃ) means there is only the measure of distress of the process that arises dependent on the single perception of forest.

"For whatever is not there" (Yañhi kho tattha na hoti) means that just as there are no elephants and so on in the Migāramātu palace, the mass of distresses of the process and distresses of defilements that arise through the perception of village and perception of man are not present in this perception of forest. "But whatever remains there" (Yaṃ pana tattha avasiṭṭhaṃ) means that just as the Saṅgha of monks remains in the Migāramātu palace, only the measure of distress of the process remains in that perception of forest. "He understands: 'This is present'" (Taṃ santamidaṃ atthīti pajānāti) means he understands that very existing distress as "This is present." "Entry into emptiness" (Suññatāvakkanti) means the arising of emptiness.

"Without attending to the perception of man" (Amanasikaritvā manussasaññaṃ): Here, the perception of village is not taken. Why? It is said that this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "By removing the perception of village through the perception of man, removing the perception of man through the perception of forest, removing the perception of forest through the perception of earth, removing the perception of earth through the perception of the base of infinite space... etc... through the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception..."
109:
(The Buddha thought:) “I will show the ultimate emptiness (Arahatta-phala) in sequence, by causing the perception of the base of nothingness to subside through insight, the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to subside through insight, and insight to subside through the Path.” Therefore, he began this discourse. In that discourse, why is the perception of forest (arañña-saññā) abandoned and the perception of earth (paṭhavī-saññā) attended to? It is because the distinction of the Path and Fruit cannot be attained through the perception of forest.

For example, if a man sees a pleasant field and thinks, ‘Rice and other crops sown here will flourish well, and I will gain great profit,’ but merely looks at that field seven times, the rice and other crops will not flourish. However, if he clears the stumps and thorns from that place, plows it, and sows seeds, then they will flourish. In the same way, even if one attends to the perception of forest seven times, thinking, ‘This is a forest, this is a tree, this is a mountain, this is a dark-green woodland,’ one can reach neither access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) nor absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). But with the perception of earth, by performing the preliminary work (parikamma) on the earth kasiṇa, which is the meditation subject one should constantly cultivate, and by producing the jhānas, one can reach Arahatta-phala by developing insight based on those jhānas. Therefore, the perception of forest is abandoned and the perception of earth is attended to. ‘Paṭicca’ means having arisen dependent on (attending to a single state).

Now, to show an illustration of how that monk possesses the perception of earth in that earth kasiṇa, he said ‘seyyathāpi’ and so on. Therein, ‘āsabhaṃ’ refers to the hide of a bull. In other cattle, there are often lumps and wounds from being struck. When their hides are stretched, they are not free of wrinkles. But because a bull is endowed with excellent characteristics, it does not have those defects. Therefore, the hide of a bull is taken as an example. ‘Saṅkusatena’ means (struck) with a hundred pegs. ‘Suvihataṃ’ means well-stretched and struck. A hide stretched with fewer than a hundred pegs cannot be free of wrinkles. A hide struck with a hundred pegs is as free of wrinkles as the surface of a drum. Therefore, he said this.

‘Ukkūlavikkūlaṃ’ refers to high and low ground, such as uplands and depressions. ‘Nadīviduggaṃ’ refers to rivers and places difficult to traverse. ‘Paṭhavīsaññāṃ paṭicca manasi karoti ekattaṃ’ means attending to a single perception that arises dependent only on the kasiṇa earth. ‘Darathamattā’ means it should be understood as mere disturbance arising in all the stages from this point onwards.

‘Animittaṃ cetosamādhiṃ’ refers to the concentration of the mind associated with insight. That concentration is called ‘signless’ (animitta) because it is devoid of the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta) and so on. With the phrase ‘imam-eva kāyaṃ,’ he shows the object of insight. Therein, ‘imam-eva’ refers to this very body composed of the four great elements.
110:
*Saḷāyatanikaṃ* means that which is connected with the six sense bases (*āyatana*). *Jīvitapaccayā* means that as long as the life faculties (*jīvitindriya*) continue to exist, there is a mere disturbance (*daratha*) that occurs because of the cause known as life. Again, the word *animittaṃ* is spoken to show insight into insight (*paṭivipassanā*). *Kāmāsavaṃ paṭicca* means that disturbances arising dependent on the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) do not exist here in this Dispensation, nor do they exist in the Noble Path (*Ariya Magga*) or the Noble Fruit (*Ariya Phala*). The phrase *imameva kāyaṃ* is spoken to show the remaining disturbance (*upādisesa-daratha*). In this way, having removed the perception of a village (*gāmasaññā*) with the perception of a human (*manussasaññā*)... etc... having removed insight (*vipassanā*) with the Path (*Magga*), the ultimate emptiness (*accanta-suññatā*) called Nibbāna is shown in due order.

*Parisuddhaṃ* means free from the defilement of impurities. *Anuttaraṃ* means that which has nothing superior to it, the most excellent of all things. *Suññataṃ* refers to the attainment of the fruit of emptiness (*suññata-phala-samāpatti*). *Tasmā* means: because in the past, recluses and brahmins known as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples (*sāvaka*); in the future; and in the present, have dwelt, will dwell, and do dwell having entered upon this pure, supreme, and unsurpassed fruit of emptiness; therefore (it is said). The remaining meanings are clear in all places.

## The Explanation of the Cūḷasuññata Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Mahāsuññata Sutta
