The sutta beginning with *Evaṃ me sutaṃ* is the *Mahāsuññata Sutta*. In that sutta, *Kāḷakhemakassa* means: that Sakyan was called *Kāḷa* because of his dark complexion, but *Khemaka* was his original name. *Vihāra* refers to a dwelling built within that very Nigrodhārāma monastery, enclosed by a wall, with a gatehouse constructed, and where dwellings such as *haṃsavaṭṭaka*, circular halls (*maṇḍalamāḷa*), dining halls, and so on were established. *Sambahulāni senāsanāni* means that many lodgings such as couches, stools, bolsters, pillows, mats, pieces of skin, grass mats, leaf mats, and straw mats were spread out. With couch touching couch... etc... straw mat touching straw mat, those places were like the dwelling place of a group of monks (*gaṇabhikkhu*).
111:
Regarding the phrase "Sambahulā nu kho" (Are there many?), there is no doubt for the Exalted One because he had already completely uprooted all defilements at the very seat of enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka). This is a question preceded by thought (vitakka), and here the particle "nu" is a mere functional word (nipāta). When the teaching reaches its conclusion, there is nothing left undecided. Indeed, prior to this time, the Exalted One had never seen twelve monks living together in one place.

Then, this thought occurred to the Exalted One: "This so-called living in a group (gaṇavāsa) is a habit constantly practiced in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). It is like water descending into a river. Living in a group is the habit in hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), and the host of asuras, as well as in the human world, the deva worlds, and the brahma worlds." Indeed, hell, which is ten thousand yojanas wide, is packed with beings without any gap, like a tube filled with lead powder. In the place where beings are tortured with the fivefold binding, there is no limit or boundary to their number. Likewise, in the places where they are carved with cleavers and such, they suffer as a group without limit. In the animal realm, there is no limit or boundary to the number of termites in a single mound. Likewise, there is no limit to the number of ants and such in each individual hole. In the animal realm too, living in a group is the habit. Peta cities of one gāvuta or half a yojana in size are also filled with petas. Thus, in the peta realm too, living in a group is the habit. The asura realm, ten thousand yojanas wide, is like the ear-hole for a needle placed in the ear. Thus, in the host of asuras too, living in a group is the habit. In the human world, there are five million seven hundred thousand households in Sāvatthī. In the city of Rājagaha, eighteen crores of people lived inside and outside the city. Thus, in other places as well, living in a group is the habit in the human world. Starting from the terrestrial devas, living in a group is the habit in the deva and brahma worlds as well. For each son of the devas, there are twenty-five million or ninety million dancers. Ten thousand Brahmas also live in a single place.

Then he thought: "For four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, I fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs) for the sake of destroying this living in a group. Yet these monks, from this point on, are forming groups and delighting in them, doing what is inappropriate." Thus, spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in him. Again, he thought: "If it were possible to prescribe a training rule (sikkhāpada) stating 'Two monks shall not live in one place,' I would prescribe it. However, it is not possible to prescribe such a rule. Now, I shall preach the discourse known as the Practice of Great Emptiness (Mahāsuññata).

That discourse will be like the prescription of a training rule for noble sons who desire training, and like a full-body mirror placed at a city gate. For example, just as kings and others see their own faults in that mirror and, having abandoned them, become faultless; so too, for five thousand years after my Parinibbāna, noble sons who reflect on this Mahāsuññata Sutta, abandon group-living, and delight in solitude, will reach the end of the round of rebirth by means of this sutta."
112:
"I shall preach the sutta which will be like the prescription of a training rule for noble sons who desire the three trainings, and like a full-body mirror placed at a city gate. For that reason, just as kings and others see their own faults in that mirror and, having abandoned those faults, become faultless; in the same way, for five thousand years after my Parinibbāna, noble sons who reflect on this sutta, dispel group-living, and delight in solitude, will make an end to the suffering of the round of rebirth."

As if fulfilling the Exalted One's wish, the noble sons who reflected on this sutta, dispelled delight in groups, ended the suffering of the round, and attained Parinibbāna, are beyond counting. At the Vālikapiṭṭhi Monastery, the Elder Abhaya the Abhidhamma expert (Ābhidhammika Abhayatthera) recited this sutta together with many monks during the time of entering the rains retreat and said, "The Fully Enlightened One makes us act in this way; what shall we do?" All those monks dispelled group-living during the rains retreat, delighted in solitude, and attained Arahatship. This sutta is indeed called the sutta that destroys group-delight.

"Ghaṭāya" means in the monastery of the Sakyan of this name. This monastery should be understood as being built in a portion of the Nigrodhārāma, similar to the monastery built by the Sakyan named Kālakkhema. "Cīvarakamma" (robe-work) refers to the preparation made by patching and washing worn-out and soiled robes, which is appropriate. It also refers to the arrangement of cloth obtained for robes, such as planning and sewing, which has not yet been completed, and this is also appropriate. However, in this sutta, the arrangement that is not yet completed is intended. People gave robe-cloth to the Elder Ānanda. Therefore, the Elder took many monks and performed robe-work there. Those monks sat there from the early morning when the eye of a needle could be seen, and rose only when it could no longer be seen. They did not arrange their lodgings, thinking, "We will arrange the lodgings only after the needle-work is finished." Regarding the phrase "Cīvarakāra-samayo no" (Is it not the time for robe-making?), the Elder thought: "Surely these monks have not tidied their lodgings, and the Exalted One will see this. When the Teacher, being displeased, wishes to strongly rebuke them, I will be a support for these monks." Therefore, he spoke thus. The intention here is: "Venerable Sir, these monks are not merely delighting in work; they are living like this only because of the business of robes."

"Ānanda, whether it be a time for work or not, a time for robe-making or not, a monk who delights in company (saṅgaṇikārāma) does not shine at all. Do not be a support in a matter where support should not be given." In that context, "saṅgaṇikā" means associating with one's own group. "Gaṇa" means associating with various people. Thus, whether one delights in one's own group...
113:
Whether delighting in various people or delighting in a large group in every way, a monk bound by the ties of a group does not shine. However, a monk who, after the meal, sweeps his day-quarters, washes his hands and feet thoroughly, takes up his original meditation subject, and devotes himself to delighting in solitude, shines in the Buddha's Dispensation.

Nekkhamma-sukha is the happiness of one who has emerged from sensual pleasures. Paviveka-sukha is also the happiness born of seclusion from sensual pleasures. It is called upasama-sukha because it leads to the calming of passion and so forth. It is called sambodhi-sukha because it leads to the realization of the Four Noble Truths through path-knowledge. Nikāmalābhī means one who obtains as much as desired. Akicchalābhī means one who obtains easily without hardship. Akasiralābhī means one who obtains abundantly.

Sāmāyika means liberation from defilements at the time of attainment. Kanta means pleasant. Ceto-vimutti refers to the liberation of the mind belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (jhāna). For it is said: "The four jhānas and the four immaterial attainments—this is temporary liberation (sāmāyika-vimokkha)." Asāmāyika does not mean liberation from defilements by way of time, but rather refers to the supramundane (lokuttara) which is permanently liberated. For it is said: "The four noble paths and the four fruits of recluseship—this is non-temporary liberation (asāmāyika-vimokkha)." Akuppa is the state that cannot be disturbed by defilements.

What is being taught by this much? A monk who delights in company and is bound by the ties of a group is unable to produce either mundane or supramundane virtues. But a monk who dispels the group and delights in solitude is able to do so. Indeed, while the Bodhisatta Vipassī was wandering for seven years surrounded by eighty-four thousand monks, he was unable to attain the quality of omniscience. Only after dispelling the group, delighting in solitude for seven days, and ascending the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), did he attain the quality of omniscience. Our Bodhisatta, too, while wandering for six years with the group of five, was unable to attain the quality of omniscience. Only when they had departed and he delighted in solitude and ascended the seat of enlightenment, did he attain the quality of omniscience.

Having thus shown the lack of attainment of virtues for one who delights in company, he now spoke the words beginning with "Nāhaṃ Ānanda," wishing to show the arising of faults. In that passage, rūpa means the physical body. I do not see any such body in which, for one who is attached to it by the power of lust, sorrow and so forth would not arise. On the contrary, just as sorrow and so forth arose for the wanderer Sañjaya due to the change—namely, the becoming of disciples of the Buddha—of Sāriputta and Moggallāna, and just as for the Nigaṇṭha due to the change of the householder Upāli becoming a disciple of the Buddha...
114:
...as for the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta due to the change of the householder Upāli, and as for the merchant and others in the Piyajātika Sutta, sorrows certainly arise.

What is the connection (anusandhi) of the words "Ayaṃ kho panānanda"? If some foolish newly ordained monk should say, "The Sammāsambuddha removes us from the group just like driving cows out of a field and urges us to be alone, yet he himself stays surrounded by kings and great ministers," this discourse was started to cut off the opportunity for such talk and to show that "even when sitting in the midst of an assembly reaching to the edge of the universe, the Tathāgata is truly alone."

In that text, sabba-nimittānaṃ means not attending to conditioned signs such as forms and so forth. Ajjhattaṃ means the internal sphere, which is the fruit attainment. Suññataṃ means the void fruit attainment. In the phrase tatra ca, the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative. Again, tatra means staying in the midst of the assembly. Viveka-ninnena means with a mind inclined toward Nibbāna. Byantībhūtena means with a mind that has departed from, is released from, and is dissociated from the states that are grounds for the taints (āsava). Uyyojanika-paṭisaṃyuttaṃ means connected with words of dismissal such as "You may go."

At what time does the Blessed One speak such words of dismissal? He speaks them at the time of duties after the meal (pacchābhatta-kicca) or during the first watch. For after the meal, the Blessed One takes the lion's sleep in the Fragrant Chamber, and after rising, he sits down having entered the fruit attainment. At that time, the assembly gathers to hear the Dhamma. Then the Blessed One, knowing the time, comes out of the Fragrant Chamber, sits on the noble Buddha-seat, and teaches the Dhamma. Without letting the time pass, like one taking a medicinal oil decoction, he dismisses the assembly with a mind inclined toward solitude. In the first watch too, he dismisses them saying, "Vāseṭṭhas, the night is far spent; you may go when you think it is time." For the Buddhas, from the time of attaining enlightenment, even the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness are inclined toward Nibbāna. "Tasmātiha Ānanda" means because the void-abiding (fruit attainment) is peaceful and sublime.

Ajjhattameva means keeping the mind only on internal objects such as wholesome states. Ajjhattaṃ suññataṃ means contemplating the voidness based on the five aggregates within one's own continuity. Sampajāno hoti means being clearly comprehending by knowing the incompleteness of the meditation subject. Bahiddhā refers to the five aggregates of others. Ajjhatta-bahiddhā means sometimes internally and sometimes externally. Aneñjaṃ (the imperturbable) means attending to the immaterial attainments with the thought, "I shall be a person liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)." The words "Tassmiṃyeva purime" are combined as a single foot of verse, and the Blessed One...
115:
Externally as well, one attends to the imperturbable (āneñja), which is the formless attainment (arūpa-samāpatti), with the thought, 'I shall be one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta).'

The phrase 'in that very first foundation jhana' is spoken in reference to the foundation jhana (pādakajjhāna) which is the basis for insight (vipassanā). For one who has emerged from a foundation jhana that has not been well-practiced and attends to emptiness (suññatā) within one's own continuity (internal), the mind does not enter or settle into that emptiness. At that time, one attends externally, thinking, 'How is it in the continuity of others?' Even when attending thus, the mind does not enter. Then, one attends both internally and externally, thinking, 'How is it sometimes in my own continuity and sometimes in the continuity of others?' Even when attending thus, the mind does not enter. Then, desiring to be one liberated in both ways, one attends to the imperturbable, thinking, 'How is it in the formless attainment?' Even when attending thus, the mind does not enter. Now, thinking 'My mind does not enter,' one should not slacken one's effort and follow behind attendants and such; rather, one should well and repeatedly attend to the foundation jhana itself. To show that just as an axe that cannot perform the task of cutting for a person cutting a tree can perform that task when it is sharpened again, so too, attending to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) can lead to the Path and Fruit, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'in that very foundation jhana.' Now, wishing to show that for the practitioner who practices in this way, the attention is successful in whatever state he attends to, the Buddha said, 'it enters.'

'By this dwelling' means by this dwelling in tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā). 'Thus, one who has clear comprehension therein' means that even while walking, when the meditation subject is successful, one is clearly comprehending by knowing 'My meditation subject is successful.' 'Sleeps' means lying down to sleep. Here, after walking for some time and knowing 'Now I shall be able to walk for this much time,' one should remain standing without abandoning the posture. This method is the same in all sections. By knowing 'I will not speak,' one becomes one who acts with clear comprehension therein.

Again, for the second time, by knowing 'I will speak such speech,' one becomes one who acts with clear comprehension. For this monk, tranquility and insight are still tender; therefore, to protect those states—
'The dwelling, the resort, the speech, the person, the food, the climate, and the posture: these are the seven suitable things (sappāya) that should be cultivated.'
This was said to show those suitable things. In the sections on thoughts (vitakka), clear comprehension should be understood by knowing both unapplied thought and applied thought.
116:
Having thus taught the two Paths (Stream-entry and Once-returning) by the abandoning of thoughts, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with 'Ananda, these five are the cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa),' wishing to show the insight for the third Path (Non-returning). 'Āyatana' refers to the cause of the arising of defilements in those very five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Samudācāra' refers to the defilements that have not been abandoned due to repeated occurrence. 'Evaṃ santaṃ' means those very defilements that are clearly present. 'Sampajāna' (clearly comprehending) means one who knows through the non-success of the meditation subject. In the second instance, 'evaṃ santametaṃ' means this (the abandoning of desire and lust) being so. 'Sampajāna' means one who knows through the success of the meditation subject. For this monk, when reviewing, 'Is desire and lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure abandoned by me or not?' knows the state of it not being abandoned, exerts effort, and uproots that desire and lust with the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). Then, immediately after the Path, the Fruit (phala) occurs. Emerging from the Fruit and reviewing, he knows the state of it being abandoned. Because of that knowing, it is said, 'he becomes clearly comprehending.'

Now, wishing to show the insight for the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Ananda, these five are the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā).' In that passage, 'that state is abandoned' means that in the aggregate of form (rūpa), the conceit 'I am' (asmi-māna), the desire 'I am' (asmi-chanda), and the underlying tendency 'I am' (asmi-anusaya) are abandoned. Likewise, in the aggregates of feeling and so on, clear comprehension (sampajannatā) should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

'Ananda, these states' is said in reference to the states of tranquility, insight, Path, and Fruit mentioned below. 'Kusalāyatikā' means wholesome states (kusala) that have come from wholesome states. Wholesome states are sometimes just wholesome, and sometimes both wholesome and kusalāyatikā. For example: the first jhana is wholesome; the second jhana is both wholesome and kusalāyatikā... the sphere of nothingness is wholesome; the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is both wholesome and kusalāyatikā. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is wholesome; the Path of Stream-entry is both wholesome and kusalāyatikā... the Path of Non-returning is wholesome; the Path of Arahantship is both wholesome and kusalāyatikā. Likewise, the first jhana is wholesome, and the states associated with it are both wholesome and kusalāyatikā... the Path of Arahantship is wholesome, and the states associated with it are both wholesome and kusalāyatikā.

'Noble' (ariya) means states that are free from defilements and pure. 'Supramundane' (lokuttara) means states that are superior and beyond the world. 'Not overcome by the Evil One' means states that the Evil One, Mara, cannot enter or overwhelm.
117:
Māra cannot see the mind of a monk who dwells having attained the eight attainments which are the basis for insight (vipassanā); he is unable to know, 'It proceeds depending on such and such an object.' Therefore, it is said, 'They are not overwhelmed.'

Why was this said: 'What do you think of this?' It was said to show that there is another benefit of seclusion even within a group. *Anubandhituṃ* means to follow after, to attend upon.

In the phrase 'Not so, Ānanda,' although the Blessed One has made a learned noble disciple like a warrior endowed with five weapons, saying, 'Monks, the learned noble disciple who is a hearer of the Dhamma abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity' (A. VII, 67), if that person, despite having learned the scriptures (pariyatti), does not practice the conformable path (anuloma-paṭipadā) suitable for that learning, then that learning does not become a weapon for him. It becomes a weapon only for one who practices. Therefore, showing that it is not worthy to follow for this purpose, he said, 'Not so, Ānanda.'

Now, to show the purpose for which one should follow, he said 'But that which...' (Yā ca kho), etc. Thus, in this sutta, the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu) appear in three places. They appear by way of suitability and unsuitability in 'I will speak such talk'; they appear by way of scriptural learning in 'This sutta is a geyya'; and they appear here by way of fulfillment. Therefore, one who speaks the ten subjects of talk in this sutta should do so standing in this place.

Now, because the goal is not achieved even for some who dwell alone, referring to such a person and wishing to show the danger of living alone, he said, 'Ananda, this being so,' etc. Therein, 'this being so' means when there is such living alone.

'Satthā' means an external sectarian teacher (titthakara). 'Anvāvattanti' means they repeatedly come, they approach. 'Mucchaṃ kāmayati' means he desires the craving of infatuation, he brings it about. 'Ācariyūpaddavena' means the teacher's affliction through the affliction of defilements arisen within. In the remaining afflictions, the method is the same. 'They killed him' means the death of his spiritual qualities is spoken of.
118:
'Vinipātāya' means for the sake of falling well (falling into the four woeful states). But why is only the danger to the practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārūpaddava) said to 'lead to a more painful result, a more bitter result, and to falling into the woeful states'? Indeed, going forth outside the Sasana has little gain; therein, there are no great qualities to be produced, there are only the eight attainments and the five mundane direct knowledges. Thus, just as one who falls from the back of a donkey does not experience great pain but merely gets smeared with dust on the body, so too, in an external system, one merely falls away from mundane qualities; therefore, the first two dangers were not spoken of in this way. But going forth in the Sasana has great gain; therein, there are great qualities to be attained, namely the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna. Thus, just as a royal prince well-born on both sides, while traveling through the city mounted on the back of a noble elephant, meets with great suffering if he falls from the elephant's back, so too, one who falls away from the Sasana falls away from the nine supramundane states. Therefore, this danger to the practitioner of the holy life was spoken of in this way.

'Tasmā' (Therefore) means because the danger to the practitioner of the holy life has a more painful result than the other dangers, or because one who transgresses by acting as an enemy (towards the teacher) conducts himself for his own harm and suffering for a long time, while acting as a friend leads to welfare. Thus, it should be understood by connecting it with both the preceding and following meanings. 'Mittavatāya' means by way of acting as a friend. 'Sapattavatāya' means by way of acting as an enemy.

'Vokkamma ca satthusāsanā' means that even one who intentionally transgresses a mere dukkaṭa or dubbhāsita offense is said to conduct himself by deviating from the Teacher's Sasana. One who does not transgress those same offenses is said not to conduct himself by deviating.

'Ānanda, I will not strive with you in that way (like a potter)' means I will not act towards you in that way. 'Āmake' means an unbaked pot. 'Āmakamatte' means in a pot that is raw and not yet dry. For a potter holds a raw, not-yet-dry, unbaked pot gently with both hands, thinking, 'May it not break.' Thus, just as a potter acts towards those pots, I will not act towards you in that way. 'Rebuking again and again' (niggayha niggayha) means I will not remain silent after advising only once; I will advise and instruct again and again, rebuking repeatedly. 'Removing again and again' (pavayha pavayha) means by repeatedly washing away faults. Just as a potter, among baked pots, [discards] those that are broken, cracked, or worn out...
119:
Just as one discards [faulty pots], gathers them together, and takes only the well-baked pots by repeatedly striking them, even so, I will repeatedly advise and instruct by repeatedly discarding [faults]. "Whatever is the essence, that will remain"—this means that for you, my dear sons, who are being advised by me in this way, whatever is the essence of the Path and Fruit (Magga-Phala), that will remain. Alternatively, even mundane virtues are intended here as 'essence'. The rest of the words have a clear meaning everywhere.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Mahāsuññata Sutta is finished.
## 3. Explanation of the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" etc. is the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta. In that sutta, the phrase "yatra hi nāma" is a particle used in the sense of wonder. It means "the one named the Tathāgata". In the term "chinnapapañca", the 'papañca' refers to these three defilements: craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi). In the term "chinnavatuma", the word "vatuma" refers to the round of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. The term "pariyādinnavaṭṭa" is a synonym for that same term. "Sabbadukkhavītivatta" means the Buddha who has transcended all suffering known as the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa). The word "anussarissati" is in the future tense due to the power of the particle "yatra", but the meaning here should be understood in the past tense. This is because the Blessed One has already recollected those Buddhas; he will not recollect them now. "Evaṃjaccā" means that Buddhas like Vipassī were of the Khattiya (warrior) caste, while Buddhas like Kakusandha were of the Brāhmaṇa (priestly) caste. "Evaṃgottā" means that Buddhas like Vipassī were of the Koṇḍañña clan, while Buddhas like Kakusandha were of the Kassapa clan. "Evaṃsīlā" means they possessed such virtue through mundane and supramundane virtue. In the term "evaṃဓမ္မာ", states associated with concentration (samādhi) are intended. It means they possessed such concentration through mundane and supramundane concentration. "Evaṃpaññā" means they possessed such wisdom through mundane and supramundane wisdom. In the term "evaṃvihārī", since states associated with concentration were already mentioned above, "dwelling" (vihāra) is already included. If asked why it is mentioned again, it is not just repeating what was taken. This term is used to show the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Therefore, the meaning here is "they used to dwell in such attainment of cessation."
120:
In the term "evaṃvimuttā", there are five kinds of liberation (vimutti): liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti). Among those five, the eight attainments (samāpatti) are called liberation by suppression because they are liberated from hindrances (nīvaraṇa) etc., which are suppressed by them. The seven contemplations (anupassanā), such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), are called liberation by substitution of opposites because they are liberated from the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) etc., which are abandoned by the power of their respective opposing factors. The four noble paths (ariya-magga) are called liberation by eradication because they are liberated from defilements which are completely cut off by them. The four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are called liberation by tranquilization because they arise when defilements are tranquilized by the power of the path. Nibbāna is called liberation by escape because it is the escape from all defilements, the departure from them, and standing far away from them. Thus, the meaning of "evaṃvimuttā" should be understood through these five kinds of liberation.

"Tasmātiha" means: since you say "The Tathāgatas are wonderful," may the wonderful and marvelous qualities of the Tathāgata become even more clear to you. In the term "sato sampajāno", there are two kinds of clear comprehension (sampajañña): that which occurs in the human world and that which occurs in the celestial world. Among those two, in the Vessantara Jātaka, after giving his two sons to the Brahmin, and on the next day giving his queen to Sakka, when Sakka was pleased and offered eight boons, [Vessantara] took the boons saying: "When I am released from this body, may I go to heaven, reaching a distinguished heaven, and may I not return from there; I choose this as the eighth boon." Thus, he took the boon, "May my rebirth be in the Tusita heaven." From that time on, knowing "I will be reborn in the Tusita heaven" is clear comprehension in the human world. When he passed away from the existence as Vessantara and was reborn in the Tusita heaven, knowing "I have been reborn" is clear comprehension in the celestial world.

If asked, "Do other deities not know?", it is not that they do not know. However, those deities know only when they look at the gardens, mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees, or when they are awakened by the sound of music from celestial dancers and reminded, "Friend, this is the celestial world; you have been reborn here." The Bodhisatta does not know during the first impulsion (javana), but he knows from the second impulsion onwards. Thus, the Bodhisatta has a unique way of knowing that is not shared with other deities.
121:
## He Dwelt (Aṭṭhāsīti)

In this context, other deities besides the Bodhisatta also know they are dwelling in that celestial realm, thinking, "We are dwelling here." However, those deities, being overwhelmed by powerful pleasant objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) at the six sense doors, lose their mindfulness and, not even knowing they have finished eating and drinking, pass away due to the exhaustion of nutriment (āhārūpaccheda). Does the Bodhisatta not have such objects? It is not that he does not; he does. Indeed, that Bodhisatta surpasses the other deities in ten ways; he does not allow himself to be overwhelmed by objects, but rather dwells having overcome those objects. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Ananda, mindful and clearly comprehending, the Bodhisatta dwelt in the Tusita body."

Regarding the term "for the full life span" (yāvatāyukaṃ): Does he not stay for the full life span in other existences? Indeed, he does not. The reason is that at other times, when reborn in a long-lived celestial world, the Bodhisatta realizes he cannot fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) there; thus, closing his eyes, he performs what is called a "voluntary passing" (adhimuttikālaṅkiriyā) and is reborn in the human world. This kind of passing does not happen to other deities. At this particular time, however, there was no gift not yet given and no virtue not yet guarded; because he had fulfilled all the perfections, he remained for the full life span.

According to the words, "Mindful and clearly comprehending, having passed away from the Tusita body, he entered the mother's womb," the Bodhisatta, having first fulfilled all the perfections, remained for the full life span at that time. For the deities, five preliminary omens (pubbanimittāni) appear, indicating: "According to human reckoning, passing away will occur seven days from now." These are: the flowers wither, the clothes become soiled, sweat flows from the armpits, a loss of physical beauty occurs in the body, and the deity cannot remain on the celestial seat.

Among those omens, "flowers" (mālā) refers to the flowers worn on the day of rebirth. It is said that those flowers remain without withering for fifty-seven crores and six million years (576,000,000), and only then wither when the time of passing is near. The same principle applies to the clothes. For this entire duration, the deities feel neither cold nor heat. But when the time of passing is near, sweat flows from their bodies in drops. For this entire duration, no loss of beauty such as broken teeth or gray hair is apparent in their bodies; the goddesses appear as if they are sixteen years old, and the gods appear as if they are twenty years old. At the time of death, however, their physical forms (attabhāva) take on a weary appearance. For this entire duration, for those deities in the celestial realm...
122:
Deities never experience boredom during their lives; however, at the time of death, they sigh and yawn, and they find no delight in their own seats.

These preliminary omens appear only to powerful deities, just as in the world, omens such as falling meteors, earthquakes, and lunar eclipses are apparent only to those of great merit, such as kings and great ministers, and not to everyone. Among humans, only those such as astrologers know the preliminary omens, not everyone; similarly, not all deities know those omens, only the wise ones do. Among them, those deities born due to weak wholesome kamma become frightened when these omens appear, thinking, "Who knows now where we shall be reborn?" Those of great merit, however, do not fear, reflecting: "Based on the gifts we have given, the virtue we have guarded, and the meditation we have developed, we shall experience prosperity in the higher celestial realms."

The Bodhisatta also saw those preliminary omens and did not fear, reflecting: "Now, in the very next existence, I shall become a Buddha." Then, when those omens had appeared, the deities of the ten thousand world systems assembled and entreated him: "O Great One, when you fulfilled the ten perfections, you did not fulfill them desiring the prosperity of Sakka, or the prosperity of Mara, Brahma, or a Cakkavatti king; you fulfilled them desiring Buddhahood for the sake of delivering the world. Now, Great One, is the time for your Buddhahood; Great One, it is the proper occasion for your Buddhahood."

Then the Great Being, without yet giving his word to the deities, performed the Five Great Investigations (pañcamahāvilokana) regarding the time, the continent, the region, the family, and the mother's life span. Among those five, he first investigated the time, thinking, "Is it the right time or not?" In that investigation, a time when the lifespan is longer than one hundred thousand years is not the right time. Why? Because at that time, birth, aging, and death are not apparent to beings. The Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas is never free from the Three Characteristics (tilakkhaṇa); when they teach that things are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, beings do not think to listen or believe, asking, "What is this they are saying?" Therefore, there is no realization of the Truth (abhisamaya). In the absence of that, the Dispensation (sāsana) does not lead to liberation (aniyyānika). Therefore, that is not the right time. A time when the lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not the right time. Why? Because at that time, beings have abundant defilements, and advice given to those with abundant defilements does not remain in the place of advice. It disappears quickly, like a line drawn on water with a stick. Therefore, that also is not the right time.
123:
The period when the human lifespan is between one hundred thousand years and one hundred years is called the (proper) time (for a Buddha to appear). At that time, the human lifespan was one hundred years. Then the Great Being (Bodhisatta) observed the time, thinking, "It is the time to be conceived."

Then, while observing the island, he looked at the four great islands with their surrounding islands and observed: "Buddhas are not born in the three (other) islands; they are born only in Jambudīpa."

Then, thinking, "Jambudīpa is a large island, ten thousand yojanas in extent; in which region are Buddhas born?", he observed the regions and saw the Majjhimadesa (Middle Country). The Majjhimadesa is indeed described in the Vinaya texts in this manner: "To the east is the market town named Gajaṅgala," and so forth. That Majjhimadesa is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in breadth, and nine hundred in circumference. It is in this region that the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddhas) appear after fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable periods (asaṅkheyyas) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappas). Paccekabuddhas appear after fulfilling perfections for two incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons. Great Disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna appear after fulfilling perfections for one incalculable period and a hundred thousand aeons. Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti kings) who rule over the four great islands and two thousand small islands appear here. Other powerful and wealthy nobles (Khattiya), brahmins (Brāhmaṇa), and householders (Gahapati) of great status (Mahāsāla) also appear here. "In this Majjhimadesa is the city named Kapilavatthu; there I shall be conceived," he thus came to a decision.

Then, while observing the family, he thought: "Buddhas are born in a family esteemed by the world. Now, the Khattiya (warrior-noble) class is the family esteemed by the world; I shall be born in that class. King Suddhodana shall be my father." Thus he observed the family.

Then, while observing the mother, he thought: "The mother of a Buddha is not flighty or addicted to intoxicants. She must have fulfilled perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and kept the five precepts unbroken from the time of her birth. This Queen Mahāmāyā is such a person. She shall be my mother. How long is her remaining lifespan?" Upon reflection, he saw: "It is only ten months and seven days."
124:
Having thus made these five great observations, he gave his word to the deities, intending to favor them, saying, "Friends, the time has come for me to become a Buddha." Having dismissed those deities, he entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita heaven, surrounded by the Tusita deities. Indeed, in all deva realms, there is a Nandana Grove. There, the deities wandered about, reminding him of the opportunities of his past meritorious deeds, saying, "When you pass away from here, go to a happy destination (sugati); when you pass away from here, go to a happy destination."

While wandering in that grove, surrounded by deities reminding him of his merit, he passed away (deceased). When passing away thus, he knew, "I am passing away," but he did not know the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). Even after taking rebirth, he did not know the rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta), but he did know, "I have taken rebirth in this place." Some elders, however, say, "Since he should obtain the turn of reflection (āvajjana), he would know at the second or third thought-moment."

However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said: "The rebirth of Great Beings is not like the rebirth of others; their mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) reach the highest point. But because it is impossible to know that very consciousness with the same consciousness, he does not know the death-consciousness. At the moment of death, he knows, 'I am passing away.' Even after taking rebirth, he does not know the rebirth-consciousness, but he knows, 'Rebirth has been taken in such a place.' At that time, the ten thousand world systems tremble." Thus, mindful and clearly comprehending, our Bodhisatta entered his mother's womb. Among the nineteen types of rebirth-consciousness, he took rebirth with a great resultant consciousness (mahāvipāka-citta) similar to the unprompted wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge (somanassa-sahagata ñāṇa-sampayutta asaṅkhārika kusala-citta), preceded by loving-kindness. Elder Mahāsīva, however, said, "He took rebirth with a consciousness accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata)."

When taking rebirth, he did so on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, under the Uttarāsāḷha nakshatra. At that time, it is said that Queen Mahāmāyā, starting from seven days before the full moon, had been celebrating the festival, abstaining from intoxicants and adorned with garlands and perfumes. On the seventh day, she rose early in the morning, bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all ornaments, ate choice food, undertook the Uposatha vows, and entered the royal bedchamber. As she fell asleep on the royal bed, she saw this dream:

It seemed that the four Great Kings (Mahārājas) lifted her up together with her bed, carried her to Lake Anotatta, and placed her to one side. Then, the queens of those Great Kings came and bathed her to remove human impurities, dressed her in celestial garments, anointed her with perfumes, and adorned her with celestial flowers. Not far from that Lake Anotatta, there was a Silver Mountain, and inside it was a golden mansion. In that golden mansion...
125:
They laid her down with her head towards the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered on a golden mountain not far from that silver mountain. Descending from the golden mountain and ascending the silver mountain, he approached from the north, entered the golden mansion, circumambulated his mother three times, and seemed to enter her womb by piercing her right side.

Then the Queen, having awakened, informed the King of that dream. When the night had turned to dawn, the King summoned sixty-four eminent Brahmins. On a ground smeared with fresh cow-dung and honored with auspicious offerings such as parched rice, he had seats prepared suitable for noble persons. To the Brahmins seated there, he filled gold and silver bowls with excellent milk-rice (pāyāsa) prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, covered them with gold and silver lids, and offered them. He also satisfied those Brahmins with other gifts such as new clothes and tawny cows. Then, having satisfied them with all desired objects, he informed them of the dream and asked, 'What will be the result?' The Brahmins said, 'Do not worry, Great King; a conception has taken place in the Queen's womb. That conception is of a male child, not a female. A noble son will be born to you. If he lives the household life, he will become a Cakkavatti King. If he leaves the household life and goes forth into homelessness, he will become a Buddha in the world, one who removes the veil [of defilements].' Thus, the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending, passed away from the Tusita heaven and descended into his mother's womb.

In this context, by the phrase 'mindful and clearly comprehending,' it is shown that he descends by the fourth type of descent into the womb. There are four types of descent into the womb (gabbhāvakkanti).

'Venerable sir, there are these four types of descent into the womb. Here, venerable sir, someone descends into the mother's womb without clear comprehension, stays in the mother's womb without clear comprehension, and exits the mother's womb without clear comprehension. This is the first descent into the womb.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone descends into the mother's womb with clear comprehension, but stays in the mother's womb without clear comprehension, and exits the mother's womb without clear comprehension. This is the second descent into the womb.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone descends into the mother's womb with clear comprehension, stays in the mother's womb with clear comprehension, but exits the mother's womb without clear comprehension. This is the third descent into the womb.'
126:
'Furthermore, venerable sir, here someone descends into the mother's womb with clear comprehension, stays in the mother's womb with clear comprehension, and exits the mother's womb with clear comprehension. This is the fourth descent into the womb' (D. iii. 147).

Among these four, the first type belongs to ordinary worldlings. The second type belongs to the eighty Great Disciples (mahāsāvaka). The third type belongs to the two Chief Disciples (aggasāvaka) and to the Paccekabodhisattas. It is said that, due to the kamma-born winds (kammajavāta), they are turned feet-upwards and head-downwards, and they experience infinite suffering as they emerge through the birth canal, which is extremely narrow like the hole of a key, as if falling into a bottomless abyss or like an elephant exiting through a keyhole. Therefore, they do not have the clear comprehension that 'we are exiting.' The fourth type belongs to the Omniscient Bodhisattas. They know when they are taking conception in the mother's womb, they know while staying there, and at the time of birth, the kamma-born winds are unable to turn them feet-upwards and head-downwards; they emerge standing, with both hands stretched out and eyes open.

In the phrase 'mātukucchiṃ okkamati,' it means he has already descended into the mother's womb. This knowledge occurs only after having descended, not at the moment of descending. 'Appamāṇo' means immeasurable, in the sense of being vast. 'Uḷāro' is a synonym for that same 'appamāṇo.' In the phrase 'devānubhāvaṃ,' the majesty of the devas is as follows: the radiance of their garments extends for twelve yojanas; likewise the radiance of their bodies, their ornaments, and their mansions. It means 'surpassing that majesty of the devas.'

'Lokantarikā' refers to the inter-cosmic hells located between every three world-systems (cakkavāḷa), like the space in the middle of three cartwheels or three alms-bowls placed touching each other. That Lokantarika hell is eight thousand yojanas in extent. 'Aghā' means constantly open space. 'Asaṃvutā' means having no support below. 'Andhakārā' means a region of blinding darkness. 'Andhakāratimisā' means being possessed of a blinding gloom that prevents the arising of eye-consciousness, like being blind. It is said that eye-consciousness does not arise there. 'Evaṃmahiddhikā' means the moon and the sun have such great power that they can appear simultaneously in three continents. They have such great majesty that they can dispel darkness and show light for nine hundred thousand yojanas in a single direction. 'Ābhāya nānubhonti' means that the moon and the sun cannot shine with their own radiance [in that place]. The moon and the sun only circulate around the middle of Mount Sineru (Cakkavāḷa mountain). Beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountain, in the place where the Lokantarika hell is situated, the moon and the sun cannot shine with their own radiance.
127:
The sun and the moon are unable to illuminate that region with their own radiance. Since those suns and moons revolve only in the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Lokantarika hell is situated beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the light of the sun and moon cannot reach that hell. 

Regarding the phrase "the beings who are there," it refers to the beings born in that Lokantarika Great Hell. As for the question, "By performing what kamma are they born there?"—they are born there because of committing grave and cruel offenses against their parents and against righteous recluses and brahmins, and because of performing daily acts of violence such as killing living beings, similar to the bandits Abhaya and Nāga in the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Their physical bodies are three gāvutas in height, and they have long nails like bats. They cling to the base of the Cakkavāḷa mountains with their nails, just as bats cling to trees. While crawling about, when they come within a hand's reach of one another, they think, "We have found food!" and in their struggle to seize and eat each other, they lose their grip and fall into the water that supports the world. Like Madhuka fruits falling when the wind blows, they break off and fall into the water. As soon as they fall, they dissolve like a lump of flour in that extremely salty water.

On that day [of the Bodhisatta's birth], they see one another and say, "Friends, it seems there are other beings besides us!" thinking, "Just as we experience great suffering, so too other beings are born here experiencing this suffering." This radiance does not last even for the duration of drinking a single cup of gruel; it lasts only as long as it takes for a person waking from sleep to perceive an object. However, the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīghabhāṇakas) say that it flashes forth like a bolt of lightning for only a finger-snap, and while they are still saying, "What is this light?", it disappears.

"Saṅkampati" means it trembles all around. The other two terms are merely synonyms of the first. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Appamāṇo ca" was spoken for the purpose of conclusion.

In the passage, "Four sons of devas approached from the four directions for protection," the word "four" refers to the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā). In the ten thousand world-elements, if four are taken for each, there are forty thousand Great Kings. Among those forty thousand Great Kings, the Great Kings residing in this Cakkavāḷa came with swords in hand to protect the Bodhisatta and entered the auspicious chamber, while the others, starting from the chamber door...
128:
...having driven away the hosts of spirits such as the lowly dust-heap-dwelling ogres (pamsu-pisāca), they took up protection as far as the Cakkavāḷa boundary.

For what purpose did this protection come? In truth, from the moment of conception at the stage of the embryonic drop (kalala), even if a hundred thousand Māras were to come lifting a hundred thousand Mount Sinerus to cause harm to the Bodhisatta or the Bodhisatta’s mother, all those dangers would vanish in mid-air. This was also stated by the Blessed One in the episode concerning the causing of [the Buddha's] blood to flow (Lohituppādaka-vatthu): "Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that anyone could deprive a Tathāgata of life through an external effort. Monks, Tathāgatas attain Parinibbāna without such effort. Go, monks, to your respective dwellings; Tathāgatas, monks, do not need protection." (Cūḷavagga, 341). Even though this is so, there is no danger to their lives through the efforts of others. However, there are non-human beings of deformed and ugly appearance, and birds of terrifying form; upon seeing their forms or hearing their sounds, fear or terror might arise in the Bodhisatta’s mother. To prevent such fears, they took up protection. Furthermore, in truth, out of reverence born from the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, and urged by their own sense of respect, those Great Kings provided such protection.

Do those four Great Kings who entered and stood within the chamber show themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother or not? They do not show themselves when she is performing bodily functions such as bathing, adorning herself, or eating. However, they show themselves when she has entered the auspicious chamber and is lying on the noble couch. In that regard, although the sight of non-human beings is generally terrifying to humans, the Bodhisatta’s mother does not fear them when she sees them, due to the power of her own merit and that of her son. Her mind regards them just as she would the ordinary palace guards.

"Pakatiyā sīlavatī" means she was naturally endowed with virtue by her very nature. It is said that before the arising of a Buddha, people would pay homage to ascetics and wanderers and, sitting in a crouching position, receive the precepts. The Bodhisatta’s mother also used to receive the precepts from the ascetic Kāla-devila. However, once the Bodhisatta has entered the womb, it is not proper for her to sit at the feet of another. Sitting on an equal seat to receive precepts would also be a sign of disrespect. Therefore, it is said that she took the precepts by herself.
129:
The term 'among men' (purisesu) means that no lustful thoughts (rāga) arose in any men, starting from the Bodhisatta's father, towards the mother. This absence of lust was due to their respect for the Bodhisatta, and not because their defilements had been eradicated. Even highly skilled artists are unable to replicate the beauty of the Bodhisatta's mother in statues and the like; therefore, it cannot be said that lust would not arise in men upon seeing her. However, if a man with a lustful mind intended to approach her, his feet would fail to carry him, as if he were bound by divine shackles. For this reason, it is said 'she was not to be transgressed' (anatikkamanīyā), and so forth.

Regarding 'the five cords of sensual pleasure' (pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ): previously, by the phrase 'associated with the cords of sensual pleasure' (kāmaguṇūpasaṃhitaṃ), the rejection of sensual objects according to the desires of men was discussed; now, the acquisition of such objects is shown. It is said that at that time, hearing that 'such a noble son has been conceived in the Queen's womb,' kings from all directions sent gifts consisting of the five types of sensual objects, such as costly ornaments and musical instruments. Due to the abundance of merit performed by the Bodhisatta and the Bodhisatta's mother, there was no limit or measure to the gains and offerings received.

'With unwearied body' (akilantakāyā) means that unlike other women who become weary from the weight of the pregnancy and suffer from swelling of the hands and feet, she experienced no such fatigue. 'Gone into the interior of the womb' (tirokucchigataṃ) refers to the son within the womb. Having passed the stages such as the initial embryonic stage (kalala), she sees him only when he has developed major and minor limbs and has reached the state of unimpaired faculties. Why does she see him? For the sake of his comfortable dwelling. Just as a mother, while sitting or lying down with her young son, watches him thinking, 'If his hand or foot is hanging down, I will lift it and set it right,' so that he may dwell comfortably;

In the same way, the Bodhisatta's mother, while rising, walking, turning, or sitting, and while consuming hot, cold, salty, bitter, or pungent food, watches the Bodhisatta with the concern of whether any suffering has arisen for her son, desiring him to dwell comfortably. In doing so, she sees the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged. While other fetuses sit in the mother's womb pressing down on the receptacle for digested food (pakkāsaya), lifting up the receptacle for undigested food (āmāsaya), with the abdominal membrane behind them, leaning against the backbone, and sitting in a squatting position with their chin on their two fists like monkeys in a tree hollow when it rains, the Bodhisatta does not sit like that. The Bodhisatta sits with his backbone to the back, cross-legged, facing forward (eastward), like a Dhamma preacher on a Dhamma-seat. His past merit cleanses the womb, and in that pure womb, the characteristics of delicate skin and complexion appear.
130:
When this occurs, the skin of the mother's womb is unable to hide the Bodhisatta residing within; he appears clearly to the mother who looks at him, as if he were outside (like a thread passed through a clear gem). To clarify this meaning with a simile, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'Just as' (seyyathāpi). However, the Bodhisatta residing within the womb does not see his mother. Indeed, eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) does not arise for those within the womb.

'She passes away' (Kālaṃ karoti) means that her death is not due to the cause of childbirth, but solely due to the exhaustion of her lifespan. The place where a Bodhisatta has resided is like a shrine-room (cetiya-kuṭi) and is not fit to be used by others. Furthermore, it is not proper to remove the Bodhisatta's mother from the position of Chief Queen and place another in that position; therefore, the lifespan of a Bodhisatta's mother is only that long. Thus, she passes away at that time. At what age does she pass away? She passes away in middle age (majjhimavaya). In the first stage of life, the desire and lust (chandarāga) for the bodies of beings is strong; because it is so strong, a woman who conceives at that time is unable to protect the fetus, and the pregnancy is prone to many ailments. But after passing two parts of middle age, in the third part, the mother's womb is pure; children born in a pure womb are free from disease. Therefore, the Bodhisatta's mother also enjoys prosperity in her youth and, after giving birth in the third part of middle age, she passes away.

In the phrase 'nine or ten months,' the word 'or' (vā) should be understood to include other durations such as seven, eight, eleven, or twelve months. Among these, a child born at seven months survives but cannot withstand cold or heat. A child born at eight months does not survive, while those born in the remaining months do survive.

'While standing' (Ṭhitāva) means having remained standing. Queen Mahāmāyā, when the time for birth was near, informed the King, 'I wish to go to my relatives' home.' The King had the road leading from Kapilavatthu to the city of Devadaha decorated and had the Queen seated in a golden palanquin. The Sakyans, inhabitants of the entire city, surrounded her and escorted the Queen, making offerings with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Seeing the Lumbinī Sal grove not far from the city of Devadaha, the Queen desired to wander in the garden and gave a sign to the King. The King had the garden prepared and arranged for guards. As soon as the Queen entered the garden, she felt a weakness in her body; then, having prepared a glorious bed at the foot of the auspicious Sal tree, they enclosed it with curtains.
131:
Queen Mahāmāyā entered within the curtain, held a branch of the Sāla tree with her hand, and stood there. At that very moment, the birth from her womb occurred.

"The devas receive him first" means that the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), receive him. How do they receive him? Some say they take the form of midwives. Rejecting that view, it is said: At that time, the Mother of the Bodhisatta stood wearing a cloth adorned with gold and wrapped in a dukūla robe, resembling fish-eyes, down to her feet. While she stood thus, the birth from her womb occurred very easily, like water flowing from a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa). Then, those Brahmas approached in their natural Brahma forms and first received him with a golden net. From the hands of those Brahmas, humans received him with a roll made of dukūla cloth. Therefore, it is said: "The devas receive him first, and afterwards, humans."

"Four sons of gods receive him" refers to the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā). "Having received" means receiving him with a rug made of antelope skin (ajinappaveṇī). "Mahesakkha" means a being of great power, great fame, and endowed with the marks.

"He emerges purely" means that unlike other beings who emerge stuck in the birth canal, broken and in pain, he does not emerge in that way; he emerges without being stuck. "With water" means he emerges without being smeared by water. "By any impure matter" means that other beings, due to karma-born winds (kammajavāta), are turned feet-up and head-down, cast into the birth canal, as if falling into a hundred-fathom deep hell-abyss, or like an elephant being pulled through a small opening, experiencing great suffering and emerging smeared with various impurities. The Bodhisatta is not like that. The karma-born winds cannot turn the Bodhisatta feet-up and head-down. Like a Dhamma preacher descending from a Dhamma-seat, or like a man descending a ladder, that Bodhisatta emerges with both hands and both feet stretched out, standing, without being smeared by even a tiny bit of impurity from the mother's womb.

"Streams of water" refers to two streams of water. Among them, the cold stream falls into a golden bowl, and the hot stream falls into a silver bowl. This is said to show the drinking water and usable water for them, unmixed with any impurity on the ground, and the water for playing, which is not shared with others. As for the water brought in other gold and silver jars, and the water in lotus ponds where hamsa birds and ducks dwell, it is immeasurable and vast.
132:
"Sampatijāta" means one who is newly born (born just a moment ago). Although in the Pali it is shown as if he had just emerged from the mother’s womb, it should not be understood in that way. In truth, as soon as the Bodhisatta was born, first the Brahmas received him with a golden net; from the hands of those Brahmas, the Four Great Kings received him with a blessed and pleasant-to-touch antelope skin; from the hands of those kings, humans received him with a roll of dukūla cloth; and being released from the hands of humans, he stood upon the ground.

"When the white umbrella is held over him" means when the divine white umbrella is held. Here, the five royal regalia (kakudhabhaṇḍa), such as the sword and so on, which are the retinue of the umbrella, also arrived. However, in the Pali, only the umbrella is mentioned, like a king when a king travels. Among them, only the umbrella is visible, not the umbrella-bearers. Similarly, only the sword (khagga), the palm-leaf fan (tālavaṇṭa), the peacock-feather fan (morahatthaka), the yak-tail whisk (vāḷabījanī), and the turban (uṇhīsa) are visible, not their bearers. It is said that deities with invisible forms held all those royal regalia. This has also been said:

The devas held the umbrella in the sky,
Which has many branches and a thousand circles;
Golden-handled whisks wave to and fro,
But the bearers of the whisks and umbrella are not seen.

"And all directions" (surveying all directions)—this is said as if he surveyed all directions while standing after taking seven steps, but it should not be understood in that way. In truth, when the Great Being (Mahāsatta) was released from the hands of humans, he looked towards the front (the East), and many thousands of world-systems became like a single open space. There, devas and humans, worshipping him with scents and garlands, said: "O Great Man (Mahāpurisa), there is no one even equal to you here; how could there be anyone superior?" In this way, having surveyed the ten directions—the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, the downward direction, and the upward direction—and seeing no one equal to himself, he thought, "This is the North," and proceeded by taking seven steps. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

"Āsabhi" means noble speech. "Aggo" means being foremost of all in virtues. The remaining two words are just synonyms of this word "Aggo". By the two phrases "This is the last birth; there is no further rebirth," he proclaimed the Arahantship (Arahatta-phala) to be attained in this very existence.
133:
In this context, standing on the earth with level feet is the precursor (pubbanimitta) to attaining the four bases of power (iddhipāda). Facing the North is the precursor to going forth by overwhelming and surpassing the masses. Taking seven steps is the precursor to attaining the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The holding of the divine white parasol is the precursor to attaining the parasol of liberation (vimutti) (the fruit of Arahatship). The five royal regalia are the precursor to liberation from defilements through the five kinds of release (vimutti). Looking around at the directions is the precursor to attaining unimpeded knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). Uttering the bull-like speech (āsabhī vācā) is the precursor to turning the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) which cannot be turned back by others. Uttering the lion's roar (sīhanāda), "This is my last birth," should be understood as the precursor to final passing away (parinibbāna) into the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa nibbāna-dhātu). These sections appear in the Pali; the Sambahulavāra (the section of various occurrences) also appears and is presented here by drawing from various commentaries.

Indeed, on the day the Bodhisatta (Great Being) was born, the ten-thousandfold world system shook. The deities in the ten-thousandfold world system gathered in a single universe. First the deities received him, and then humans. Lutes strung with strings and drums covered with skin sounded by themselves without anyone playing them. The shackles and bonds of humans broke into pieces. All diseases vanished like copper rust washed away by acid. Those born blind saw forms. Those born deaf heard sounds. The lame became swift-footed. Mindfulness was established even in those born mute or dull-witted. Ships traveling to foreign lands reached safe harbors. Jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shone with their own radiance. Enemies felt a heart of loving-kindness. The fire in the Avīci hell was extinguished. Light appeared in the inter-world spaces. Water in the rivers ceased to flow. In the great oceans, the water became sweet like honey. The wind stopped blowing. Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees descended to the ground. The moon shone with exceeding beauty. The sun was neither too hot nor too cold, becoming pure and endowed with a pleasant season. Deities, standing at the doors of their celestial mansions, celebrated with great festivities such as clapping, whistling, and tossing their garments. A great rain fell across all four continents. The masses were not oppressed by hunger or thirst. Door panels opened by themselves. Trees capable of flowering and fruiting became laden with blossoms and fruits. The ten-thousandfold world system became like a single mass of banners and garlands.

Among those events, the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system is the precursor to attaining omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). The gathering of deities in a single universe is the precursor to their gathering all at once to receive the Dhamma when the Wheel of Dhamma is turned. First...
134:
The deities receiving him is the precursor to attaining the four fine-material absorptions (rūpāvacara jhāna). Humans receiving him afterwards is the precursor to attaining the four immaterial absorptions (arūpa jhāna). The spontaneous sounding of stringed lutes is the precursor to attaining the successive dwellings (anupubbavihāra). The sounding of skin-covered drums is the precursor to the proclamation of the Great Drum of Dhamma. The breaking of shackles and bonds is the precursor to the total eradication of the conceit "I am" (asmimāna). The cessation of all diseases is the precursor to the cessation of all defilements (kilesa). The seeing of forms by those born blind is the precursor to attaining the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). The hearing of sounds by those born deaf is the precursor to attaining the divine ear element (dibba-sotadhātu). The swiftness of the lame is the precursor to the attainment of the four bases of power (iddhipāda). The establishment of mindfulness in the dull-witted is the precursor to attaining the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). The arrival of ships traveling to foreign lands at safe harbors is the precursor to the attainment of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The shining of jewels with their own radiance is the precursor to showing the light of Dhamma to the people of the world.

The attainment of a heart of loving-kindness by enemies is the precursor to attaining the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra). The extinguishing of the fire in Avīci hell is the precursor to the extinguishing of the eleven fires. The appearance of light in the inter-world spaces is the precursor to dispelling the darkness of ignorance (avijjā) and seeing the light of knowledge (ñāṇa). The sweetness of the great ocean is the precursor to the state of having a single taste through the flavor of Nibbāna. The stillness of the wind is the precursor to the destruction of the sixty-two types of wrong views (diṭṭhi). The birds going to the ground is the precursor to the masses hearing the instruction and taking refuge for as long as life lasts. The exceeding brilliance of the moon is the precursor to being beloved and cherished by many. The sun being free from heat and cold and having a pleasant season is the precursor to the arising of physical and mental happiness. The deities playing at the doors of their mansions with clapping and so on is the precursor to uttering the joyful inspired utterance (udāna) upon reaching Buddhahood. The falling of the great rain across the four continents is the precursor to the falling of the great rain of Dhamma. The absence of oppression by hunger is the precursor to attaining the deathless (amata) through mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). The absence of oppression by thirst is the precursor to being happy with the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha). The spontaneous opening of door panels is the precursor to the opening of the door of the Eightfold Path. The bearing of flowers and fruits by trees is the precursor to blossoming with the flowers of liberation and being laden with the weight of the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). It should be understood that the ten-thousandfold world system being filled with banners and garlands is the precursor to being adorned with the banners of the Noble Path and the Noble Truths. This is known as the Sambahulavāra.

In this regard, a question is asked: "When the Great Being stood on the ground, faced the North, and spoke the noble words, at that time on the ground..."
135:
Did he walk on the ground, or through the air? Did he walk with a visible body, or an invisible one? Did he walk naked, or was he adorned and prepared? Did he walk as a youth, or as an adult? After taking the seven steps, did he remain in that state, or did he become a small infant again? (These were the questions asked). This problem was indeed answered by the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷābhaya at an assembly of the Saṅgha beneath the Lohapāsāda. It is said that the Elder, in this matter, spoke extensively regarding the doctrines of fatalism (niyati), past actions (pubbekata-kamma), and creation by a lord (issaranimmāna), and finally gave this explanation: 'The Great Being walked on the ground, yet to the great multitude, it appeared as if he were walking through the air. He walked with a visible body, yet to the great multitude, it appeared as if he were invisible. He walked naked, yet to the great multitude, he appeared as if he were adorned and prepared. He walked as a youth, yet to the great multitude, he appeared as if he were sixteen years of age. Afterwards, however, he became a small infant; he did not remain in that grown-up state.' When this was said, the assembly was delighted, saying, 'Friends, the Elder has answered the question as if he were the Buddha himself.' The section on the 'interval between worlds' (lokantarika) is as previously explained.

'Known' (viditā) means having become manifest. Just as disciples, during times of bathing, washing the face, eating, or drinking, are in a situation where they cannot fully comprehend past formations (saṅkhāra) without remainder, and can only contemplate when the opportunity arises, the Buddhas are not like that. The Buddhas, having contemplated the formations existing within a seven-day period from the very beginning and having applied the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), then answer the questions. For those Buddhas, there is no such thing as a phenomenon (dhamma) not seen with insight. Therefore, it is said 'viditā'. The rest of the text is clear in all respects.

## The Commentary on the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.
## 4. Bākulasutta-vaṇṇanā

'Thus have I heard' (evaṃ me sutaṃ) and so forth refers to the Bākula Sutta. In that context, 'Bākula' is used where 'Dvikula' (of two families) should be said, just as 'bāvīsati' and 'bāttiṃsa' are said when 'dvāvīsati' and 'dvattiṃsa' are meant. That Elder indeed had two families. It is said that after passing away from the deva world, he was reborn in the city of Kosambī...
136: I pay homage to the Buddha. I pay homage to the well-expounded Dhamma. I pay homage to the Saṅgha of good conduct. This discourse beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Bākula Sutta. In this Bākula Sutta, the meaning of the term 'Bākula' should be understood as follows: Just as people in the world speak of 'twenty-two' (bāvīsati) and 'thirty-three' (bāttiṃsa), he is called 'Bākula' because he is said to be of 'two families' (dvikula). I shall now relate the story of that Elder Bākula. That Elder had previously belonged to two families. Having passed away from the celestial realm, the Elder Bākula was reborn into the family of a great merchant in the city of Kosambī. On the fifth day, they performed the head-washing ceremony for the child and took him to play in the river Gaṅgā. While the nurses were letting the child play by dipping him in and out of the water, a fish saw the child and, thinking 'This is my food,' it opened its mouth and approached. The nurses abandoned the child and fled. That fish swallowed the child. The meritorious child did not suffer any pain but felt as if he had entered a bedchamber and was lying down. Due to the child's merit, the fish felt as if it had swallowed a hot frying pan; being greatly distressed, it swam swiftly for a distance of thirty yojanas and entered the net of a fisherman living in the city of Vārāṇasī. Usually, large fish die when they are caught in a net and struck, but this fish died only after being taken out of the net, due to the child's power. Although fishermen usually cut open and sell large fish when they catch them, due to the child's power, they did not cut this fish but carried it whole on a pole, wandering through the city saying, 'We will sell this for a thousand pieces of money.' No one bought it. In that city, there was a merchant family with a wealth of eighty crores who had no children. When the fishermen reached the door of that house and were asked, 'For how much will you give it?', they replied, 'For a thousand kahāpaṇas.' The merchants paid the money and bought it. Although the merchant's wife did not usually care for fish on other days, on that day she placed the fish on a board and cut it open herself. While fish are normally cut from the belly, she cut it from the back; seeing the golden-hued child inside the fish's belly, she cried out, 'I have obtained a son from the belly of a fish!' and taking the child, she went to her husband, the merchant. The merchant immediately had the drums beaten and, taking the child, went to the King and said, 'Great King, I have obtained a child from the belly of a fish; what should I do?' The King replied, 'This child who could live in a fish's belly without illness is one of great merit; raise him.' The other family heard that 'a merchant family in Vārāṇasī has obtained a child from the belly of a fish' and went there. When the child's [original] mother saw the child adorned and playing, she said, 'This child is truly delightful,' and approaching, she told the whole story. The second mother said, 'This child is my son.' When asked, 'Where did you get him?', she replied, 'From the belly of a fish.' The first mother said, 'He is not your son, he is only my son.' When asked, 'Where did you get him?', she explained, 'I carried him in my womb for ten months, and then while letting him play in the river, a fish swallowed him.' The other replied, 'Another fish might have swallowed your son, but this child was obtained from the belly of a large fish.' Thus they disputed and both went to the King's palace. The King said, 'Since this woman carried him in her womb for ten months, it cannot be said she is not the mother. Since this woman who bought the fish obtained him from the fish's belly—and no one catches a fish by removing its entrails beforehand—it cannot be said she is not the mother either. Therefore, let the child be the heir to both families, and both of you shall care for him.' Thus, both families cared for him. When he reached the age of discretion...
137: ...while playing in the river, a fish swallowed him. 'Your son must have been swallowed by another fish, but I obtained this child from the belly of this fish,' they said, and both went to the royal palace. The King said, 'Because this woman carried him in her womb for ten months, she cannot be dismissed as the mother. Since there is no one who catches a fish by first removing its entrails, this woman who obtained him from the fish's belly also cannot be dismissed as the mother. Let the child be the heir to both families; both of you should look after him.' So both families cared for him. When he reached the age of maturity, they had palaces built for him in both cities and provided him with troupes of dancers. He lived for four months in each city. When he had completed four months in one city and was to move to the other, they would set up a pavilion and place him there along with the dancers. Enjoying such prosperity, he would travel to the other city. The residents of that city would come halfway to meet him with dancers. They would greet him, surround him, and lead him to their own palace. The dancers who had come from the other city would then turn back and return to their own city. After staying there for four months, he would return to the other city in the same manner. In this way, enjoying such prosperity, he reached eighty years of age. Then, the Blessed One, while wandering on a walking tour, arrived at Vārāṇasī. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, he gained faith and was ordained. After ordaining, he remained a worldling (puthujjana) for only seven days, and on the eighth day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus, he had two families. For that reason, he came to be known as 'Bākula.' 'Purāṇagihisahāyo' means a companion from his former life as a layman. This Acela Kassapa was also long-lived, and when he went to see the Elder Bākula after his ordination, he was already eighty years old. By the phrase 'methuno dhammo' (sexual intercourse), the foolish naked ascetic (Acela Kassapa) was asking a foolish question; it was not a matter concerning the Dispensation (Sāsana). Now, standing in the method provided by the Elder, he asked, 'By these things, your...' The words beginning with 'yampāyasmā' were established and fixed in all sections by the Elders who conducted the Dhamma Council (Dhammasaṅgāhaka). In that context, it should be understood that perception (saññā) is merely what has arisen, while thought (vitakka) performs the differentiation of the pathways of action (kammapatha).
138:
The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, however, said: "Why do they do them separately? Both of these (perception and thought) are indeed destroyers of the path of action (kammapatha)."

"Gahapaticīvara" refers to the robes offered to monks who have completed the rains retreat. "Satthena" means (cutting) with a knife. "Sucitā" means he does not remember (it never happened) having ever sewn while holding a needle. "Kathinacīvara" refers to the Kathina robe; since the Kathina robe is also categorized as a rains-residence robe, he said regarding that Kathina robe as well, "I do not remember sewing it."

Regarding where the Venerable Bākula obtained robes during all this time when he did not delight in robes offered by lay devotees and did not perform cutting or sewing—he obtained them from two cities (Kosambī and Vārāṇasī). The Elder Bākula had a great following and fame; his children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren would have robes made from fine cloth, dyed, placed in caskets, and sent to him. When the Elder bathed, they would place them in the bathhouse. The Elder would wear those new robes and give the old robes to any newly ordained monks who arrived.
