After asking about his friend's health, he had a drum beaten (to announce): "From this day forward, whether they be merchants on foot or merchants with carts who come from my friend's city, from the moment they enter my territory, let them be given lodging and rations from the royal granary. Let their taxes be waived, and let no harm whatsoever be done to them." King Bimbisāra also had a drum beaten in his city in the same manner. Then King Bimbisāra sent a message to King Pukkusāti: "In the border regions (paccantadesa), treasures such as rubies and pearls are produced. Whatever treasure, worthy of being seen or heard of, arises in my friend's kingdom, let him not be stingy towards me regarding it." King Pukkusāti also sent a reciprocal message: "The Middle Country is a great region. Whatever treasure of such a nature arises there, let my friend not be stingy towards me regarding it." In this way, as time passed, they became firm friends even though they had never seen each other.
196:
While these two kings lived according to their agreement, first, a gift arrived from King Pukkusāti. The King had obtained eight priceless woolen blankets (kambala) of five colors. He thought, "These blankets are exceedingly excellent; I will send them to my friend King Bimbisāra." He had eight caskets made of heartwood, about the size of a lacquer ball, placed the blankets inside them, sealed them with lacquer, wrapped them in white cloth, placed them in baskets, wrapped them again in cloth, sealed them with the royal seal, and sent ministers, saying, "Give these to my friend." He also gave instructions: "This gift should be viewed in the middle of the city, surrounded by ministers and others." They went and presented them to King Bimbisāra.

Upon hearing the instructions, King Bimbisāra had a drum beaten to assemble the ministers and others. Surrounded by ministers and others in the middle of the city, seated on a noble throne under a white parasol, he broke the seal, removed the cloth, opened the basket, unwrapped the inner bundle, and seeing the lacquer balls, he thought, "My friend Pukkusāti probably sent this gift thinking, 'My friend is fond of gambling.'" He took one ball, rolled it in his hand, and weighing it, realized it was not very heavy and that there was a cloth bundle inside. Then he struck it against the leg of the throne, and the lacquer immediately fell off. The King opened the casket with his fingernail, and seeing the precious blanket inside, he had the others opened as well; all were woolen blankets. Then he had them spread out; they were perfect in color and texture, sixteen cubits long and eight cubits wide. When the people saw them, they snapped their fingers and shouted in triumph, waving their clothes. They were delighted, saying, "Our King's unseen friend, King Pukkusāti, has sent such a gift without even meeting him; it is truly fitting to be friends with such a king." The King had each blanket valued; all were priceless treasures. Among them, he sent four to be offered to the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha and kept four in his palace. Then he thought, "One who sends a gift later should send something superior to the gift sent first. My friend has sent a priceless gift; what shall I send?"

If one asks, "Was there no treasure superior to that in Rājagaha?" it is not that there was none; the King was of great merit. However, for King Bimbisāra, from the time he became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), apart from the Triple Gem, no other treasure was capable of producing joy. Treasures are of two kinds: animate (saviññāṇaka) and inanimate (aviññāṇaka). Among these, gold, silver, and so on are called inanimate treasures. Living beings are called animate treasures. Inanimate treasure is only for the sake of animate treasure...
197:
No, there is a treasure superior to that blanket. King Bimbisāra then strove to select a treasure. What is called a treasure is of two kinds: animate and inanimate. Among those two, gold, silver, and the like are called inanimate treasures, while beings endowed with life-faculties are called animate treasures. Inanimate treasures serve merely as requisites, such as ornaments, for animate treasures; therefore, of these two kinds, the animate treasure alone is superior. Animate treasures are also of two kinds: animal treasures and human treasures. Among those two, the elephant treasure and the horse treasure are called animal treasures; even those animal treasures arise only for the use of humans; therefore, of these two, the human treasure alone is superior.

Human treasures are also of two kinds: the female treasure and the male treasure. Among those two, even the female treasure that arises for a Wheel-turning King (Cakkavatti) is merely for the use of the male; therefore, of these two, the male treasure alone is superior. Male treasures are also of two kinds: the lay treasure and the monastic treasure. Among those two, even a Wheel-turning King, a lay treasure, pays homage with the five-point prostration to a young novice who has been ordained only today; therefore, of these two, the monastic treasure alone is superior. Monastic treasures are also of two kinds: the trainee treasure (sekha) and the adept treasure (asekha). Among those two, even a hundred thousand trainees cannot reach a fraction of the quality of an adept; therefore, of these two, the adept treasure alone is superior. That adept treasure is also of two kinds: the Buddha treasure and the disciple treasure (sāvaka). Among those two, even a hundred thousand disciple treasures cannot reach a fraction of the quality of the Buddha treasure; therefore, of these two, the Buddha treasure alone is superior.

The Buddha treasure is also of two kinds: the Paccekabuddha treasure and the Omniscient Buddha (Sabbaññū-Buddha) treasure. Among those two, even a hundred thousand Paccekabuddhas cannot reach a fraction of the quality of the Omniscient Buddha; therefore, of these two, the Omniscient Buddha treasure alone is the most supreme. Indeed, in the world with its devas, there is no treasure equal to the Buddha treasure. Therefore, thinking, 'I will send this peerless treasure to my friend,' the King asked the ministers residing in the city of Takkasilā, 'Friends, are these three treasures—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—manifest in your country?' They replied, 'Great King, even the sound of the words "Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha" does not yet exist in that country; how could there be the opportunity to see them?'

'Friends, that is well,' the King said, being delighted. He thought, 'To favor the people, it would be appropriate to invite the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) to the city of Takkasilā where my friend resides. However, the Buddhas do not usually stay in border regions until dawn. Therefore, it is not possible for the Teacher to go. It might be appropriate to invite the Great Disciples such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna.'
198:
I also thought, 'Even if I hear that the noble elders reside in border regions, it is only proper to send people to invite those noble elders to one's presence and serve them.' Therefore, the Great Disciple elders cannot go either. 'I will send a message in such a manner that when the message is sent, it will be as if the Teacher and the Great Disciples have gone themselves,' he planned.

Having thought thus, he had a gold plate made, four cubits in length and about one span in width, neither too thin nor too thick, saying, 'I shall write the letters on that gold plate today.' Early in the morning, having washed his head and undertaken the Uposatha precepts, and having eaten his breakfast, he removed his scents, flowers, and ornaments. Taking red vermilion (cinnabar) in a golden bowl, he closed the doors starting from the ground floor, ascended the palace, opened the lion-window facing the East, and sitting in the open air, he wrote the letters on the gold plate as follows:

'In this world, the Buddha, the Blessed One, has appeared—the one who is worthy of special offerings (Arahaṃ), the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), endowed with the three and eight kinds of knowledge and the fifteen kinds of conduct (Vijjācaraṇasampanno), the Well-gone (Sugato), the Knower of the worlds (Lokavidū), the Incomparable (Anuttaro), the Trainer of persons fit to be tamed (Purisadammasārathi), the Teacher of gods and humans (Satthā devamanussānaṃ), the Enlightened One (Buddho), the Blessed One (Bhagavā).' Thus, he first wrote a portion of the Buddha's qualities.

Then he wrote: 'Having thus fulfilled the ten perfections, passing away from the Tusita heaven, he took conception in his mother's womb. Thus the opening of the world occurred. While residing in his mother's womb, this named miracle occurred. While living in the midst of the household life, this named luxury existed. He went forth with such a Great Renunciation. He strove with such Great Effort. Having performed such difficult practices and ascended the terrace of the Great Bodhi tree, sitting on the Unconquered Throne, he realized Omniscient Wisdom. For the Blessed One who realized Omniscient Wisdom, thus occurred the lack of obstruction in the three worlds. In the world with its devas, there is no treasure of such a nature other than the Buddha-treasure.'

'Whatever wealth there be here or beyond,
or whatever precious treasure in the heavens,
there is none equal to the Tathāgata.
In the Buddha is this precious treasure.
By this truth, may there be well-being!'

Having thus written a portion of the Buddha's qualities, the King, wishing to praise the Dhamma-treasure for the second time, wrote: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One... to be personally realized by the wise.' 'The four foundations of mindfulness... the Noble Eightfold Path.' 'The Dhamma taught by the Teacher is of such and such nature.' Thus, he wrote a portion of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), and then—
199:
“The Supreme Buddha praised that pure concentration (of the Path); that concentration is said (by the Buddha and the virtuous) to yield its fruit immediately. There is no other concentration equal to that. This too is a precious jewel in the Dhamma. By this truth, may there be well-being.”

Having thus written the qualities of the Dhamma in part, and wishing to praise the third jewel, the Saṅgha-ratana, he wrote: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well... (and so on) ...is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” He wrote: “Sons of good family, having heard the Dhamma-talk of the Teacher, thus go forth from the household life and renounce. Some renounce giving up the white umbrella of kingship; some give up the vice-regency; some give up the position of general and so forth. Having renounced, they fulfill this practice.” Thus, he wrote in part the Cūḷasīla, Majjhimasīla, and Mahāsīla. He then wrote in part about the restraint of the six sense-doors, mindfulness and clear comprehension, contentment with the four requisites, the nine types of lodgings, the abandoning of the hindrances, the preliminary work, the jhānas and supernormal knowledges, and the thirty-eight meditation subjects up to the destruction of the taints. However, he wrote the sixteen-fold mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) meditation in full detail and then wrote: “The Saṅgha of the Teacher's disciples is endowed with such qualities as these.

Those eight individuals praised by the virtuous constitute four pairs. Those disciples of the Sugata are worthy of offerings; gifts given to them yield great fruit. This too is a precious jewel in the Saṅgha. By this truth, may there be well-being.”

Having thus written the qualities of the Saṅgha in part, he wrote: “The Dispensation of the Blessed One is well-expounded and leads out of suffering. If my friend is able, let him go forth from the household life and renounce.” Then, he rolled up the gold plate, wrapped it in a fine cloth, and placed it in a box made of sandalwood heartwood. He then placed that box into a gold box, the gold box into a silver box, the silver box into a ruby box, the ruby box into a coral box, the coral box into a red ruby box, the red ruby box into a masāragalla (emerald/cat's eye) box, the masāragalla box into a crystal box, the crystal box into an ivory box, the ivory box into an all-jewels box, and the all-jewels box into a wicker box. Finally, he placed that wicker box into a casket made of sandalwood heartwood.
200:
Again, he placed the sandalwood casket into a gold casket and so on, following the previous method, until he placed the all-jewels casket into a wicker casket. Furthermore, he placed the wicker casket into a sandalwood chest and so on, following the previous method, until he placed the all-jewels chest into a wicker chest. He then wrapped it externally with cloth, sealed it with the royal seal, and commanded his ministers: "Decorate the road within the reach of my authority. Let the road be eight usabhas wide; let a four-usabha width be merely cleared, but the middle four usabhas should be grandly prepared with royal majesty."

Then, having decorated the auspicious elephant, he prepared a throne upon it and raised the white umbrella. He had the city streets sprinkled with water and swept, and well-adorned with raised banners and flags, banana trees, full water pots, perfumes, incense, flowers, and so forth. He sent swift messengers to the local governors, saying, "Perform such worship in your respective territories." He himself, adorned with all ornaments, said, "I shall send this gift escorted by a full military force and all kinds of musical instruments." He went to the border of his territory and gave a verbal message to the minister: "Dear friend, when my companion King Pukkusāti receives this gift, let him not receive it in the midst of the harem, but let him ascend the palace and receive it."

Having given this message, he thought, "The Teacher is going to the border regions," and he returned after paying homage with the five-fold prostration. The local governors also prepared the road in the same manner and conveyed the gift.

King Pukkusāti also had the road prepared from the beginning of his kingdom in the same manner, had the city decorated, and went out to welcome the gift. The gift arrived at Takkasilā on an Uposatha day. The minister who brought the gift also conveyed the message spoken by the King. Upon hearing it, the King arranged the necessary hospitality for the ministers who came with the gift. He then took the gift, ascended the palace, and ordered guards at the door, saying, "Let no one enter here." He opened the lion's window, placed the gift on a high seat, and sat himself on a low seat. He broke the seal, removed the cloth wrapping, and opened the containers one by one, starting from the wicker chest. When he saw the sandalwood chest, he thought, "Such a grand preparation cannot be for any ordinary jewel; surely a jewel worthy of being heard has appeared in the Middle Country." Then, he opened that chest, broke the royal seal, and after drawing aside the fine cloth from both sides, he saw the gold plate.
201:
The king spread out the gold plate and began to read, starting with: "How delightful indeed are the letters, how uniform the tops, how even the rows, and how square-shaped!" As he read the virtues of the Buddha, "The Tathāgata has appeared in the world," a powerful joy arose in him, and ninety-nine thousand pores of his body stood on end. He was unaware of whether he was standing or sitting. Then, a more powerful rapture arose in him as he thought, "Through my friend, I have gained the opportunity to hear of this Dispensation (Sāsana), which is difficult to encounter even in a hundred thousand crores of aeons." Being unable to continue reading further, he remained sitting until the surge of rapture subsided. Then he began to read the virtues of the Dhamma: "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One." While reading the virtues of the Dhamma, the same thing happened to him. Again, he sat until the surge of rapture subsided, and then began to read the virtues of the Saṅgha: "The Saṅgha has practiced well." While reading the virtues of the Saṅgha, the same thing happened as before. Finally, after reading the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), he attained the fourfold and fivefold jhānas and spent his time in the bliss of jhāna. No one else was allowed to see him; only a single young attendant could enter. In this way, he spent about half a month.

The citizens gathered in the royal courtyard and shouted, "Since the day the gift was received, there have been no military displays or theatrical performances, and no administration of justice. Let the king show the gift sent by his friend to whoever desires it. Kings are known to try to seize a kingdom for themselves by deceiving others through gifts. What is our king doing?" Hearing the shouting, the king thought, "Shall I uphold the kingdom or shall I uphold the Teacher?" Then the thought occurred to him, "The life of ruling a kingdom cannot be reckoned even by accountants or chief ministers of accounts. I shall only uphold the Teacher's Dispensation." He took the sword kept at his bed, cut off his hair, opened the lion-window (sīhapañjara), and threw the lock of hair along with the jeweled crest (cūḷāmaṇi) into the midst of the assembly, saying, "Take this and rule the kingdom!" The multitude lifted the lock of hair and cried out all at once, "O King, kings who receive gifts from a friend are indeed like you!" Only two inches of hair and beard remained on the king. It is said that he looked just like the Bodhisatta at his renunciation.
202:
Then, he sent the young attendant to fetch two saffron-colored robes and a clay alms-bowl from the market. Dedicating himself to the Teacher, he thought, "Whoever are the Arahants in the world, for their sake is my renunciation." He put on one saffron robe, draped the other over his shoulder, placed the bowl on his left shoulder, took a staff, and paced back and forth a few times on the upper terrace of the palace, reflecting, "Does my renunciation look graceful or not?" Thinking, "My renunciation is indeed graceful," he opened the door and descended from the palace.

As he was descending, the dancers and harem women stationed at the three gates saw him but did not recognize him as their king. They thought, "A certain Paccekabuddha has come to give a Dhamma talk to our king." However, when they went up to the palace and saw the places where the king used to stand and sit, they realized the king had gone and wailed all at once, like people on a ship sinking in the middle of the ocean. As soon as the noble son (King Pukkusāti) reached the ground, the eighteen guilds, all the citizens, and the army surrounded him and wailed loudly.

The ministers also addressed him, saying, "Your Majesty, the kings of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) are very deceitful. Please send a message first to find out whether the Buddha-gem has truly appeared in the world or not, and only then depart. Please turn back, Your Majesty!" He replied, "I believe the word of my friend. Between me and that friend, there is no such thing as double-tongued speech. You all stay back." They continued to follow him nonetheless.

The noble son drew a line with his staff and asked, "To whom does this kingdom belong?" "It belongs to you, Your Majesty," they replied. He said, "Whoever crosses this line shall be punished by royal authority." Just as Queen Sīvalī in the Mahājanaka Jātaka could not bear to cross the line made by the Bodhisatta and rolled on the ground following him, the multitude followed the path she took. But the people did not dare to cross that line; they placed the line at the head of their path and rolled on the ground, wailing.

The noble son departed without taking even a single servant, thinking, "This boy might provide me with a tooth-stick or water for washing my face wherever I arrive." He thought, "My Teacher also renounced through the Great Renunciation and became a monk alone," so he went alone. Thinking, "I am ashamed before the Teacher," and "My Teacher, having renounced, did not ride a vehicle," he did not wear even a single-layered sandal, nor did he carry a leaf-parasol. The people climbed trees, walls, and watchtowers, watching him, saying, "There goes our king." The noble son, thinking, "I must travel a long distance, and it is not possible to complete the journey alone," followed a certain caravan leader. To the delicate noble son...
203: The feet of that delicate gentleman traveling were blistered and burst due to the hardness of the ground, and painful feelings arose. When the caravan traders set up camp and rested, the gentleman left the path and sat at the foot of a tree. There was no one to massage his feet or back at that place. That gentleman, entering the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), dispelled the exhaustion and heat of the journey and spent the time in the bliss of jhāna.  At dawn the next day, after attending to his bodily needs, he followed the caravan again. At breakfast time, the traders took the gentleman's bowl and filled it with food. That food was sometimes undercooked, sometimes overcooked, sometimes contained gravel, and was either saltless or too salty. The gentleman, contemplating only the passage of the throat, consumed it like ambrosia. In this manner, he traveled 192 yojanas (eight yojanas short of two hundred). Even when passing near the gateway of Jetavana Monastery, he did not ask, 'Where does the Teacher reside?' Why? Because of his respect for the Teacher and the influence of the message sent by the King. For the King had sent the message as if the Tathāgata had appeared in Rājagaha, saying, 'The Tathāgata has appeared in the world here.' Therefore, without asking anyone, he bypassed the 45-yojana distance.  When he reached Rājagaha at sunset, he asked, 'Where does the Teacher reside?' They asked, 'Venerable sir, where have you come from?' He replied, 'I have come from the north.' Then they told him, 'On the path you came, 45 yojanas from here, there is a city named Sāvatthī; the Teacher resides there.' The gentleman thought, 'It is now an improper time; it is impossible to go. I will stay here today and go to the Teacher tomorrow.' Then he asked, 'Where do monks who arrive at an improper time stay?' They said, 'Venerable sir, they stay in this potter's shed.' Then he requested permission from the potter, entered, and sat there.  The Blessed One, surveying the world at dawn that day, saw King Pukkusāti and thought: 'This gentleman, having read only the message sent by his friend, has renounced a great kingdom of over 300 yojanas and ordained for my sake. He will reach Rājagaha after traveling 192 yojanas. If I do not go, he will die a helpless death after staying one night, without realizing the three fruits of recluseship. But if I go...'
204: 'If I go, he will realize the three fruits of recluseship. I have fulfilled the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand eons only for the sake of helping beings; I shall help him.' Thinking thus, he attended to his bodily needs early in the morning, wandered for alms in Sāvatthī surrounded by the community of monks, and after returning from the alms round, entered the Gandhakuṭi and rested for a moment to dispel bodily fatigue.  The Blessed One reflected: 'This gentleman has performed a difficult task out of respect for me. He renounced a kingdom of over a hundred yojanas and left alone, without even taking a servant to provide water for washing his face.' Without informing any monk such as Sāriputta or Moggallāna, he took his own bowl and robes and set out alone. While traveling, he did not fly through the air nor did he contract the earth. He thought: 'This gentleman, out of respect and modesty toward me, did not ride any vehicle such as an elephant, horse, chariot, or golden palanquin. He did not even wear single-layered sandals or carry a palm-leaf umbrella. It is fitting that I too should go on foot.' Thus, he traveled on foot.  The Blessed One, concealing his Buddha-glory—endowed with the eighty minor marks, the fathom-wide radiance, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man—traveled in the guise of an ordinary monk, like the full moon obscured by clouds. In the period after a single meal, he covered the 45-yojana distance and reached the potter's shed just as the gentleman had entered at sunset. Referring to this, it was said: 'At that time, monks, a gentleman named Pukkusāti, out of faith, had gone forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of the Blessed One. He was the first to arrive at that potter's dwelling.'  Even after arriving, the Blessed One did not enter the potter's shed by force, saying 'I am the Fully Enlightened Buddha.' Standing at the door, he asked the gentleman for permission, saying, 'Monk, if (you are willing)...' and so on. 'Urunda' means secluded and not cramped. The gentleman gave permission, saying, 'May the venerable one stay as he pleases,' meaning he may stay in whatever posture is comfortable. How could this gentleman, who renounced a kingdom of over a hundred yojanas to ordain, be stingy toward another fellow practitioner in this shed abandoned by the potter?  Some men in this Dispensation, who are empty of the paths and fruits, having ordained, are overcome by the stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsamacchariya) and strive to prevent others from staying, saying, 'This is my monastery, my precinct.' 'He sat down' means that the Lord of the World, the Blessed One, who is extremely delicate, left the Gandhakuṭi which is like a divine mansion, and in the potter's shed—which was like a calf-stable, soiled with scattered ashes, broken pots, grass, straw, rubbish, and the droppings of chickens and pigs—he spread a mat of grass, laid out his rag-robe, and sat down. He sat in the potter's shed just as he would enter and sit in the Gandhakuṭi. Thus, the Blessed One was born of the unbroken Mahāsammata royal lineage, and the gentleman Pukkusāti was also...
205:
Why should one be stingy towards another fellow practitioner regarding a discarded potter's shed? Indeed, some foolish men who have gone forth in this Dispensation, overcome by stinginess regarding dwellings and such, strive to prevent others from staying, saying, "This is my monastery, this is my precinct" in their own living places. "He sat" (nisīdi) means the Lord of the World, who is extremely delicate, left the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) which is like a celestial mansion. In that potter's shed, which was like a rubbish heap, soiled with scattered ashes, broken pots, grass, straw, and the droppings of chickens and pigs, He spread a mat of grass, laid out His rag-robe (paṃsukūla), and sat down just as if He were entering and sitting in the Perfumed Chamber, which is like a celestial mansion and filled with divine fragrances.

Thus, the Blessed One was born into the unbroken Mahāsammata lineage, and the clansman (Pukkusāti) was also raised in a kshatriya womb. The Blessed One was endowed with the resolution (abhinīhara), and the clansman was also endowed with the resolution. The Blessed One went forth after renouncing a kingdom, and so did the clansman. The Blessed One was golden-hued, and so was the clansman. The Blessed One was an attainer of meditative attainments (samāpatti), and so was the clansman. Thus, because these two kshatriyas, both endowed with the resolution, both royal renunciants, both golden-hued, and both attainers of meditative attainments, entered and sat in the potter's shed, that shed was exceedingly beautiful. It should be understood through the simile of two lions entering a jeweled cave. Among those two, the Blessed One, without even giving rise to the thought, "I am delicate, extremely delicate; I have come forty-five yojanas after a single meal; I will rest in the lion's posture for a moment to relieve the fatigue of the journey," entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) while still sitting. The clansman also, without giving rise to the thought, "I have come a journey of one hundred and ninety-two yojanas; I will lie down for a moment to dispel the fatigue of the journey," entered the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) while still sitting. Aiming at this, it was said, "Then the Blessed One, having [spent] much of the night..." and so forth.

Did the Blessed One not come to preach the Dhamma to that clansman? Why did He not preach? Because the clansman's fatigue from the journey had not yet subsided, and he would not yet be able to receive the Dhamma teaching. Thinking, "Let his fatigue subside first," He did not preach. Others say, "Rājagaha is crowded with people and not quiet, filled with the ten sounds; those sounds subside only after about a watch and a half of the night; He did not preach while waiting for those sounds to quiet down." That is not the reason. For the Blessed One, by His own psychic power, could [quiet] even a sound that reached the Brahma realm...
206:
...could quiet it with His power, but He did not preach only because He was waiting for the fatigue of the journey to subside.

In that context, "much of the night" (bahu deva rattiṃ) means a period of about a watch and a half. "This thought occurred" (etadahosi) means the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of fruition, opened His eyes adorned with the five sensitivities (pasāda-rūpa), like opening a jeweled lion-window in a golden mansion, and looked. Then, seeing the clansman sitting like a golden statue, motionless like a firmly planted sacrificial post (indakhīla), free from fidgeting of hands, fidgeting of feet, or shaking of the head, this thought occurred: "This [monk] is indeed graceful (pāsādika)," and so forth. In that context, "pāsādika" means bringing about inspiration (pasāda). This word "pāsādika" is a neuter abstract noun (bhāva-napuṃsaka), meaning he dwells with a posture that brings about inspiration. The meaning here is that he dwells in such a way that his posture becomes inspiring. Indeed, among the four postures, three postures are not [inherently] beautiful. For a monk who is walking, the hands move, the feet move, and the head moves. For one who is standing, the body is stiff. For one who is lying down, the posture is unpleasant to others. But the posture of one who, after the meal, has swept the day-quarters, spread a leather mat, and with well-washed hands and feet, sits with legs crossed in the fourfold-jointed posture (catusandhika-pallaṅka), is truly beautiful and elegant. This clansman also sat having crossed his legs and attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. Thus, the Blessed One, being pleased by his posture alone, thought, "He is indeed graceful."

Why did He think, "What if I were to ask?" Did the Blessed One not know that he had gone forth on His account? It is not that He did not know; He certainly knew. However, if a question is not asked, a conversation does not start; if a conversation does not start, the [intended] talk does not arise. Therefore, He asked for the purpose of establishing a conversation.

Regarding "Would you know if you saw [him]?", everyone knows "This is the Buddha" when seeing the Tathāgata shining with the glory of a Buddha. Such knowing is not wonderful. However, when He wanders in the guise of an ordinary alms-collecting monk, concealing the glory of a Buddha, He is difficult to recognize. Therefore, the Venerable Pukkusāti spoke according to his own nature, saying, "I would not know." Because of this, he did not recognize even the Blessed One who was sitting in the same potter's shed.

"This thought occurred" means He had the thought after knowing that the fatigue of the journey had subsided. "It is so, friend" means the clansman, having read only the message sent by his friend...
207:
King Pukkusāti, while renouncing his kingdom to become a monk, thought: "I shall get to hear the sweet and noble Dhamma teaching of the Buddha (Dasabala)." After becoming a monk and traveling such a long distance, he had not found anyone who would say even a few words like, "Monk, I will teach you the Dhamma." When the Blessed One said, "Monk, I will teach you the Dhamma," why would King Pukkusāti not listen respectfully? Indeed, this King Pukkusāti was like a drunkard longing for liquor, or like a thirsty elephant. Therefore, acknowledging that he would listen respectfully, he said, "Very well, friend."

With the words "Cha dhāturo ayaṃ," the Blessed One, without teaching the fifteen practices (caraṇa) that constitute the preliminary stage of insight for that young man of good family, began to teach from the very beginning only the characteristics of insight (vipassanā), which is absolute emptiness (suññatā) and the proximate cause for the fruit of Arahatship. If a person's preliminary practice is not yet pure, the Buddha first teaches this preliminary practice consisting of restraint in virtue (sīlasaṃvara), guarding the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven noble qualities (saddhamma), and the four jhānas. However, if this practice is already pure for someone, the Buddha does not teach that preliminary practice but teaches only insight (vipassanā), which is the proximate cause for the fruit of Arahatship. For King Pukkusāti, the preliminary practice was already pure. Because it was pure, after reading the message sent by King Bimbisāra, this king attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) while still in his noble palace. That fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing fulfilled the function of a vehicle for the king as he traveled the distance of 92 yojanas. His novice virtue (sāmaṇera-sīla) was also complete. Therefore, without teaching the preliminary practice, the Buddha began to teach him only the characteristics of insight, which is absolute emptiness and the proximate cause for the fruit of Arahatship.

In the term "Cha dhāturo," the elements (dhātu) exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha), but the person (puggala) does not exist in the ultimate sense. The Blessed One, in some instances, shows the non-existent through the existent; in some, the existent through the non-existent; in some, the existent through the existent; and in some, the non-existent through the non-existent. This should be understood in detail according to the method explained in the Sabbāsava Sutta. In this Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, however, wishing to show the non-existent person through the existent elements, He spoke in this way. If the Blessed One had discarded the designation (paññatti) "person" and established the mind only by saying "elements," King Pukkusāti would have fallen into doubt, reached great confusion, and would not have been able to accept the teaching. Therefore, the Blessed One gradually led him to abandon the designation "person," saying, "The terms 'being,' 'man,' or 'person' are merely designations; in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a 'being.'" Thus, establishing the mind only on the collection of elements, [to realize] the three lower fruits...
208:
Like a great teacher skilled in various languages as mentioned in the Anangaṇa Sutta, who teaches a craft using those respective languages, the Buddha spoke in this way, thinking, "I shall make him penetrate [the three lower fruits]."

In that passage, "Cha dhāturo" means that those six elements belong to that person. This is what is meant: "O man, that which you perceive as a 'man' is merely a collection of six elements; in the ultimate sense, there is no 'man' here; 'man' is merely a designation (paññatti)." The same method should be understood for the remaining terms. In the term "Caturādhiṭṭhāno," "adhiṭṭhāna" means a foundation (patiṭṭhā); thus, it means one who has four foundations. This is what is meant: "That monk, this person of six elements, six bases of contact (phassāyatana), and eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra), when he turns away from saṃsāra and takes hold of Arahatship, which is the supreme success, he does so by standing on these four foundations." Thus, he is called "Caturādhiṭṭhāno."

"Yattha ṭhitaṃ" means when one stands on those foundations (wisdom, truth, relinquishment, and peace). "Maññassā vā nappavattanti" means the streams of conceit (māna) do not occur. "Muni santo'ti vuccati" means the sage (muni) whose defilements are exhausted is called "peaceful" and "extinguished" (nibbuta). "Paññaṃ nappamajjeyya" means that for the sake of penetrating with the wisdom of the fruit of Arahatship, one should not neglect the wisdom of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) from the very beginning. "Saccamanurakkheyya" means that for the sake of realizing Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca), one should guard verbal truth (vacī-sacca) from the very beginning. "Cāgamanubrūheyya" means that for the sake of relinquishing all defilements through the path of Arahatship, one should increase the relinquishment of defilements from the very beginning. "Santimeva so sikkheyya" means that for the sake of calming all defilements through the path of Arahatship, one should train in the calming of defilements from the very beginning. Thus, to attain the foundations of wisdom and so on, these preliminary foundations of tranquility, insight, wisdom, and so on are taught.

"Phassāyatanaṃ" means the foundation or the source of contact (phassa). Terms like "Paññādhiṭṭhāna" should be understood by way of the wisdom of the fruit of Arahatship and so on mentioned previously.

Now, by way of the laid-down outline (mātikā), He should have said, "Yattha ṭhitaṃ maññassā vā nappavattanti," but once Arahatship is reached, there is no further work to be done with "Paññaṃ nappamajjeyya" and so on. Therefore, although the Blessed One set aside the order of the outline, wishing to analyze it according to the nature of the Dhamma, He spoke "Paññaṃ nappamajjeyya" and so on. In that passage, who neglects wisdom and who does not? One who, having gone forth in this Dispensation, makes a living through the twenty-one types of improper search, such as medical practice, and cannot maintain a mind suitable for a monk, is said to neglect wisdom.

One who, having gone forth in this Dispensation, stands in virtue, learns the words of the Buddha, stands in concentration, takes up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that pleases his mind, resorts to a secluded place, performs the preliminary work for a kasina, and brings about meditative attainments (samāpatti), and then dwells developing insight with the thought, "I shall take hold of the fruit of Arahatship this very day"—such a person is said not to neglect wisdom. In fact, in this sutta, the monk's non-neglect of wisdom is taught by way of the meditation on elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna). I shall say another point: the explanation regarding the meditation on elements in this sutta has already been detailed below in the Hatthipadopama Sutta and others. In this sutta, the meaning of "Atha paraṃ viññāṇameva avasissati" is also the conclusion. To speak in detail, the meditation on materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) was taught previously; now, the meditation on the immaterial (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) [will be taught] by way of feeling (vedanā).
209:
One who makes a living through improper search and is unable to establish a state of mind suitable for monkhood is said to be negligent of wisdom. However, one who ordains in the Dispensation, remains established in virtue, learns the Buddha's word, undertakes suitable ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), takes up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) pleasing to the mind, resorts to a secluded lodging, performs the preliminary work for kasina, attains meditative absorptions (samāpatti), and dwells developing insight (vipassanā) thinking, "Today itself I shall reach Arahantship"—this person is said to be non-negligent of wisdom. In this Sutta, non-negligence in wisdom is taught by way of the meditation on elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna). Everything that should be said regarding this meditation on elements has already been taught below in the Hatthipadopama Sutta and others.

"Then only consciousness will remain"—this statement is also a separate connection (anusandhi) in this context. Since the meditation on material forms (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) was taught below, this teaching is now begun to show the meditation on the formless (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by way of feeling (vedanā). Alternatively, this noble son (the King) possesses consciousness that performs the task of insight by way of the insight that leads to the elements such as the earth element; this teaching is begun to show that consciousness by analyzing it by way of the consciousness element (viññāṇa-dhātu). In that context, for what purpose is it said "it will remain"? It remains for the purpose of the Teacher's explanation and for the noble son's penetration (realization). "Parisuddhaṃ" means free from defilements. "Pariyodātaṃ" means radiant. "He knows: 'It is pleasant'" means when experiencing a pleasant feeling, he knows, "I experience a pleasant feeling." The same method applies to the other two terms. If this discourse on feeling had not been taught below, it would be appropriate to teach it here. However, since this discourse on feeling was already taught in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, it should be understood according to the method taught in that Sutta. The words beginning with "sukhavedaniyaṃ" are taught to show the arising and passing away by way of causes. In that context, "sukhavedaniyaṃ" refers to contact (phassa) which is the cause of pleasant feeling. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

"Then only equanimity will remain"—in this statement, to give a simile: just as a skilled master of pearls pierces a pearl with a diamond needle, drops it onto a piece of leather, and the apprentice takes it and strings it, making pearl necklaces, pearl nets, and so on; even so, this noble son, reflecting again and again on the meditation subject taught and given step by step by the Blessed One, has become proficient in it. For him, both the meditation on material forms and the meditation on the formless...
210:
(For King Pukkusāti, the meditation on material forms and the meditation on the formless) became proficient (mastered). When that happened, the Blessed One said, "Thereafter, only equanimity will remain."

For what purpose does it remain? It remains for the purpose of the Teacher's explanation (by way of exposition). Some teachers say, "It remains for the purpose of the noble son's (King Pukkusāti's) penetration"; that statement should not be accepted. The reason is that the noble son, after reading the news from his friend (King Bimbisāra), while still standing on the palace roof, had already produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). That fourth jhāna served as the function of a vehicle for that noble son who traveled this distance (of 192 yojanas). It remains only for the purpose of the Teacher's explanation. In this context, the Teacher praised the fine-material sphere jhāna (rūpāvacara jhāna) of the noble son. The meaning of what is about to be said is: "Monk, this fourth rūpāvacara jhāna of yours is well-practiced (mastered)." The words beginning with "parisuddhā" are indeed the praise of that very equanimity of the fourth jhāna.

"Ukkhaṃ bandheyya" means one should prepare a crucible (fire-pot). "Ālimpeyya" means one should put fuel into that crucible, apply fire, and blow with a tube to kindle the fire. "Ukkāmukhe pakkhipeyya" means one should stir the embers and place (the gold) on top of the embers or put it into a small pot. "Nīhaṭaṃ" means having faults removed (free from impurities). "Ninnītakasāvaṃ" means having subtle impurities removed. "Evameva kho" means just as that (pure) gold can be fashioned into any desired ornament, even so, this equanimity of the fourth jhāna serves the purpose of whatever one desires among these benefits: insight (vipassanā), direct knowledge (abhiññā), cessation (nirodha/nibbāna), and descending into a good destination (sugati). Thus, He praised the virtues (of the fourth jhāna).

Why did the Blessed One praise the fourth rūpāvacara jhāna instead of speaking of its lack of merit in order to exhaust the attachment (nikanti) to it? The reason is that the noble son's arousal of attachment to the fourth jhāna was strong. If He had spoken of its lack of merit, the noble son might have fallen into doubt and confusion, thinking: "This fourth jhāna served as a vehicle for me who ordained and traveled a distance of 192 yojanas. I came this long distance with the bliss of jhāna and delight in jhāna. The Blessed One speaks of the lack of merit of such a sublime state. Does He speak knowing or without knowing?" Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of its praise.

In the term "tadanudhammaṃ," the formless sphere jhāna (arūpāvacara jhāna) is called "Dhamma," and because it follows that formless jhāna, the fine-material sphere jhāna is called "Anudhamma." Alternatively, the resultant (vipāka) jhāna is called "Dhamma," and the wholesome (kusala) jhāna is called "Anudhamma." "Tadupādānā" means because of grasping that (the sphere of infinite space). "Ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ" means for twenty thousand aeons (kappas). This is said by way of the resultant (vipāka). The same method should be understood for the sections above this (such as the sphere of infinite consciousness, etc.).
211:
## 
Having thus praised the virtues of the formless-sphere meditative absorptions (arūpāvacara-jhāna) through four turns, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with "He understands thus" (so evaṃ pajānāti), wishing to show the faults of those very formless-sphere absorptions. In that passage, the phrase "this is conditioned" (saṅkhatametaṃ) means that although there is a lifespan of twenty thousand eons in this Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana), this absorption is conditioned and prepared by causes; it arises only when one makes an effort. It is not permanent like Nibbāna; it is unstable, not eternal, and lasts only for a moment. It is of the nature to fall away, to perish, and to be destroyed. It is followed by birth, oppressed by aging, afflicted by death, and established in suffering. It is without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and is always devoid of a true refuge. The same method should be understood for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and the other absorptions.

Now, wishing to conclude the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "He neither constructs that..." (so neva taṃ abhisaṅkharoti). For example, it is like a skilled physician who, seeing the manifestation of poison, causes vomiting to move the poison from its place, and prevents it from reaching the upper parts like the shoulders or the head, eventually bringing the poison down and casting it onto the ground. In the same way, the Blessed One praised the virtues of the formless-sphere absorptions to the noble son. Hearing those words, the noble son abandoned his attachment to the fine-material sphere absorptions (rūpāvacara-jhāna) and developed a longing for the formless-sphere absorptions.

The Blessed One, knowing that longing, spoke to the monk who had not yet reached or attained those formless-sphere absorptions, saying: "There is indeed what is called 'success' in these realms such as the Sphere of Infinite Space. Among those Brahmas, the lifespan in the first Brahma world is twenty thousand eons, in the second forty thousand, in the third sixty thousand, and in the fourth eighty-four thousand eons. However, that absorption is impermanent, unstable, not eternal, and temporary. It is of the nature to fall away, to perish, and to be destroyed. It is followed by birth, oppressed by aging, afflicted by death, and established in suffering. It is without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and is devoid of refuge. Even after enjoying success there for such a long time, if one dies as a worldling (puthujjana), one must fall again into the four woeful states (apāya)." Thus, the Buddha explained all these faults with the single phrase "this is conditioned" (saṅkhatametaṃ). When the noble son heard about those faults, he ended his attachment to the formless-sphere absorptions. The Blessed One, knowing that the noble son's attachment to both the fine-material and formless-sphere absorptions had ended, spoke the words beginning with "He neither constructs that..." wishing to take the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Alternatively, it is like a great warrior who, having pleased a king, receives a noble village yielding a revenue of one hundred thousand. Later, the king, remembering the warrior's power, thinks, "This warrior is of great power; what he has received is too little." He then says, "Friend, this village is not yet suitable for you; take another village yielding four hundred thousand..."
212:
"This village is not yet suitable for you; take another village yielding four hundred thousand." The warrior would say, "Very well, your majesty," and giving up that village, would take the other. Even before the warrior reached that village, the king would have him summoned and say, "What benefit is there for you in that village? The plague (ahi-vātaka-roga) occurs there. But in such a place, there is a great city; raise the white umbrella there and rule as king." The warrior would do as told.

In this simile, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha should be seen as the king. The noble son named Pukkusāti should be seen as the great warrior. The fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-catuttha-jhāna) should be seen as the first village received. The teaching of the formless states after causing the end of attachment to the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing should be seen as the time when it was said, "Give up that village and take another." The act of turning back the longing for those formless attainments (samāpatti) before they were even reached—by teaching their faults, saying "this is also conditioned" (saṅkhatametaṃ) regarding the formless realm—and then taking the conclusion of the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship above that, should be seen as the time when it was said, "What benefit is there for you in that village? The plague occurs there. In such a place there is a city; raise the white umbrella and rule as king."

In that teaching, "he neither constructs" (neva abhisaṅkharoti) means he does not strive for the sake of increase or decrease, nor does he accumulate. "He does not volitionally construct" (na abhisañcetayati) means he does not prepare or plan. "For existence or non-existence" (bhavāya vā vibhavāya vā) means for growth or for decline; this should also be applied by way of the views of eternalism and annihilationism. "He clings to nothing in the world" (na kiñci loke upādiyati) means he does not grasp or misapprehend even a single phenomenon among forms and so on in the world through craving. With the words "He understands: '...there is no further state here'" (nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti), the Blessed One, established in his own Buddha-range, took the pinnacle of Arahantship in the teaching. The noble son, however, penetrated the three fruits of the ascetic life (sāmaññaphala) according to his own supporting conditions (upanissaya).

For example, while a king is eating food of various flavors from a golden bowl, he might roll a large ball of food according to the size of his own mouth. When a young prince sitting on his lap shows desire for that ball of food, the king would offer it to him. The prince would take only a small mouthful according to the size of his own mouth. The king would then eat the rest himself or put it back into the dish. Similarly, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, took the pinnacle of Arahantship which is his own measure and delivered the teaching; the noble son penetrated the three fruits of the ascetic life according to his own supporting conditions.

Even before attaining this fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmi-phala), when the Buddha was delivering this kind of discourse on the aggregates, elements, and bases as being utterly empty (accanta-suññata) and struck by the three characteristics, the noble son had no doubt or uncertainty. Nor was there any sluggishness or speculative wandering such as, "So it is said, indeed, my teacher said so."
213:
It is not as one might think. Indeed, in some places where there are beings to be tamed, the Buddhas wander in an unrecognized form. Doubt and uncertainty such as "Is this person truly a Sammāsambuddha?" did indeed occur. Only when King Pukkusāti realized the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala) did he reach the conclusion, "This Blessed One is my teacher." If he reached that conclusion, why did he not confess his fault? It was because there was no opportunity. This is because the Blessed One was preaching the Dhamma continuously, like the celestial Ganges descending, following the established outline (mātikā).

"So" (He) refers to an Arahant. "Anajjhosita" means knowing that it is not proper to swallow and take as one's own. "Anabhinandita" means knowing that it is not proper to delight in through the power of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi).

"Visaṃyutto naṃ vedeti" (He feels it detached) means: If for that person, the underlying tendency to lust (rāgānusaya) arose based on pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) based on painful feeling, or the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) based on neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, then he would be feeling it joined with underlying tendencies. But because they do not arise, he feels that feeling detached from them; he is one who has escaped and is freed from underlying tendencies. "Kāyapariyantika" means a feeling that ends with the body. It means a feeling that occurs as long as the body persists (kāyapavatti) and does not occur after the body breaks up. The same logic applies to the second term (jīvitapariyantika). "Anabhinanditāni sītībhavissanti" (Un-delighted in, they will become cool) means: Because there is no special indulgence in defilements in the twelve bases (āyatana), they are not delighted in through craving and views, and will cease right here in these twelve bases. Even though defilements cease upon reaching Nibbāna, they are said to cease in those twelve bases where they no longer exist. This meaning should be shown by the problem of origin (samudaya): "When this craving ceases here, it ceases." Therefore, the Blessed One said that even the defilements that have become cool upon reaching Nibbāna "will become cool right here in this life." If it is objected, "Is it not feelings that are spoken of here, not defilements?", feelings also become cool only because of the absence of defilements. Otherwise, there is no such thing as the cooling of those feelings. Therefore, this is well-spoken.

"Evameva kho" (Even so): Here is the comparison between the simile and the thing illustrated. For example, a man pours oil into a burning oil lamp when the oil is exhausted, and puts in a wick when the wick is exhausted; by doing so, the flame continues without interruption. Even so, a worldling (puthujjana) staying in one existence performs wholesome and unwholesome deeds; because of that kamma, he is reborn in happy destinations and in woeful states. Thus, of feelings...
214:
...the non-interruption of the flame occurs. But especially, if a man becomes weary of the flame and, thinking "Because of this man the flame continues without interruption," hides and cuts off that man's head. When he cuts it off, the wick and oil can no longer be supplied, and the flame, being without fuel, goes out. Even so, a practitioner (yogāvacara) who is weary of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa) completely cuts off wholesome and unwholesome kamma through the path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). Because they are completely cut off, after the breakup of the body of the monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), feelings to be felt do not arise again.

"Tasmā" (Therefore): Because the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphalapaññā) is superior to the initial concentration (samādhi) and insight wisdom (vipassanāpaññā). "Evaṃ samannāgato" (Thus possessed): This refers to one possessed of this noble foundation of the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship. Although the "knowledge of the destruction of all suffering" (sabbadukkhakkhaye ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, in this sutta, the knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship is intended. That is why it is said: "His liberation, being established in truth, is unshakable (akuppa)."

Here, "liberation" (vimutti) is the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship, and "truth" (sacca) is the ultimate truth, Nibbāna. It is called "unshakable" (akuppa) because it takes the unshakable Nibbāna as its object. "Musā" means a false thing; "mosadhamma" means having the nature of perishing. That "truth" means having a non-false nature, and "amosadhamma" means having the nature of not perishing.

"Tasmā" (Therefore): Because the ultimate truth, Nibbāna, is superior to the truth of speech (vacīsacca) resulting from initial calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), and superior to the truth of suffering and the truth of origin. "Evaṃ samannāgato" (Thus possessed): This refers to one possessed of this noble foundation of ultimate truth.

"Pubbe" (Before): This refers to the time when one was a worldling (puthujjana). "Upadhī honti" (Acquisitions exist): This refers to the existence of these acquisitions: the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), the acquisition of defilements (kilesūpadhi), the acquisition of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārူpadhi), and the acquisition of the five cords of sensual pleasure (pañcakāmaguṇူpadhi). "Samattā samādinnā" means acquisitions that are fully taken up and grasped. "Tasmā" (Therefore): Because the abandonment of defilements through the path of Arahantship is superior to the abandonment of defilements through initial calm and insight, and superior to the abandonment of defilements through the path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), etc. "Evaṃ samannāgato" (Thus possessed): This refers to one possessed of this noble foundation of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna).

In the terms "āghāta" etc., "āghāta" is by way of resentment, "byāpāda" is by way of ill-will, and "sampadosa" is by way of malevolence. By these three terms, only the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa) is meant. "Tasmā" (Therefore): Because the initial...
215:
The cessation of defilements through the Path of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga) is particularly noble, even more so than the cessation through the power of Samatha and Vipassanā, or through the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) and the subsequent paths. Therefore, "endowed in this way" means being endowed with this noble foundation of the cessation of defilements.

"Conceiving" (maññita) can refer to all three types: conceiving through craving (taṇhā), conceiving through conceit (māna), and conceiving through views (diṭṭhi). However, in the context of "I am this," only conceiving through craving is appropriate for the term "I am."

In terms such as "disease" (roga), it is called a disease because it oppresses; it is called a boil (gaṇḍa) because it destroys from within; and it is called a dart (salla) because it pierces. The statement "the sage is at peace" means that the sage, who is an Arahant (khīṇāsava), has extinguished defilements and is at peace. "Wherein he stands" refers to the place where he is established.

"In brief" implies that all Dhamma teachings of the Buddhas are, in fact, concise; there is no such thing as a detailed teaching. Even the Samantapaṭṭhāna discourse is considered concise. Thus, the Blessed One brought the discourse to its conclusion according to the sequence of connections. Among the four types of individuals, such as the *ugghāṭitaññū*, the clansman Pukkusāti was a *vipañcitaññū* (one who understands after a detailed explanation). Therefore, the Blessed One taught this Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta through the influence of a *vipañcitaññū* individual.

When he requested, "Venerable Sir, my bowl and robes are not yet complete," why did the miraculous bowl and robes not appear for that clansman? It was because he had not offered any of the eight requisites in his past lives. It should not be said that he had not given any dāna, for the clansman had indeed given dāna and made aspirations. However, miraculous bowls and robes only appear for those in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*); since this person was to be reborn again, they did not appear. Then, why did the Blessed One not seek them out himself and ordain him? Because there was no opportunity. The clansman's life had come to an end; it was as if a Great Brahmā, an Anāgāmī to be reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm, had come and sat in the potter's shed. Therefore, the Buddha did not seek them himself.

At what time did he depart to seek the bowl and robes? He departed at the rising of the dawn. It is said that the conclusion of the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching, the rising of the dawn, and the emission of the rays occurred at the same moment. As soon as the Blessed One finished the discourse, he emitted the six-colored rays (chabbannaraṃsi), and the entire potter's dwelling was instantly filled with light. The six-colored rays, appearing in masses and flashes, raced toward all directions, making it look as if covered with gold plates or brilliant with clusters of various colored flowers and jewels. The Blessed One resolved, "Let the townspeople see me." Upon seeing the Blessed One, the townspeople informed one another, "The Teacher has arrived; he is staying in the potter's shed," and they reported this to the King.
216:
King Bimbisāra came, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked, "Venerable Sir, at what time did you arrive?" The Buddha replied, "Great King, I arrived yesterday at the time of sunset." "For what purpose did the Blessed One come?" the King asked again. "Great King, your friend King Pukkusāti, having heard the message sent by you, went forth and ordained. Aiming to meet me, he traveled 45 yojanas beyond Sāvatthī, entered this potter's shed, and sat down. I came to favor him and delivered a Dhamma discourse; that clansman has now penetrated the three lower fruits, Great King."

"Venerable Sir, where is he now?" the King asked. "Great King, having requested ordination but lacking a complete set of bowl and robes, he has gone to seek them," the Buddha replied. The King followed in the direction the clansman had gone. The Blessed One also departed through the air and appeared in the Gandhakuṭī of Jetavana Monastery.

While seeking the bowl and robes, that clansman did not go to King Bimbisāra, nor did he go to the traveling merchants from Takkasilā. This thought occurred to him: "It is not proper for me to seek a bowl and robes by picking and choosing what is pleasing or unpleasing here and there like a cock. Avoiding the great city, I will search in water-landings, cemeteries, rubbish heaps, and alleys." Thinking thus, he first began to search for scraps of cloth in the rubbish heaps in the alleys.

Regarding the phrase "deprived him of life": while King Pukkusāti was looking for scraps of cloth at a certain rubbish heap, a young cow with a calf, which had gone wild, ran up and gored him to death with its horns. That clansman, whose internal state was one of hunger, reached the end of his life while still in the air and fell. He lay on the rubbish heap like a golden statue placed face down. After passing away, he was reborn in the Aviha Brahma realm, and at the very moment of rebirth, he attained Arahatship. It is said that seven individuals attained Arahatship at the very moment they were reborn in the Aviha Brahma realm. Thus it was said:

"Seven bhikkhus, reborn in Aviha, are liberated,
With lust and hatred destroyed, they have crossed over attachment in the world.
Who are they that crossed the mire, the realm of Death so hard to cross?
Who, having left the human body, have reached the state of celestials?"
217:
"Upaka, Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti—these three;
Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi, and Singiya;
These, having left the human body, have transcended the divine bond (reaching the Suddhāvāsa realms)." (Saṃ. Ni. 1.50, 105).

King Bimbisāra also thought, "My friend Pukkusāti, merely by reading the message I sent, abandoned the kingship of Takkasilā that was in his hands and traveled this great distance. This noble son has done what is difficult to do. I shall honor him with the honors due to a monk." Thus, he sent people here and there, saying, "Search for my friend." Those sent saw him fallen at a rubbish heap and, having seen him, returned to inform the king. When the king went and saw the noble son, he lamented, "Alas, we did not get the chance to honor our friend; my friend has become helpless." After lamenting, he had the noble son's body carried on a couch and placed in a suitable location. Not knowing how to perform honors for one who was not yet fully ordained (anupasampanna), he summoned bath-attendants, barbers, and others, had the noble son's head washed, had him dressed in clean clothes, had him adorned in royal attire, and placed him on a golden palanquin. Offering worship with all kinds of musical instruments, perfumes, and garlands, he carried him out of the city, built a great pyre (citaka) with much sandalwood, performed the funeral rites for the noble son, took the relics, and enshrined them in a stupa. In all places, the rest is clear.

## Within the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta. In that sutta, "pointing out" (ācikkhanā) means pointing out that "this is the Noble Truth of Suffering... pe... this is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering." This same method applies to the remaining terms. Furthermore, "prescribing" (paññāpanā) here means the establishing (ṭhapanā) of the Truth of Suffering and so forth. Indeed, one who prepares a seat is said in the world to "prescribe (arrange) a seat." "Setting forth" (paṭṭhapanā) is the same as "prescribing." "Revealing" (vivaraṇā) means making open (vivaṭakaraṇa). "Analyzing" (vibhajanā) means the act of dividing into parts (vibhāgakiriya). "Making plain" (uttānīkamma) means making it evident (pākaṭabhāvakaraṇa).
218:
"Anuggāhakā" refers to those who support through the two kinds of support: material support (āmisa-saṅgaha) and Dhamma support (dhamma-saṅgaha).

"Janetā" is the mother who gives birth (the biological mother). "Āpādetā" is the one who nurtures (the nursing mother). It is shown that Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is like a nurturing mother. A biological mother carries the child in her womb for nine or ten months, avoiding salty and sour foods, and after giving birth from her womb, she hands the child over to a nurturing mother or nurse. That nurse raises the child with milk, butter, and so on, and when the child grows up, they move about happily as they wish.

In the same way, Venerable Sāriputta supports those who have ordained under him or under others with the two kinds of support, tending to the sick, and engaging them in meditation. When he knows they have reached the state of a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), from the time they are freed from the dangers of the woeful states, he thinks, "Now these people will produce the higher paths through their own individual effort," and becomes indifferent toward them, instead instructing other new people. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also supports those who have ordained under him or under others in the same way and engages them in meditation, but even when they have reached the lower three fruits, he does not yet reach the state of indifference. Why? Because it is said that he has this thought: The Blessed One said, "Monks, just as even a small amount of excrement is foul-smelling... pe ... even a small amount of urine, saliva, pus, or blood is foul-smelling; in the same way, monks, I do not praise existence (bhava) even for a tiny amount, even for the duration of a finger-snap."

Therefore, as long as they do not reach Arahantship, he does not reach the state of indifference, and only when they reach Arahantship does he become indifferent. For that reason, the Blessed One said: "Monks, Sāriputta is like the mother who gives birth. Moggallāna is like the nurse who rears the born. Sāriputta, monks, disciplines in the fruit of Stream-entry; Moggallāna disciplines in the highest goal (Arahantship)."

"Pahoti" means "is able."

Knowledge of Suffering means the knowledge of hearing (savana), reflection (sammasana), and penetration (paṭivedha). The same applies to the Origin of Suffering. In the Cessation of Suffering, it should be said as the knowledge of hearing and penetration. The same applies to the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

In "nekkhamma-saṅkappa" (renunciation-thought) and so on, it is called renunciation-thought because of its nature of opposing sensuality (kāma), or because of the state of being escaped from sensuality, or because it arises in one who is reflecting on sensuality, or because it arises while performing the destruction or stilling of sensuality, or because it arises in seclusion from sensuality. In the remaining two terms (right thought) as well, the method is the same. All of these are obtained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage (before the path); however, at the moment of the Path (magga-kkhaṇa), they are obtained in a single consciousness. In that path-moment, only one Thought (Sammā-saṅkappa) which totally eradicates the volition of Wrong Thought (Micchā-saṅkappa) is obtained, not various thoughts.
219:
(Right Intention) is attained. Right Speech and the others are also attained in various consciousnesses in the preliminary stage; however, in the path-moment, they are attained in a single consciousness in the manner already described. What has been stated here is merely a summary; for a detailed explanation, one should look into the Saccakathā in the Visuddhimagga and the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta is finished.
## 12. Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasutta Vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta. In that sutta, regarding the name "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī," "Gotamī" is the clan name. On the day of her naming, the Brahmins in attendance, seeing her possession of auspicious marks, prophesied: "If this princess has a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a Universal Monarch. If she has a son, he will become a Universal Monarch. Thus, in either case, her progeny (pajā) will be great." Therefore, they gave her the name "Mahāpajāpatī." In this sutta, however, she is referred to as "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī," combining it with her clan name. "Navaṃ" refers to something new that has not yet been soiled. "Sāmaṃ vāyitaṃ" (woven by herself) does not mean she wove it entirely with her own hands; rather, it refers to a day when, surrounded by a group of nurses, she went to the weavers' workshop, took hold of the end of the shuttle, and made the gesture of weaving. It is said in reference to that.

At what time did the thought of offering a pair of cloths to the Blessed One arise in Gotamī? It was when He first returned to Kapilavatthu after attaining Buddhahood. At that time, King Suddhodana invited the Blessed One, who had entered for alms, into his palace. Then, seeing the beauty of the Blessed One's physical form, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī thought, "How beautiful is my son's physical form!" and a powerful joy arose in her. Then she thought, "While my son lived at home for twenty-nine years, I never gave him even so much as a banana; now I will give him a set of robes." She further thought, "Although there are many costly cloths in this palace, they do not satisfy me. Only what is made by my own hands will satisfy me. Therefore, I will make it with my own hands and offer it."
220:
After thinking thus, she had cotton brought from the market, and by her own hands, she performed the tasks of ginning and carding, and then spun fine thread. She had a weaving shed built within the palace grounds, summoned weavers, and had them weave the cloth, providing them with the same fine food and snacks that she herself consumed. From time to time, surrounded by a group of nurses, she would go and hold the end of the loom to assist. When the weaving was finished, she gave great rewards to the weavers, placed the pair of cloths in a perfumed casket to let the fragrance permeate, and thinking, "I will take these robes for my son (Prince Siddhattha)," she informed King Suddhodana. The King had the road to the Nigrodhārāma monastery prepared. He ordered the streets to be swept, water-pots to be placed, and banners and flags to be raised, arranging the path from the royal palace to the Nigrodhārāma and sprinkling it with flowers. Mahāpajāpatī, adorned with all her ornaments and surrounded by nurses, carried the casket on her head, went to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, this is a new pair of cloths of mine," and so forth.

"Dutiyaṃ pi kho" (For a second time) means—when the Buddha said, "Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha," she invited and pleaded, saying, "Venerable Sir, I am able to give robes to a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand monks from the cloth storehouse. However, this cloth was spun and woven by my own hands specifically for the Blessed One. Therefore, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One please accept it." Although she pleaded in this way up to three times, the Blessed One continued to refuse.

Why did the Blessed One have the robes that were being given to him offered to the Saṅgha? It was out of compassion for his aunt. This thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Because of me, three types of volitions—preliminary volition (pubba-cetanā), actual volition (muñca-cetanā), and subsequent volition (para-cetanā)—have arisen in my aunt. Let these volitions also arise in her because of the Saṅgha. In this way, her six volitions will combine and lead to her welfare and happiness for a long time." However, a Vitaṇḍavādī (sophist) says, "It was said so because giving to the Saṅgha is of great fruit." That person should be asked: "Do you say that giving to the Saṅgha is more fruitful than giving to the Teacher?" If he says, "Yes, I say so," then tell him, "Bring forth a Sutta passage." The Vitaṇḍavādī brings forth the passage: "Gotamī, give it to the Saṅgha; when it is given to the Saṅgha, I will be honored, and the Saṅgha will be honored too." When asked, "Is this the only meaning of this Sutta?" he admits, "Yes, that is all." If that were the case, then according to the statements, "Ānanda, give the cake to the scavengers (vighāsāda)," and "Kaccāna, give the molasses to the scavengers," giving to scavengers would also be especially fruitful. This is also true: the Blessed One often has things given to him bestowed upon others. Therefore, you (the Vitaṇḍavādī) should not hold such a view. Kings and great ministers often have the gifts brought to them given to elephant trainers and others. Are those elephant trainers superior to the kings? Therefore, do not hold such a view. Because it is taught, "In this world or the next, there is no one superior or equal to the Buddha; he has reached the pinnacle of those worthy of offerings and gives great fruit to those desiring merit," there is no individual worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya) superior to the Buddha.
221:
Regarding the statement, 'He causes what is offered to him to be given to others,' kings, great ministers, and the like also cause the gifts brought to them to be given to elephant keepers, cowherds, and so on. Do those elephant keepers and others then become superior to the kings and such? Therefore, do not hold the view [that the recipient is more noble].

'Neither in this world nor in the world beyond,
Does there exist one superior to or equal to the Buddha;
He has reached the pinnacle of those worthy of offerings,
For those seeking merit and searching for vast fruits.'

Because of this teaching, there is no recipient of offerings more excellent or superior to the Teacher. Intending that the six-fold volition of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī would thus become unified and lead to her welfare and happiness for a long time, the Buddha refused her three times and caused her to give it to the Saṅgha.

He also spoke thus to inspire respect for the Saṅgha in future generations. It occurred to the Buddha: 'I will not remain for long, but my Sāsana will be established in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha; let future generations develop respect for the Saṅgha.' Thus, he refused three times and caused her to give it to the Saṅgha. If this is so, future generations will think, 'The Teacher caused even what was offered to himself to be given to the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha is indeed a worthy recipient of offerings.' Having developed respect for the Saṅgha, they will consider it proper to offer the four requisites. The Saṅgha, without being weary for the four requisites, will learn the Word of the Buddha and practice the Dhamma of a recluse. In this way, my Sāsana will endure for five thousand years. From the request, 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept [the offering],' it should also be understood that there is no recipient of offerings superior to the Teacher. Indeed, the Elder Ānanda had no grudge or enmity toward Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. Nor did the Elder wish that her offering should not be of great fruit. The Elder, being wise, learned, and having attained the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) of a trainee (sekha), clearly saw the great fruit of an offering given to the Teacher and thus pleaded for him to accept it, saying, 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept it.'

Furthermore, a Vitandavādī (sophist) says: 'Because of the statement, "If it is given to the Saṅgha, I will be honored and the Saṅgha too," is the Teacher not included within the Saṅgha?' That person should be asked: 'Do you know how many refuges there are, and how many kinds of unshakeable faith (aveccappasāda) there are?' If he knows, he will say 'three.' Then he should be told: 'According to your doctrine, since the Teacher is included in the Saṅgha, there would be only two.' If that were the case, [the passage] 'Monks, I allow the going forth and the higher ordination by these three refuges...' (Mahāvagga, 34).
222:
'I allow the going forth and the higher ordination by these three refuges' (Mahāvagga, 34)—under the Vitandavādī's view, neither this going forth nor this higher ordination would be valid. If that were so, you would be neither a monk nor a layman. Furthermore, while the Fully Enlightened One is residing in the Gandhakuṭī, the monks perform the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and other legal acts of the Saṅgha (Saṅghakamma). If the Teacher were included in the Saṅgha, those acts would be invalid [due to his absence from the assembly], but they are not. Therefore, it should not be said that 'the Teacher is included in the Saṅgha.'

'Āpādikā' means one who makes one grow (a nurturer). It means one who cared for and made your hands and feet grow when they could not yet perform their functions. 'Posikā' means one who reared you by bathing, feeding, and giving you drink two or three times a day.
