## The Explanation of the Chachakka Sutta is finished.
## 7. Explanation of the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta

The Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta begins with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ'. In that sutta, 'Mahāsaḷāyatanika' refers to the discourse (dhamma-pariyāya) that illuminates the six great (highly beneficial) bases (āyatana).

'They do not know' (ajānanti) means not knowing through the Path together with insight (vipassanā). 'They go to accumulation' (upacayaṃ gacchanti) means they reach growth, meaning they reach mastery (vasībhāva). 'Bodily' (kāyikā) refers to the distress (daratha) occurring in the five doors. 'Mental' (cetasikā) refers to the distress occurring in the mind door. The same method applies to terms such as 'fever' (santāpa).

'Bodily happiness' (kāyasukkhaṃ) refers to the happiness occurring in the five doors. 'Mental happiness' (cetosukkhaṃ) refers to the happiness occurring in the mind door. Here, there is no entering into (samāpatti) or emerging from (vuṭṭhāna) [attainment] by way of the five-door impulsion (javana); it is merely what has arisen. Everything occurs by way of the mind door. The powerful insight that is the condition for emerging from the Path also occurs only by way of the mind door.
248:
"Tathābhūtassa" refers to a person endowed with mental happiness associated with wholesome consciousness together with insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). "Pubbeva kho panassa" means that the right speech, right action, and right livelihood of that monk are purified from the very beginning, known as "purified beforehand" (pubbasuddhika). The five factors known as right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are called "factors that accomplish the task of constructing the entire path" (sabbattha-kakārāpakāṅga). Thus, the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga) consists of either eight factors or seven factors.

A sophist (vitanḍavādī), however, taking only this portion of the sutta, "yā yathābhūtassa diṭṭhi," says, "The supramundane path has only five factors." He should be refuted by this very subsequent statement: "Thus, this Noble Eightfold Path goes to the fulfillment of cultivation (bhāvanā-pāripūri)." Furthermore, he should be made to understand: "There is no such thing as a five-factored path; rather, these five basic factors fulfill [the path] at the moment of the path (magga-khaṇa) by way of abstinence (virati)." For among the abstinences described as "abstaining and refraining from the four types of verbal misconduct," one who is endowed with the Noble Path abandons wrong speech and cultivates right speech. For one thus cultivating right speech, these five factors are not fulfilled without abstinence, but are fulfilled only together with abstinence. The same method applies to right action and right livelihood. Thus, verbal actions and so on must be pure from the beginning. Since these five basic factors are fulfilled by way of abstinence, there is no such thing as a five-factored path. This was also stated in the Subhadda Sutta: "Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma-Vinaya the Noble Eightfold Path is found..." And in many hundreds of other suttas, only the eightfold path is mentioned.

The four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) also refer to the four foundations of mindfulness associated with the path. The same method applies to the right efforts (sammappadhāna) and so on. "Yuganandhā" (yoked together) refers to the yoking of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) occurring in a single moment of the path. Although these states may occur at different moments—attainment at one time and insight at another—in the Noble Path, they occur together in a single moment.

"Knowledge and liberation" (vijjā ca vimutti ca) refers to the wisdom associated with the path of Arahantship and the fruition of Arahantship. The rest of the terms are clear in all places.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta is concluded.
249:
## 8. Nagaravindeyya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Nagaravindeyya Sutta. Therein, "samavisamaṃ caranti" means practicing evenly at times and practicing unevenly at times. "Samacariyampi hetaṃ" should be analyzed as "samacariyaṃ pi hi etaṃ."

"Ke ākārā" means what reasons? "Ke anvayā" means what kind of following knowledges (insights)? Why is it said "natthi kho pana tattha" (there is nothing there)? Is it not true that in the forest there are the five cords of sensual pleasure, such as very delightful forms consisting of grass, trees, jasmine groves, and so on? There are; however, this is not said with reference to the forest thicket, but with reference to the forms of women and so on. For those forms of women remain captivating the mind of a man. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, I do not see even one other form that remains captivating the mind of a man as does this form of a woman. The form of a woman, monks, remains captivating the mind of a man." This should be understood in detail. The rest of the words are clear in all places.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Nagaravindeyya Sutta is concluded.

## 9. Piṇḍapātapiārisuddhi Sutta Vaṇṇanā
This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Piṇḍapātapiārisuddhi Sutta. Therein, "paṭisallānā" means due to the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).

"Vippasannāni" is spoken by way of opportunity. For one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition, the place where the five sensitive materialities (pasāda-rūpa) reside is clear, and the complexion is pure. Therefore, it is said thus. "Suññatavihārena" means dwelling by way of the attainment of the fruition of emptiness. "Mahāpurisavihāro" means the dwelling of Great Beings, namely, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the Great Disciples of the Tathāgata. In the passages beginning with "yena cāhaṃ maggena," the journey from the monastery up to the village gate-post (indakhīla) is called the "path entered" (paviṭṭhamagga). The area from entering the village, wandering from house to house, until exiting through the city gate is called the "area to be wandered" (caritabbapadesa). The journey from the outside of the gate-post back to the monastery is called the "path returned" (paṭikkantamagga). "Paṭighaṃ vāpi cetaso" means reflecting whether there is even a slight impingement (paṭigha) in the mind.

"Anုsikkhantena bhikkhunā" refers to a monk who practices constantly by day and by night. In the passages beginning with "pañca kāmaguṇe pahīname," the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. The reflection of a single monk and the reflection of various monks are each distinct. How? A certain monk...
250:
One should reflect whether there is even a slight amount of the collection of defilements that cause impingement in the mind. "Ahorattānusikkhinā" means a monk who practices continuously by day and by night.

In the passages beginning with "Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?", the reflection of a single monk is of various kinds, and the reflections of various monks are also of various kinds. How is this? A certain monk, after his meal, having returned from his alms round and put away his bowl and robes, sits in a secluded place and reflects: "Have the five strands of sensual pleasure been abandoned by me?" Knowing that "they are not yet abandoned," he arouses energy and, having completely eradicated the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure through the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmimagga), he attains the Fruit (phala) immediately after the Path, and the Path immediately after the Fruit. When he reflects upon emerging from that state, he knows distinctly: "They have been abandoned." The same method applies to the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth. The abandonment of these hindrances and so forth occurs through the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga). In this way, there are various reflections for a single monk. Among these reflections, one monk reflects on one kind of reflection, and another monk reflects on another. In this way, there are various reflections for various monks. All the remaining words are clear.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta is finished.
## 10. Explanation of the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta. Therein, "Gajaṅgalāyaṃ" means in the market town of that name. "Suveḷuvane" means he was staying in a great forest grove covered with the species of trees called Suveḷu. "He does not see a form with the eye, he does not hear a sound with the ear" means that (the young man Uttara) speaks with the intention that one should not look at a form with the eye, and one should not listen to a sound with the ear.

By the words "It is otherwise in the Discipline of the Noble One," the Blessed One provided the opportunity to teach the incomparable development of the faculties in his own Dispensation. Then, the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, "The Teacher has shown the opportunity; let me now cause the Teacher to give a talk on the development of the faculties to the Saṅgha of monks in this assembly," and wishing to request the Blessed One...
251:
The Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Bhagavā." Then, the Blessed One, wishing to teach the development of the faculties to the Venerable Ānanda, spoke the words beginning with "Tena hānananda."

In that teaching, "upekkhā" refers to that which is called insight-equanimity (vipassanūpekkhā); it means that this insight-equanimity is peaceful, sublime, and untainted (by craving and views). Thus, this monk, regarding the forms at the eye-door—a pleasant mind towards a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa), an unpleasant mind towards an undesirable object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa), and a mind that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant towards a neutral object (majjhattārammaṇa)—without allowing lust, hatred, or delusion to arise towards those respective objects, defines them with wisdom and maintains insight in equanimity. "Cakkhumā" means one who has perfect eyes, one with pure vision. For a person with an eye disease, the opening and closing of the eyes cannot occur upwards; therefore, such a person is not taken here.

"Īsakaṃpoṇe" refers to that which stands raised like the pole of a chariot.

In the phrases beginning with "paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī" (perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive), one dwells with the perception of non-repulsiveness in a repulsive object either by the radiation of loving-kindness (mettā) or by attending to it as elements (dhātu). One dwells with the perception of repulsiveness in a non-repulsive object either by the radiation of foulness (asubha) or by attending to it as impermanent (anicca). The same method should be understood for the remaining terms. "Avoiding both of those" means: what does one who wishes to dwell as one who is equanimous do? When desirable and undesirable objects come into range, he is neither joyful nor dejected. This matter is taught (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga) as follows:

"How does one dwell perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive? He radiates with loving-kindness towards an undesirable object, or he attends to it as elements; thus he dwells perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive. How does one dwell perceiving the non-repulsive as repulsive? He radiates with foulness towards a desirable object, or he attends to it as impermanent; thus he dwells perceiving the non-repulsive as repulsive. How does one dwell perceiving both the repulsive and the non-repulsive as non-repulsive? He radiates with loving-kindness towards both undesirable and desirable objects, or he attends to them as elements. Thus he dwells perceiving both the repulsive and the non-repulsive as non-repulsive. How does one dwell perceiving both the non-repulsive and the repulsive as repulsive? He radiates with foulness towards both desirable and undesirable objects, or he attends to them as impermanent; thus he dwells perceiving both the non-repulsive and the repulsive as repulsive. How, regarding both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, avoiding both of those..."
252:
He dwells. How does he dwell with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, having avoided both the repulsive and the non-repulsive objects? Here, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad, but dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. ... Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad, but dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. Thus, he dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, having avoided both the repulsive and the non-repulsive objects (so He said).

Among these three methods, in the first method, the state of defilement (saṃkilesa) called agreeable, disagreeable, or both agreeable and disagreeable is appropriate; the state of non-defilement is also appropriate. In the second method, the state of defilement is appropriate. In the third method, both the state of defilement and the state of non-defilement are appropriate. Furthermore, it was said: "The first method is appropriate for the state of defilement; the second method is appropriate for both the state of defilement and the state of non-defilement; the third method is appropriate only for the state of non-defilement." The remaining words are clear in all respects.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Fifth Vagga is finished.
## The Uparipaṇṇāsa Commentary is finished.

This Majjhima Nikāya, which is good in the beginning because it starts with "Monks, I will teach you the root of all things," good in the middle because of the teaching of "Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla," and good in the end because of the statement "The Noble One is one who has developed the faculties," is thus good in three ways and is called "Mahā-vipassanā." This Majjhima Nikāya is now complete in terms of its commentary.
253:
## Concluding Remarks
By this much sequence of words—

Requested by the Elder Buddhamitta of excellent wisdom, with whom I formerly resided in the city of Mayūradūtapaṭṭana, I endeavored to compose this commentary named Papañcasūdanī, which is an explanation of the noble Majjhima Nikāya that destroys opposing doctrines. This commentary has reached completion by taking the essence of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. The Majjhima Nikāya Pāḷi consists of 107 recitation sections (bhāṇavāra). The Visuddhimagga, composed to explain the meaning of the Agamas, consists of 59 recitation sections. Therefore, together with that Visuddhimagga, this commentary should be known to consist of 166 recitation sections according to the method of counting verses. This commentary, measuring 166 recitation sections, illustrates the tradition of the dwellers of the Mahāvihāra. By the merit of my composing this commentary by taking the essence of the original commentary (Mūla-aṭṭhakathā), may all beings be happy at all times.

Adorned with exceedingly noble and especially pure faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a collection of virtues such as morality, conduct, rectitude, and gentleness; capable of plunging into the thicket of one's own and others' doctrines; possessed of clear and sharp wisdom; having the power of unimpeded knowledge in the Dispensation of the Teacher consisting of the Three Piṭakas together with the commentaries; a great grammarian; possessed of the beauty of sweet and noble speech that flows happily from the perfection of vocal instruments; a speaker of appropriate and liberated words; an eminent proponent of doctrines; a great poet; surrounded by the retinue of analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā); adorned with qualities such as the six direct knowledges (abhiññā); well-established in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma); a lamp of the lineage of elders; an ornament to the lineage of the great elders residing at the Mahāvihāra; possessed of vast and pure wisdom; the Elder who is given the name Buddhaghosa by venerable teachers, has composed this commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī—
254:
May it remain in the world as long as the name 'Buddha' of the Blessed One—who is of pure mind, who is such (tādi), who is the foremost in the world, and who is the Great Seer—remains in the world, showing the way for the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) to the sons of good family who seek liberation from the world.

## The Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya
## Named Papañcasūdanī is finished in every respect.
